## Note
**Electronic filing of amended employment tax returns (p. 3).** An amended Form 940, Form 941-X, Form 943-X or Form 945-X can be filed electronically through Modernized e-File (MeF). For now MeF cannot be used for Form 944-X or Form CT-1 X. The page points to IRS.gov/EmploymentEfile for more on electronic filing.

**Pub. 15 is for all employers (p. 3).** All employers use Pub. 15, agricultural employers and employers in the U.S. territories among them. Pub. 51, Pub. 80 and Pub. 179 have been discontinued. If you prefer a Spanish version of Pub. 15, the page refers to Pub. 15 (sp).

**Form references (p. 3).** Unless otherwise noted, the publication’s references to Form W-2 cover Forms W-2AS, W-2CM, W-2GU and W-2VI and Form 499R-2/W-2PR. References to Form W-2c cover Form 499R-2c/W-2cPR, those to Form W-3 cover Form W-3SS and Form W-3 (PR), and those to Form W-3c cover Form W-3C (PR).

**COVID-19 related credit for qualified sick and family leave wages (pp. 3–4).** This credit applies only to leave taken after March 31, 2020, and before October 1, 2021, and can no longer be claimed on Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944. Generally, two credits have expired. The first, under the Families First Coronavirus Response Act (as amended and extended by the COVID-related Tax Relief Act of 2020), covered leave taken after March 31, 2020, and before April 1, 2021. The second, under sections 3131, 3132 and 3133 of the Internal Revenue Code (enacted under the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021), covered leave taken after March 31, 2021, and before October 1, 2021. Even so, employers that in 2024, 2025 or 2026 pay qualified sick and family leave wages for leave taken after March 31, 2020, and before October 1, 2021, are eligible to claim a credit for those wages in 2024, 2025 or 2026. For tax periods beginning after 2023 the lines for claiming the credit are gone from Form 941, Form 943 and Form 944, because it would be extremely rare for an employer to pay such wages after 2023 for leave taken in that earlier period. An employer eligible because it paid the wages after 2023 for an earlier applicable leave period claims the credit for the wages paid that year by filing Form 941-X, Form 943-X or Form 944-X. Filing one of those before the Form 941 for the quarter, or the Form 943 or Form 944 for the year, may lead to errors or delays in processing it.

**Form 941 (sp), Form 943 (sp) and Form 944 (sp) (p. 4).** Form 941 (sp), Form 943 (sp) and Form 944 (sp) can be filed by anyone who prefers the form and its instructions in Spanish.

**Qualified small business payroll tax credit for increasing research activities (p. 4).** For tax years beginning before 2023, a qualified small business may elect to treat up to $250,000 of its credit for increasing research activities as a payroll tax credit. For tax years beginning after 2022 the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (the IRA) raises that election amount to $500,000. The election must be made on or before the due date of the originally filed income tax return (including extensions). The part of the credit used against payroll taxes is allowed in the first calendar quarter that begins after the qualified small business filed its income tax return. Form 6765 is where the election and the determination of the credit amount to use against the employer’s payroll taxes are made, and that amount must then be reported on Form 8974. From the first quarter of 2023, the credit first reduces the employer share of social security tax, by up to $250,000 per quarter. Any credit remaining then reduces the employer share of Medicare tax for the quarter, and whatever is left after both reductions carries forward to the next quarter. Form 8974 determines how much of the credit can be used in the current quarter, and its line 12 amount (or, if applicable, its line 17 amount) is reported on Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944. The page points to IRS.gov/ResearchPayrollTC, and to the line 16 instructions in the Instructions for Form 941 (line 17 instructions in those for Form 943, line 13 instructions in those for Form 944) on reducing your record of tax liability for this credit.

**Disaster tax relief (p. 4).** Relief is available for those affected by disasters, and the page points to IRS.gov/DisasterTaxRelief.

**2026 withholding tables (p. 4).** Pub. 15-T, available at IRS.gov/Pub15T, holds the Percentage Method and Wage Bracket Method withholding tables, the employer instructions on figuring employee withholding, and the amount to add to a nonresident alien employee’s wages when figuring federal income tax withholding.

**Certification program for professional employer organizations (PEOs) (p. 4).** The Stephen Beck, Jr., Achieving a Better Life Experience (ABLE) Act of 2014 required the IRS to set up a voluntary certification program for PEOs. PEOs take on various payroll administration and tax reporting duties for business clients, and are typically paid a fee based on payroll costs. To become and remain certified, a certified professional employer organization (CPEO) must meet various requirements, which sections 3511 and 7705 and related published guidance describe. A CPEO’s certification may affect the employment tax liabilities of the CPEO and of its customers. For employment tax purposes a CPEO is generally treated as the employer of any individual who performs services for a customer of the CPEO under a contract between the CPEO and the customer that is described in section 7705(e)(2) (a CPEO contract). That treatment reaches only the wages and other compensation the CPEO itself pays the individual. An organization must apply through the IRS Online Registration System to become a CPEO; the page points to IRS.gov/CPEO and to Revenue Procedure 2023-18, 2023-13 I.R.B. 605.

**Outsourcing payroll duties (p. 4).** As an employer you are generally responsible for seeing that returns are filed and deposits and payments are made, even when you contract with a third party to do these things, and you stay responsible if the third party fails to perform a required action. Before you outsource payroll and related tax duties to a third-party payer (a payroll service provider or reporting agent, for instance), meaning withholding, reporting and paying over social security, Medicare, FUTA and federal income taxes, the page points to IRS.gov/OutsourcingPayrollDuties for helpful information. Where a CPEO pays wages and other compensation to an individual who performs services for you under a CPEO contract, the CPEO is generally treated as the employer, but only for what the CPEO pays that individual. For certain employees covered by a CPEO contract, though, you may also be treated as their employer and may therefore be liable for federal employment taxes on the wages and other compensation the CPEO pays them. The page refers to section 16 for the different types of third-party payer arrangements.

**Aggregate Form 941 or Form 943 filers (pp. 4–5).** Approved section 3504 agents and CPEOs filing an aggregate Form 941 or Form 943 must complete the applicable Schedule R: Schedule R (Form 941), Allocation Schedule for Aggregate Form 941 Filers, or Schedule R (Form 943), Allocation Schedule for Aggregate Form 943 Filers. The page names these filers of an aggregate quarterly Form 941 or annual Form 943:
- An agent the IRS has approved under section 3504 of the Internal Revenue Code. An agent seeking approval to act for an employer files Form 2678 with the IRS, unless you are a state or local government agency acting as an agent under the special procedures in Revenue Procedure 2013-39, 2013-52 I.R.B. 830.
- Also a CPEO approved by the IRS under section 7705; an organization applies through the IRS Online Registration System at IRS.gov/CPEO to become one. CPEOs file Form 8973 to tell the IRS that they have started or ended a service contract with a client or customer. A CPEO must generally file Form 941 or Form 943, and the applicable Schedule R, electronically, and for that requirement the page refers to Revenue Procedure 2023-18.

Another third-party payer that files an aggregate quarterly Form 941 or annual Form 943, such as a non-certified PEO, must complete and file the applicable Schedule R if its clients are claiming any employment tax credit; the qualified small business payroll tax credit for increasing research activities is one example.

**Aggregate Form 940 filers (p. 5).** For an aggregate Form 940, approved section 3504 agents and CPEOs must complete Schedule R (Form 940), Allocation Schedule for Aggregate Form 940 Filers. Agents acting for recipients of home care services provided through a program run by a federal, state or local government can file aggregate Forms 940. To request approval to act as such an agent, the agent files Form 2678 with the IRS, unless you are a state or local government agency acting under the special procedures in Revenue Procedure 2013-39. CPEOs approved by the IRS under section 7705 file aggregate Forms 940 as well, and file Form 8973 to notify the IRS that a service contract with a client or customer has started or ended. They must generally file Form 940 and Schedule R (Form 940) electronically, and the page refers to Revenue Procedure 2023-18 for that requirement.

**Work opportunity tax credit for qualified tax-exempt organizations hiring qualified veterans (p. 5).** A qualified tax-exempt organization that hires eligible unemployed veterans may be able to claim the work opportunity tax credit against its payroll tax liability, using Form 5884-C. The page points to IRS.gov/WOTC.

**Medicaid waiver payments (p. 5).** Under Notice 2014-7, certain Medicaid waiver payments are excludable from income for federal income tax purposes. The page points to Notice 2014-7, 2014-4 I.R.B. 445, and to IRS.gov/MedicaidWaiverPayments for more, including questions and answers.

**Disability payments for injuries from a terrorist attack (p. 5).** A disability payment for injuries incurred as a direct result of a terrorist attack directed against the United States (or its allies) is not included in income. Federal income tax withholding is only required when a payment is includible in income, so none should be withheld from these payments. The page refers to Pub. 907 and Pub. 3920.

**Voluntary withholding on dividends and other distributions by an Alaska Native Corporation (ANC) (p. 5).** A shareholder of an ANC may ask the ANC for voluntary federal income tax withholding on the dividends and other distributions it pays, by giving it a completed Form W-4V. The page refers to Notice 2013-77, 2013-50 I.R.B. 632.

**Definition of marriage (p. 5).** For federal tax purposes:
- a marriage is recognized if the state or territory of the United States where it was entered into recognizes it, regardless of legal residence;
- a relationship that is a marriage under the laws of a foreign jurisdiction or an American Indian tribe is recognized as one if at least one state or territory of the United States would recognize it as a marriage, regardless of legal residence;
- individuals in a registered domestic partnership, civil union or similar relationship that the law of the state or territory where it was entered into does not call a marriage are not lawfully married, regardless of legal residence.

**Differential wage payments (p. 5).** Qualified differential wage payments made by employers to individuals serving in the U.S. Armed Forces carry federal income tax withholding, but not social security, Medicare or FUTA tax. The page refers to section 5.

**Severance payments (p. 5).** Severance payments are wages, so social security and Medicare taxes, federal income tax withholding and FUTA tax apply to them.

**You must receive written notice from the IRS to file Form 944 (p. 5).** An employer that has been filing quarterly Forms 941, believes its employment taxes for the calendar year will be $1,000 or less and would like to file an annual Form 944 instead must contact the IRS during the first calendar quarter of the tax year to ask for it. Written notice from the IRS to file Form 944 in place of quarterly Forms 941 is required before you may file Form 944. The page refers to the Instructions for Form 944 for the methods and deadlines for making a request.

**Employers can request to file quarterly Forms 941 instead of an annual Form 944 (p. 5).** An employer that has received IRS notice to file Form 944 but prefers quarterly Forms 941 must contact the IRS during the first calendar quarter of the tax year to ask for that. Written notice from the IRS to file quarterly Forms 941 in place of Form 944 is required before the employer may file them. The page refers to the Instructions for Form 944 for the methods and deadlines for making a request.

**Correcting Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 (p. 5).** An error found on a previously filed Form 941 is corrected with Form 941-X, one on Form 943 with Form 943-X, and one on Form 944 with Form 944-X. These X forms are filed separately from the original forms, and employers use them, rather than Form 843, to claim refunds or abatements of employment taxes. The page refers to section 13.

**Zero wage return (p. 6).** Where you have not filed a “final” Form 940 and a “final” Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944, or you are not a “seasonal” employer (Form 941 only), you must continue filing Form 940 and Forms 941, Form 943 or Form 944, even for periods in which you paid no wages. The IRS encourages electronic filing of these “zero wage” returns, and the page points to IRS.gov/EmploymentEfile.

**Federal tax deposits must be made by electronic funds transfer (EFT) (p. 6).**
- All federal tax deposits must be made by EFT. An EFT can be made using the Electronic Federal Tax Payment System (EFTPS), IRS Direct Pay or your IRS business tax account.
- If you prefer not to use one of those methods, a tax professional, financial institution, payroll service or other trusted third party can be arranged to make electronic deposits on your behalf. Your financial institution can also be arranged to initiate a same-day wire payment on your behalf.
- EFTPS is a free service of the Department of the Treasury, and payments through IRS Direct Pay or your IRS business tax account are free too. A tax professional, financial institution, payroll service or other third party may charge a fee.
- The page refers to How To Deposit in section 11 for more on making federal tax deposits, to IRS.gov/DirectPay for IRS Direct Pay, and to IRS.gov/BusinessAccount for a payment through your IRS business tax account. For more on EFTPS or to enroll, it gives EFTPS.gov and the numbers 800-555-4477, 800-244-4829 (Spanish) and 303-967-5916 (toll call). A person who is deaf, hard of hearing or has a speech disability can reach EFTPS through Telecommunications Relay Services (TRS) by dialing 711 and then giving the TRS assistant the number 800-555-4477 or 800-733-4829. Pub. 966 has additional information about EFTPS.

**Residents of the Philippines working in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) (p. 6).** Employers must withhold and pay social security and Medicare taxes on wages and other compensation paid for services as employees in the CNMI to residents of the Philippines who do not hold an H-2 status, unless those workers qualify for exemption from the taxes under an exception listed in section 15. The page refers to Announcement 2012-43, 2012-51 I.R.B. 723.

**Federal employers in the CNMI (p. 6).** In December 2006 the U.S. Treasury Department and the CNMI Division of Revenue and Taxation made an agreement under 5 U.S.C. section 5517. Under it, all federal employers (the Department of Defense included) must withhold CNMI income taxes instead of federal income taxes, and deposit them with the CNMI Treasury. This applies to employees who are subject to CNMI taxes and have their regular place of federal employment in the CNMI. The page points to IRS.gov/5517Agreements for more, including details on completing Form W-2. Federal employers must also file quarterly and annual reports with the CNMI Division of Revenue and Taxation, and questions go to that division.

**Pub. 5146 explains employment tax examinations and appeal rights (p. 6).** Pub. 5146 tells employers how the IRS picks employment tax returns for examination, what happens in an exam, and what options an employer has in responding to its results, including how to appeal. It also covers worker classification issues and tip exams.

**Related:** 5. Wages and Other Compensation — the pay that counts as wages subject to federal employment taxes, in cash or in other forms (p. 18)

## Note
**Getting forms (p. 10).** Most of the forms, instructions and publications you may need can be viewed, downloaded or printed at IRS.gov/Forms. Otherwise, IRS.gov/OrderForms can be used to place an order and have them mailed to you. The IRS will process an order as soon as possible, and requests already sent should not be resubmitted. Forms, instructions and publications can be had faster online.

**Filing Forms W-2 and W-3 electronically (p. 10).** In place of ordering paper Forms W-2 and W-3, the page suggests considering the SSA’s free e-file service. To learn more about BSO, it points to the SSA’s Employer W-2 Filing Instructions & Information webpage at SSA.gov/employer. Forms W-2 can be created online and submitted to the SSA by typing wage information into fill-in fields. Completed copies of Forms W-2 can also be printed for filing with state or local governments, for giving to employees and for your records. Form W-3 is created for you from your Forms W-2.

**Puerto Rico (p. 10).** The SSA’s BSO is independent of the Government of Puerto Rico’s electronic filing system. Puerto Rico employers must go to Hacienda.pr.gov for additional information.

**Related:** Electronic Filing and Payment — filing and paying federal taxes electronically, including electronic filing of Forms W-2 with the SSA (p. 6)

text:
## Note
**Reporting cash tips (p. 22).** Withholding generally applies to cash tips an employee gets from customers. The employee must report them to you by the 10th of the month following the month in which they were received. Tips paid by cash, check, debit card or credit card all count as cash tips. A report should cover tips you paid over to the employee for charge customers, tips received directly from customers, and tips received from other employees under a tip-sharing arrangement. Directly and indirectly tipped employees alike must report tips to you. For a month in which tips total less than $20, no report is required.

**The employee's statement (p. 22).** When you give your employees no specific reporting method (an electronic tip reporting system is the page's example), they must give you a statement of their tips, signed and dated by the employee. The statement has to contain:
- The employee's name, address and SSN.
- Your name and address.
- The month and year covered (or the beginning and ending dates, if the statement covers less than 1 calendar month).
- The total of tips received during that month or period.

You are permitted to set up a system for employees to report tips electronically; the page refers to Regulations section 31.6053-1(d). You may also suggest that employees see Pub. 531, Reporting Tip Income.

**Collecting taxes on tips (pp. 22–23).** Three taxes must be collected on an employee's tips: federal income tax (the page refers to Federal income tax withholding on tips, later), employee social security tax and employee Medicare tax. The rules for withholding the employee's share of Medicare tax on tips apply equally to the Additional Medicare Tax once wages and tips go above $200,000 in the calendar year. These taxes can come out of the employee's wages (not counting tips) or out of other funds the employee makes available; the page refers to Tips are treated as supplemental wages in section 7. The employee share of social security tax stops being collected when wages and tips for tax year 2026 reach $184,500, whereas income tax and employee Medicare tax are collected for the whole year on all wages and tips. Your own responsibility is the employer social security tax on wages and tips until they (tips included) reach the limit, and the employer Medicare tax on all wages and tips for the whole year. Tips count as paid when the employee reports them to you. Deposit taxes on tips according to your deposit schedule, as described in section 11 (pp. 22–23). Form 941 or Form 944 is the form for reporting withholding and employment taxes on tips (p. 23).

**Ordering rule (p. 23).** Suppose that by the 10th of the month after the month covered by an employee's tip report you lack enough employee funds to deduct the employee tax: you then no longer have to collect it. Where funds fall short, taxes are withheld in this sequence:
1. Regular wages and other compensation.
2. Social security and Medicare taxes on tips.
3. Income tax on tips.

**Federal income tax withholding on tips (p. 23).** P.L. 119-21 lets employees and self-employed individuals deduct on their income tax returns up to $25,000 of qualified tips, for tax years beginning after 2024 and ending before 2029. The tips must have been received in occupations that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024. Qualified tips are cash tips; these include voluntary cash or charged tips from customers and, for employees, tips received through tip-sharing arrangements. Mandatory service charges added to the bill are not qualified tips. Where an employee submits an updated Form W-4, employers must use it, along with the federal income tax withholding procedures in Pub. 15-T, so that the employee can account for the expected deduction and get more money in each paycheck instead of waiting for the full benefit until the income tax return is filed.

**Reporting tips on forms (p. 23).** Tips and any collected and uncollected social security and Medicare taxes go on Form W-2 (Form 499R-2/W-2PR for employers in Puerto Rico) and on Form 941, lines 5b and 5c and, if applicable, 5d (Form 944, lines 4b and 4c and, if applicable, 4d). A negative adjustment for the uncollected social security and Medicare taxes goes on Form 941, line 9 (Form 944, line 6). In box 12 of Form W-2 the uncollected social security tax is entered with code "A" and the uncollected Medicare tax with code "B." On Form 499R-2/W-2PR they go in boxes 25 and 26 respectively. Any uncollected Additional Medicare Tax stays out of box 12 of Form W-2. For more on reporting tips the page refers to section 13 and to the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3; employers in Puerto Rico are referred to the General Instructions for Forms W-3 (PR) and W-3C (PR). Revenue Ruling 2012-18 gives employers guidance on social security and Medicare taxes imposed on tips, including reporting the employer share of these taxes under section 3121(q), the difference between tips and service charges, and the section 45B credit.

**FUTA tax on tips (p. 23).** FUTA tax also applies to tips when an employee reports $20 or more of them to you in writing in a month.

**Allocated tips (p. 23).** An operator of a large food or beverage establishment must report allocated tips in certain circumstances, but must not withhold income, social security or Medicare tax on them. The page defines a large food or beverage establishment as one in the 50 states or the District of Columbia that serves food or beverages for consumption on the premises, where tipping is customary, and that normally had more than 10 employees on a typical business day during the preceding year. Allocation may follow one of three methods: hours worked, gross receipts or good-faith agreement. For these methods, and for required electronic filing of Form 8027, the page refers to the Instructions for Form 8027; for filing Form 8027 electronically with the IRS it refers to Pub. 1239.

**Tip Rate Determination and Education Program (p. 23).** Employers may take part in this program, which is built mainly on two voluntary agreements meant to improve tip income reporting by helping taxpayers understand and meet their reporting responsibilities. They are the Tip Rate Determination Agreement (TRDA) and the Tip Reporting Alternative Commitment (TRAC). For the gaming (casino) industry there is a separate tip agreement, the Gaming Industry Tip Compliance Agreement (GITCA). The page refers to Pub. 3144 for more information.

**More information (p. 23).** The page advises telling employees to see Pub. 531, or to use the IRS Interactive Tax Assistant at IRS.gov/TipIncome, to find out whether their tip income is taxable and how to report it.

**Related:** 7. Supplemental Wages — wage payments to an employee that are not regular wages, and the kinds of payment they include (p. 23)

source.title: Publication 15 (Circular E), Employer’s Tax Guide

text:
## Note
**Caution (p. 23).** Employers in American Samoa, Guam, the CNMI, the USVI and Puerto Rico can disregard the references to federal income tax withholding, unless they have employees who are subject to U.S. income tax withholding. Such employers should contact their local tax department for information about income tax withholding.

**What supplemental wages are (p. 23).** Supplemental wages are wage payments to an employee that aren't regular wages. The list is not limited to these: bonuses, commissions, overtime pay (the page refers to Overtime compensation in section 5), payments for accumulated sick leave, severance pay, awards, prizes, back pay, reported tips (the page refers to Federal income tax withholding on tips in section 6), retroactive pay increases and payments for nondeductible moving expenses. Employers may choose to treat overtime pay and tips as regular wages rather than as supplemental wages. Taxable fringe benefits, and expense allowances paid under a nonaccountable plan, are other payments that fall under the supplemental wage rules. The way you withhold depends on whether the supplemental payment is identified as separate from regular wages. The page refers to Regulations section 31.3402(g)-1 for additional guidance and to Revenue Ruling 2008-29 (pp. 23–24).

**Over $1 million of supplemental wages in a calendar year (p. 24).** Special rules come into play to the extent that supplemental wages paid to any one employee during the calendar year exceed $1 million. When a supplemental wage payment, added to the employee's other supplemental wage payments for the calendar year, brings the total above $1 million, the excess is subject to withholding at 37% (or the highest rate of income tax for the year). That 37% rate is used regardless of the employee's Form W-4. Payments from all businesses under common control are counted when determining the supplemental wages paid to the employee in the year. The page refers to Treasury Decision 9276.

**Up to $1 million of supplemental wages in a calendar year (p. 24).** Where an employee's supplemental wages for the calendar year are $1 million or less, these rules decide the income tax to withhold:
- *Supplemental wages combined with regular wages.* If supplemental and regular wages are paid together without the amount of each being specified, withhold federal income tax as though the total were one payment for a regular payroll period.
- *Supplemental wages identified separately from regular wages.* Where supplemental wages are paid separately (or combined in one payment with the amount of each specified), the withholding method depends partly on whether you withhold income tax from the employee's regular wages.

If you withheld income tax from the employee's regular wages in the current or immediately preceding calendar year, you can choose between two methods for the supplemental wages:
1. Method 1a: a flat 22% (no other percentage is allowed).
2. Method 1b: when the supplemental wages are paid concurrently with regular wages, combine the two and withhold federal income tax as though the total were one payment for a regular payroll period. When no regular wages are paid concurrently, add the supplemental wages to either the regular wages paid or to be paid for the current payroll period, or the regular wages paid for the preceding payroll period, and figure the income tax withholding on that total as one payment. Subtract the tax already withheld or to be withheld from the regular wages, and withhold the remainder from the supplemental wages. If supplemental wages were paid earlier in the same payroll period, aggregate all supplemental payments for the period with the period's regular wages, figure the tax on the total, subtract the tax already withheld from the regular wages and from the earlier supplemental payments, and withhold what is left.

If you did not withhold income tax from the employee's regular wages in the current or immediately preceding calendar year, method 1b is the one to use. Whichever method is used for income tax withholding, supplemental wages are subject to social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes.

**Examples (pp. 24–25).**
- Example 1: John Peters gets a base salary on the first of each month. His most recent Form W-4 dates from 2018; he is single, claims one withholding allowance and entered no amount for additional withholding. For January he is paid $1,000 and, with the Wage Bracket Method, Worksheet 3 and the withholding tables in section 3 of Pub. 15-T, $2 is withheld. For February he receives his $1,000 salary plus a $500 commission that is combined with regular wages and not separately identified, so withholding is figured on the $1,500 total; the tables give $53 (p. 24).
- Example 2: Sharon Warren gets a base salary on the first of each month. She submitted a 2026 Form W-4 with the Single or Married filing separately box checked and Steps 2, 3 and 4 left incomplete. Her May 1 pay is $2,000; using the Wage Bracket Method, Worksheet 2 and the withholding tables in section 2 of Pub. 15-T, $65 is withheld. On May 15 she receives a $1,000 bonus, and the employer elects method 1b: add the bonus to the wages of the most recent base salary pay date, May 1 ($2,000 + $1,000 = $3,000); the wage bracket tables give $179 of withholding on that $3,000; subtract the $65 withheld on May 1 ($179 – $65 = $114); withhold $114 from the bonus (p. 24).
- Example 3: With the facts of Example 2 but the flat rate method elected for the bonus, 22% of $1,000, or $220, is withheld from the bonus (p. 24).
- Example 4: With the facts of Example 2 plus a second bonus of $2,000 on May 29, and method 1b used, the first and second bonuses are added to the wages of the most recent base salary pay date, May 1 ($2,000 + $1,000 + $2,000 = $5,000); the wage bracket tables give $419 of withholding on that $5,000; the amounts withheld on May 1 and from the first bonus are subtracted ($419 – $65 – $114 = $240); and $240 is withheld from the second bonus (pp. 24–25).

**Tips are treated as supplemental wages (p. 25).** Income tax on tips is withheld from wages the employee earns or from other funds the employee makes available (the page refers to Federal income tax withholding on tips in section 6), and not from the employee's tips. When an employee gets regular wages and reports tips, income tax withholding is figured as if the tips were supplemental wages. If income tax was withheld from the regular wages in the current or immediately preceding calendar year, you can use method 1a or 1b, covered earlier in the section under Supplemental wages identified separately from regular wages. If it was not, add the tips to the regular wages and withhold income tax on the total by method 1b. Treating tips as regular wages instead is an option employers have. Service charges aren't tips, so taxes on them are withheld as for regular wages.

**Vacation pay (p. 25).** Withholding applies to vacation pay as though it were a regular wage payment. Vacation pay that comes on top of regular wages for the vacation period (an annual lump-sum payment for unused vacation leave, for example) is treated as a supplemental wage payment. Vacation pay covering a time longer than the usual payroll period is spread over the pay periods for which it is paid.

**Related:** 5. Wages and Other Compensation — the pay that counts as wages subject to federal employment taxes, in cash or in other forms (p. 18)

text:
## Note
**Child employed by parents (p. 16).** Payments for a child's services are not subject to social security and Medicare taxes when the child is under age 18, works for their parent in a trade or business, and the business is a sole proprietorship or a partnership whose partners are all parents of the child. If the work is not in a trade or business (domestic work in the parent's private home is the page's example), the payments escape social security and Medicare taxes until the child reaches age 21. The page refers to Covered services of a child or spouse, later. For a child under age 21 working for their parent, in a trade or business or not, the payments are not subject to FUTA tax. Income tax withholding generally applies to payments for a child of any age working for their parent. The exceptions are domestic work in the parent's home, and work outside a trade or business that either pays less than $50 in the quarter or is work the child is not regularly employed to do.

**One spouse employed by another (p. 16).** Wages for an individual's services to their spouse in a trade or business are subject to income tax withholding and to social security and Medicare taxes, but not to FUTA tax. Payments for one spouse's services to the other outside a trade or business, such as domestic service in a private home, are not subject to social security, Medicare or FUTA taxes.

**Covered services of a child or spouse (p. 16).** Income tax withholding, social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes all apply to the wages for a child's or spouse's services when they work for any of these:
- A corporation, even one controlled by the child's parent or the individual's spouse.
- A partnership, even if the child's parent is a partner, unless every partner is a parent of the child.
- A partnership, even if the individual's spouse is a partner.
- An estate, even the estate of a deceased parent.

In these situations the child or spouse is considered to work for the corporation, partnership or estate, not for you.

**Parent employed by their child (p. 16).** The rules apply when the employer is a child who employs their parent:
- Payments for a parent's services in the child's (the employer's) trade or business are subject to income tax withholding and to social security and Medicare taxes.
- A parent's services outside the child's (the employer's) trade or business: payments are generally not subject to social security and Medicare taxes.

**Domestic services subject to social security and Medicare taxes (p. 16).** These taxes do apply to payments to a parent for domestic services when every one of the following holds:
- The employer is the parent's child.
- A child or stepchild of the employer (an adopted child included) lives in the home.
- The employer is a surviving spouse, or is divorced and not remarried, or lives with a spouse whose mental or physical condition prevents caring for the child or stepchild for at least 4 continuous weeks in the calendar quarter of the service.
- The employer's child or stepchild is under age 18, or needs an adult's personal care for at least 4 continuous weeks in the calendar quarter of the service because of a mental or physical condition.

Whatever services are provided, payments to a parent employed by their child are not subject to FUTA tax (p. 17).

**Related:** Business Owned and Operated by Spouses — when spouses who jointly own and operate a business may be partners in a partnership, and the qualified joint venture (p. 15)

## Note
Part-time workers and workers hired for short periods of time are treated the same as full-time employees for federal income tax withholding and for social security, Medicare and FUTA tax purposes (p. 31).

Generally, it doesn't matter whether the part-time worker, or the worker hired for a short period of time, has another job or has the maximum amount of social security tax withheld by another employer. The page refers to Successor employer, earlier in section 9, for an exception to this rule (p. 31).

For income tax withholding, the full-time method may be used, or the part-year employment method that section 6 of Pub. 15-T explains (p. 31).

**Related:** Social Security and Medicare Taxes — the social security and Medicare taxes, the 2026 rates and wage base limit, and the Additional Medicare Tax (p. 29)

## Note
- Return transcripts for Forms 940, 941, 943, 944 and 945 for tax years 2023 and later are now available through your IRS business tax account (F03, p. 3).
- An amended Form 940, Employer’s Annual Federal Unemployment (FUTA) Tax Return, can be filed electronically using Modernized e-File (MeF) (F04, p. 3).
- Section 3504 agents and CPEOs that the IRS has approved must complete Schedule R (Form 940) when they file an aggregate Form 940 (F04, p. 5).
- Aggregate Forms 940 may be filed by agents for recipients of home care services provided through a government-administered program (federal, state or local), and by CPEOs the IRS approved under section 7705 (F04, p. 5).
- CPEOs notify the IRS on Form 8973 when a service contract with a client or customer starts or ends, and generally must file Form 940 and Schedule R (Form 940) electronically (F04, p. 5).
- Without a “final” Form 940 and a “final” Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944, you keep filing Form 940 even for periods with no wages paid (F04, p. 6).
- The IRS encourages filing a “zero wage” Form 940 electronically (F04, p. 6).
- The Employer Responsibilities list names filing Form 940 among the items under Annually (see Calendar for due dates) (F09, p. 8).
- The filing address for Form 940 generally turns on where your residence or principal place of business is located and on whether a payment goes with the return (F14, p. 9).
- Tax-exempt organizations and government entities have separate filing addresses, which are in the separate instructions for Form 940 (F14, pp. 9–10).
- Under the Calendar’s By January 31 date, Form 940 reports any FUTA tax; if you deposited all of that tax when due, you may file by February 10 (F21, p. 11).
- FUTA tax is paid by the employer alone and isn’t withheld from the employee’s wages; the page points to the Instructions for Form 940 for more information (S14, p. 43).
- The credit for amounts paid into state unemployment funds is determined using the Instructions for Form 940 (S14, p. 44).
- Where certain states leave some wage types out of state unemployment tax although FUTA tax covers them, you may have to deposit more than 0.6% FUTA tax on those wages, and the page points to the Instructions for Form 940 for further guidance (S14, p. 44).
- An employer that acquired a business from a FUTA-liable employer may be able to count that employer’s wages toward the $7,000 wage base limit; the page points to the Instructions for Form 940 (S14, p. 44).
- The quarterly FUTA liability is figured at 0.6% of taxable wages, and may need adjusting depending on the credit for state unemployment contributions; the page points to the Instructions for Form 940 (S14, p. 44).
- If the fourth-quarter FUTA liability (plus any undeposited amount from an earlier quarter) is over $500, the whole amount is deposited by Form 940’s due date (January 31); at $500 or less you may deposit, pay by credit or debit card, or pay with Form 940 by January 31 (S14, p. 44).
- A Form 940 filed electronically can be paid with EFW for any balance due (S14, p. 44).
- In years with credit reduction states, the liabilities owed for credit reduction belong with the fourth quarter deposit, and the page points to the Instructions for Form 940 (S14, p. 44).
- Form 940 is the form for reporting FUTA tax. Your 2025 Form 940 is due by February 2, 2026, or on or before February 10, 2026 if you deposited all FUTA tax when due (S14, pp. 44–45).
- Under the Form 940 e-file program, a taxpayer may electronically file an original or an amended Form 940 (S14, p. 45).
- CPEOs must file Form 940 with Schedule R (Form 940) electronically, though the IRS may waive that requirement in some circumstances (S14, p. 45).
- Reporting agents that file Forms 940 for groups of taxpayers can file them electronically (S14, p. 45).
- FUTA taxes for household employees need not be deposited unless their wages are reported on Forms 941, 943 or 944; where employment taxes for them weren’t reported on those forms, the FUTA tax goes on Schedule H (Form 1040) (S14, pp. 44–45).
- Form 2678 does not cover FUTA taxes reportable on Form 940, except where the employer is a home care service recipient receiving services under a program run by a federal, state or local government agency (S16, p. 53).
- A CPEO files Schedule R (Form 940), Schedule R (Form 941) or Schedule R (Form 943), matching the aggregate return it files, which is Form 940, Form 941 or Form 943 respectively (S16, p. 54).
- Return transcripts for Form 940 for tax years 2023 and later can be accessed through your IRS business tax account (B04, p. 57).

## Sources & References
- Source: Publication 15 (2026) — forms.csv 940

### Where it is used
- What’s New — says Form 940 return transcripts for tax years 2023 and later are available through the IRS business tax account (p. 3)
- Reminders — says an amended Form 940 can be filed electronically through MeF, covers aggregate Form 940 filers, and says to keep filing Form 940 for zero wage periods unless a final return was filed (pp. 3–6)
- Federal Income Tax Withholding — lists filing Form 940 among the employer responsibilities under Annually (p. 8)
- Filing Addresses — says the filing address for Form 940 depends on the residence or principal place of business and on whether a payment is included, with separate addresses for tax-exempt organizations and government entities (pp. 9–10)
- Calendar — says Form 940 is filed to report any FUTA tax, with filing by February 10 where all FUTA tax was deposited when due (p. 11)
- 14. Federal Unemployment (FUTA) Tax — says FUTA tax is reported on Form 940, gives its filing dates, deposit rules, e-file options and household employee treatment, and refers to the Instructions for Form 940 (pp. 43–45)
- 16. Third-Party Payer Arrangements — says Form 2678 doesn’t apply to FUTA taxes reportable on Form 940 except for home care service recipients, and that CPEOs complete Schedule R (Form 940) for an aggregate Form 940 (pp. 53–54)

text:
## Note
Two deposit schedules, monthly and semiweekly, set when a deposit is due once a tax liability arises, for social security, Medicare and withheld federal income taxes. The liability depends on the dates payments were made or wages were paid. For taxable noncash fringe benefits, the page points to the text in section 5 on when taxable fringe benefits are treated as paid.

Before each calendar year begins, you must work out which of the two schedules you are required to use. The choice rests on the total tax liability you reported during a lookback period on Form 941 (line 12), Form 943 (line 13), Form 944 (line 9) or Form 945 (line 3). How often you pay employees or make deposits does not decide it. Later in the section the page points to special rules for Forms 943, 944 and 945, and to Application of Monthly and Semiweekly Schedules.

**Caution.** FUTA tax falls outside these rules; section 14 covers depositing it.

**Lookback period.** For a Form 941 filer the lookback period is 4 quarters, running from July 1 to June 30 as Table 1 shows, and the total taxes reported on line 12 of Forms 941 for it fix the schedule for the calendar year. Reporting $50,000 or less of taxes for the lookback period makes you a monthly schedule depositor; reporting more than $50,000 makes you a semiweekly schedule depositor.

Table 1. Lookback Period for Calendar Year 2026* (p. 32), its four columns:

| Lookback quarter 1 | Lookback quarter 2 | Lookback quarter 3 | Lookback quarter 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| July 1, 2024, through Sept. 30, 2024 | Oct. 1, 2024, through Dec. 31, 2024 | Jan. 1, 2025, through Mar. 31, 2025 | Apr. 1, 2025, through June 30, 2025 |
| * The lookback period for a 2026 Form 941 filer who filed Form 944 in either 2024 or 2025 is calendar year 2024. |  |  |  |

A filer of Form 943 or Form 944 for the current year or for either of the 2 years before it looks to the total taxes reported in the second preceding calendar year, whether on Forms 941 for all 4 quarters of that year, on that year's Form 943 or on that year's Form 944. For 2026 that lookback period is calendar year 2024 for a Form 943 or Form 944 filer. Reporting $50,000 or less of taxes for it makes you a monthly schedule depositor, and reporting more than $50,000 makes you a semiweekly schedule depositor.

A Form 945 filer uses the total taxes reported on line 3 of its Form 945 for the second preceding calendar year; for 2026 that is calendar year 2024.

**Adjustments and the lookback rule.** For the lookback rule, the tax liability of earlier periods is not changed by adjustments made on Form 941-X, Form 943-X, Form 944-X or Form 945-X.

**Example.** An employer first reported a tax liability of $45,000 for the lookback period. In January 2026 it found that the tax for one lookback quarter had been understated by $10,000, and it fixed the error with Form 941-X. It is still a monthly schedule depositor for 2026, since lookback liabilities rest on the amounts first reported, and those were $50,000 or less. The $10,000 adjustment is also not counted as part of the 2026 taxes.

**Deposit period.** A deposit period is the span over which tax liabilities build up for each required deposit due date. For a monthly schedule depositor it is a calendar month; for a semiweekly schedule depositor the deposit periods run Wednesday through Friday and Saturday through Tuesday.

**Tip.** An agent with an approved Form 2678 applies the deposit rules to the total employment taxes it accumulates for its own employees and on behalf of every employer it is authorized to act for. The page refers to Revenue Procedure 2013-39 for more on such an agent.

**Related:** Monthly Deposit Schedule — who is a monthly schedule depositor and by when deposits are due (p. 33)

## Note
The special certifying requirements do not apply to federal agencies that have employees working in Puerto Rico (p. 55).

**Caution (p. 55).** In November 1988 the U.S. Treasury Department and Puerto Rico made an agreement under 5 U.S.C. section 5517. Under it, every federal employer (the Department of Defense included) must withhold Puerto Rico income taxes in place of federal income taxes, and deposit them with the Puerto Rico Treasury, for employees whose regular place of federal employment is Puerto Rico. Federal employers must also file quarterly and annual reports with the Puerto Rico tax department. The 5517 agreement does not apply to payments to pensioners, or to pay of members of the U.S. Armed Forces who are stationed in Puerto Rico but whose state of legal residence is outside Puerto Rico. The page refers to IRS.gov/5517Agreements for more information, including details on completing Form W-2.

text:
## Note
- Return transcripts for Forms 940, 941, 943, 944 and 945 for tax years 2023 and later are now available through your IRS business tax account (F03, p. 3).
- The COVID-19 related sick and family leave wage credit applies only to leave taken after March 31, 2020, and before October 1, 2021, and Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 can’t any longer be used to claim it (F04, p. 3).
- For tax periods beginning after 2023 the claim lines were removed from Form 943, Employer’s Annual Tax Return for Agricultural Employees, and from Forms 941 and 944. An employer entitled to the credit for wages paid after 2023 for an earlier applicable leave period claims it on Form 943-X (or Form 941-X or Form 944-X) (F04, pp. 3–4).
- A Form 943-X filed before the Form 943 for the year may cause errors or processing delays (F04, p. 4).
- The amount from Form 8974, line 12 or, if applicable, line 17, is reported on Form 943 (or Form 941 or Form 944); for reducing your record of tax liability for the payroll tax credit, the page points to the line 17 instructions in the Instructions for Form 943 (F04, p. 4).
- Approved section 3504 agents and CPEOs must complete Schedule R (Form 943), Allocation Schedule for Aggregate Form 943 Filers, for an aggregate Form 943 (F04, p. 4).
- An aggregate annual Form 943 is filed by an agent the IRS approved under section 3504, and also by CPEOs approved under section 7705 (F04, p. 4).
- CPEOs generally must file Form 941 or Form 943, with the applicable Schedule R, electronically (F04, p. 5).
- Other third-party payers filing an aggregate quarterly Form 941 or annual Form 943, non-certified PEOs for example, file the applicable Schedule R when their clients claim an employment tax credit (F04, p. 5).
- A mistake on a filed Form 943 is corrected with Form 943-X, which is filed on its own and separately from Form 943 (F04, p. 5).
- Unless you have filed a “final” Form 940 and a “final” Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944, you continue to file Form 943 for periods with no wages paid (the “seasonal” employer condition is for Form 941 only); the IRS encourages filing “zero wage” returns electronically (F04, p. 6).
- The Employer Responsibilities list includes filing Form 943 if required, with payment of the tax with the return when no deposit is required, among the items under Annually (see Calendar for due dates) (F09, p. 8).
- Payroll withholding (Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944) and nonpayroll withholding (Form 945) are deposited separately (F10, p. 8).
- Income tax withheld on distributions to participants from some nonqualified pension and deferred compensation plans goes on Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944, not on Form 945; distributions from such plans to a beneficiary or estate of a deceased employee aren't wages, and the income tax withheld on them goes on Form 945 (F10, pp. 8–9).
- The filing address for Form 943 generally turns on where your residence or principal place of business is located and on whether a payment goes with the return; tax-exempt organizations and government entities have separate addresses, found in the separate instructions for Form 943 (F14, pp. 9–10).
- For depositing taxes reported on Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 and Form 945, the Calendar refers to section 11 (F21, p. 10).
- Under the Calendar’s By January 31 date, agricultural employers file Form 943 for the previous calendar year and deposit any income, social security and Medicare taxes not yet deposited (F21, p. 11).
- Those taxes may be paid with Form 943 when the year’s total tax liability (Form 943, line 13) is under $2,500, and timely depositors of all taxes may file by February 10 (F21, p. 11).
- If an EIN you used on Form 943 (or Form 941 or Form 944) differs from the EIN reported on Form W-3, the page refers to Box h—Other EIN used this year in the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 (S01, p. 13).
- The deposit schedule depends on the total tax liability reported on Form 943, line 13 (and on the other forms the page lists) during a lookback period (S11.01, p. 32).
- For a Form 943 filer in the current year or either of the 2 years before, the schedule comes from the taxes reported in the second preceding calendar year; for 2026 the lookback period for a Form 943 or Form 944 filer is calendar year 2024 (S11.01, p. 32).
- A Form 943 filer whose lookback taxes (Form 943, line 13) were $50,000 or less is a monthly schedule depositor for the calendar year, and one whose taxes were more than $50,000 is a semiweekly schedule depositor (S11.01.01, p. 33; S11.01.02, p. 33).
- Monthly schedule depositors shouldn’t file Form 943 monthly (S11.01.01, p. 33).
- For Form 943 filers, liability from before the business began or was acquired counts as zero in the lookback period, so a new filer is a monthly schedule depositor in its first and second calendar years; however, the page points to the $100,000 Next-Day Deposit Rule (S11.01.01, p. 33).
- A semiweekly schedule depositor completes Form 943-A, Agricultural Employer’s Record of Federal Tax Liability, and submits it with Form 943 (S11.01.02, p. 33).
- For annual Form 943 the return period is a calendar year (S11.01.02, p. 33).
- Red Co., in the example for employers of farmworkers, reported $48,000 of taxes on its 2024 Form 943, line 13, and $60,000 on its 2025 Form 943, line 13; it is a monthly schedule depositor for 2026 because its lookback taxes ($48,000 for calendar year 2024) were not over $50,000 (S11.01.03, p. 34).
- When you deposited too much, you choose on Form 943 for that year whether the overpayment is refunded or credited to your next return (S11.02, p. 36).
- The deposit penalty information is written about Form 941 but applies to Form 943 as well (S11.03, p. 36).
- To avoid an “averaged” FTD penalty, a monthly schedule depositor lists tax liabilities (not deposits) in the monthly entry spaces on Form 943, line 17, and a semiweekly schedule depositor lists them on Form 943-A; check that the total liability on Form 943, line 17, or Form 943-A, line M, equals the liability on Form 943, line 13 (S11.03, p. 37).
- Form 943 is due for each calendar year starting with the first year in which you pay $2,500 or more for farmwork or employ a farmworker who meets the $150 test explained in section 9; these wages are not reported on Form 941, Form 944 or Form 945 (S12, p. 38).
- Your 2025 Form 943 is due by February 2, 2026, or by February 10, 2026 if timely deposits fully paid the year’s taxes (S12, p. 38).
- An employer that files Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 for business employees may add the taxes of household employees to that return, and agricultural employers report their social security, Medicare and withheld income taxes on Form 943 (S12, p. 38).
- Form 943 can be filed through the IRS e-file program, and reporting agents filing it for groups of taxpayers can file electronically (S12, p. 38).
- CPEOs, apart from the first quarter (Form 941 only) for which a CPEO is certified, must file Form 941 with Schedule R (Form 941) electronically, or where applicable Form 943 with Schedule R (Form 943); the IRS may waive electronic filing in certain circumstances (S12, pp. 38–39).
- An agricultural employer files only one Form 943 per year (S12, p. 39).
- Name and EIN on Form 943 should read exactly as on earlier returns, and the Instructions for Form 943 explain how to prepare the form (S12, p. 39).
- A business that closes files a final return for the last year in which wages are paid (S12, p. 39).
- A late Form 943 for a previous year is filed on a copy of the form (with separate instructions) with a revision date showing that year; the page gives IRS.gov/Form943 for prior year forms (S12, p. 39).
- Social security and Medicare wages and taxes are reported separately on Forms W-2 and W-3 and on Forms 941, 943 or 944, and Form W-3 is reconciled with the annual Form 943 (S12, p. 40).
- Only taxes and withholding that appear on Form W-2 belong on Forms 941, 943 or 944 (S12, p. 40).
- Where Additional Medicare Tax was withheld, the Medicare tax on Form 943, line 5, will not be double the Medicare tax withheld in box 6 of Form W-3, because that tax falls on the employee alone (S12, p. 40).
- Certain social security and Medicare amounts reported on Form 943, lines 3, 5 and 7, have to be adjusted to reach the correct tax liability, and current period adjustments are reported on Form 943, line 10 (S13, p. 40).
- Fractions-of-cents adjustments go on Form 943, line 10, and an employer paying with Form 943 rather than depositing, because the year’s total taxes are under $2,500, may also report one (S13.01, pp. 40–41).
- Under the adjustment of tax on third-party sick pay, the employer share and the employee share of social security and Medicare taxes on sick pay are reported on Form 943, lines 2 and 4; the Additional Medicare Tax goes on line 7 when the employer’s and third-party payer’s combined wages for an employee exceed $200,000 for the calendar year; and the taxes a third-party payer withheld on sick pay are a negative adjustment on line 10 (S13.01, p. 41).
- For group-term life insurance premiums over $50,000 paid for a former employee, Form 943 filers put the social security wages and Medicare wages on lines 2 and 4 and the taxes on lines 3 and 5; if the premium amount combined with other wages exceeds $200,000 for the calendar year, the Additional Medicare Tax wages go on line 6 and the tax on line 7, and the employee share is backed out as a negative adjustment on line 10 (S13.01, p. 41).
- The supporting statement for these adjustments is not attached to Form 943 (S13.01, p. 41).
- For current period adjustments you make no change to your record of federal tax liability on Form 943, line 17, or Form 943-A (S13.01, p. 41).
- An error found on a filed Form 943 is corrected on a separate Form 943-X for each Form 943 corrected, and Form 943-X is filed on its own, not with Form 943 (S13.02, p. 42).
- Treasury Decision 9405 changed how interest-free adjustments to employment taxes reported on Form 943 are made and how a refund claim is filed (S13.02, p. 42).
- Income tax withheld in a prior calendar year can’t be adjusted unless the adjustment corrects an administrative error or section 3509 applies; an administrative error is an amount entered on Form 941, 943 or 944 that differs from the amount actually withheld (S13.02, p. 42).
- Where you did not repay or reimburse the employee, you report and pay the excess when you file the Form 943 for the year in which too much tax was withheld (S13.02, p. 43).
- FUTA tax for household employees need not be deposited unless their wages are reported on Form 941, 943 or 944; where they weren’t reported there, FUTA tax for them goes on Schedule H (Form 1040) (S14, pp. 44–45).
- A CPEO completes Schedule R (Form 943) when it files an aggregate Form 943 (S16, p. 54).
- Return transcripts for Form 943 for tax years 2023 and later can be accessed through your IRS business tax account (B04, p. 57).

## Sources & References
- Source: Publication 15 (2026) — forms.csv 943

### Where it is used
- What’s New — says Form 943 return transcripts for tax years 2023 and later are available through the IRS business tax account (p. 3)

- Nonpayroll Federal Income Tax Withholding — says payroll withholding on Form 943 is deposited separately from nonpayroll withholding, and that some plan distributions are reported on Form 943 and not on Form 945 (pp. 8–9)
- Filing Addresses — says the filing address for Form 943 depends on the residence or principal place of business and on whether a payment is included (pp. 9–10)
- Calendar — says agricultural employers file Form 943 for the previous calendar year, when it may be paid with the form, and the February 10 date for timely depositors (pp. 10–11)
- 1. Employer Identification Number (EIN) — refers to the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 when the EIN used on Form 943 differs from the one reported on Form W-3 (p. 13)
- When To Deposit — says the deposit schedule rests on the taxes reported on Form 943, line 13, in a lookback period, and gives calendar year 2024 as the 2026 lookback period for a Form 943 filer (p. 32)
- Monthly Deposit Schedule — gives the $50,000 lookback limit for Form 943 filers, the first and second calendar years rule for new Form 943 filers, and says not to file Form 943 monthly (p. 33)
- Semiweekly Deposit Schedule — gives the over $50,000 lookback test for Form 943 filers, the use of Form 943-A and the calendar-year return period (p. 33)
- Example of Monthly and Semiweekly Schedules — gives the Red Co. example of an employer of farmworkers using its Form 943 taxes for the lookback period (p. 34)
- How To Deposit — says an overpayment may be refunded or credited by choosing so on Form 943 for the year (p. 36)
- Deposit Penalties — says the penalty rules, written for Form 941, apply to Form 943 too, and gives the Form 943 lines for reporting and liability (pp. 36–37)

## Note
**Social security and Medicare taxes for 2026 (pp. 1–2).** For 2026 the employer and the employee each pay social security tax at 6.2% on taxable wages, up to a wage base limit of $184,500. Each also pays Medicare tax at 1.45%, a rate unchanged from 2025, and Medicare tax has no wage base limit. The two taxes apply to household workers when you pay them $3,000 or more in cash wages in 2026, and to election workers paid $2,500 or more in 2026 in cash or an equivalent form of compensation.

**Permanent extension of individual tax rates (p. 2).** Under P.L. 119-21, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the individual income tax rates set by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (P.L. 115-97) are extended permanently. To figure federal income tax withholding, employers keep using Pub. 15-T, Federal Income Tax Withholding Methods.

**Withholding on supplemental wages (p. 2).** The rate stays at 22%, or 37% if the supplemental wages paid to an employee during the calendar year exceed $1 million. The stated reason is that P.L. 119-21 made the individual rates of P.L. 115-97 permanent. The page refers to section 7 for more on supplemental wages.

**Backup withholding (p. 2).** The backup withholding rate stays at 24%, for the same stated reason. For reportable payments under section 6041(a) or 6041A(a) that are made in calendar year 2026 and are subject to backup withholding, P.L. 119-21 lifts the aggregate reportable payment threshold from $600 to $2,000. An inflation adjustment of that threshold follows for each calendar year after 2026. The page refers to Backup withholding, later.

**Information reporting threshold (p. 2).** For payments made after calendar year 2025, P.L. 119-21 lifts the payment threshold for information reporting (for example, Forms 1099-MISC and Forms 1099-NEC) from $600 to $2,000 per calendar year. This covers certain payments to persons engaged in a trade or business, and payments for services. Wage reporting on Forms W-2 gets the same $2,000 threshold if no federal income, social security or Medicare tax was withheld. Inflation adjustments follow for each calendar year after 2026. The page refers to the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 and to the General Instructions for Certain Information Returns.

**Withholding on qualified tips (p. 2).** For tax years beginning after 2024 and ending before 2029, P.L. 119-21 permits employees and self-employed individuals to deduct up to $25,000 of qualified tips on their income tax returns, provided the tips came from occupations that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024. Qualified tips are cash tips: voluntary cash or charged tips from customers or, for employees, tips received through tip-sharing arrangements. Mandatory service charges added to the bill do not qualify. If an employee submits an updated Form W-4, the employer must use it with the withholding procedures in Pub. 15-T, so that the employee can reflect the expected deduction and receive more money in each paycheck, rather than waiting to get the full benefit when filing the income tax return. Tips of $20 or more per month are still generally subject to both shares of social security and Medicare tax. Information returns (for example, Forms W-2, 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC) must be filed by employers and other payers with the SSA or the IRS, as applicable. Tip recipients must also be given statements showing the cash tips received and the recipient’s Treasury Tipped Occupation Code(s). The IRS has granted transition relief for the tax year 2025 reporting requirements; the page refers to Notice 2025-62, 2025-48 I.R.B. 740.

**Withholding on qualified overtime compensation (p. 2).** For tax years beginning after 2024 and ending before 2029, P.L. 119-21 permits individuals (employees, and other workers not treated as employees) to deduct up to $12,500 of qualified overtime compensation, or $25,000 if married filing jointly. The deduction comes out of income subject to federal income tax and is claimed on income tax returns. Qualified overtime is pay above the regular rate that section 7 of the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) of 1938 requires an individual to be paid, such as the “half” portion of time-and-a-half. Under the FLSA, covered, nonexempt employees must generally be paid at least one-and-a-half times their regular rate for hours over 40 in a week; the page points to dol.gov/agencies/whd/overtime. If an employee submits an updated Form W-4, the employer must use it with the Pub. 15-T procedures, so that the employee can account for the expected deduction in each paycheck. Overtime pay is still generally subject to the employer and employee shares of social security and Medicare tax. Employers and other payers file information returns (for example, Forms W-2, 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC) with the SSA or the IRS, as applicable, and must also furnish overtime recipients with statements of the qualified overtime compensation paid during the year. Transition relief applies to the tax year 2025 reporting requirements, and the page refers to Notice 2025-62.

**Moving expense reimbursement (pp. 2–3).** P.L. 119-21 permanently ends the exclusion of qualified moving expense reimbursements from an employee’s income. The exclusion is available in two cases. One is an active-duty member of the U.S. Armed Forces who moves because of a permanent change of station under a military order; for that member the exclusion covers only reimbursement of moving expenses deductible had they been paid or incurred without reimbursement, and the page refers to Moving Expenses in Pub. 3, Armed Forces’ Tax Guide. The other, added by P.L. 119-21, is an employee or new appointee in the intelligence community (the term is defined in section 3 of the National Security Act of 1947, 50 U.S.C. 3003) who is not a member of the Armed Forces and moves under a change in assignment requiring relocation; the exclusion again covers only reimbursement of moving expenses they could deduct had they paid or incurred them without reimbursement.

**Employer contributions to Trump accounts (p. 3).** A Trump account is a new type of traditional individual retirement account that P.L. 119-21 allows to be set up for a child who has not reached age 18 by the end of the year the account is established. Its annual contribution limit is $5,000 (other than exempt contributions), indexed for inflation after tax year 2027. Starting July 4, 2026, an employer may put up to $2,500 a year, indexed for inflation after tax year 2027, toward that limit in the Trump account of an employee or of an employee’s dependent. The amount is excluded from the employee’s gross income if paid under a Trump account contribution program. The page refers to Pub. 15-A, Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide.

**Direct deposit of employment tax refunds (p. 3).** Executive Order (EO) 14247, Modernizing Payments To and From America’s Bank Account, was issued on March 25, 2025. It promotes operational efficiency by mandating electronic payments for all federal disbursements, and the IRS will now therefore issue employment tax return refunds by direct deposit to a checking or savings account. As an alternative to the direct deposit refund, you can still choose to have the overpayment go toward your next return, which you do by checking the appropriate box on your employment tax return. The page refers to the instructions for your employment tax return.

**Make balance due payments electronically (p. 3).** EO 14247 likewise mandates electronic payments for all payments to the federal government. The page therefore says to pay the balance due on your employment tax return electronically, and refers to the instructions for your employment tax return for the ways to do so.

**Employment tax return transcripts (p. 3).** Return transcripts of Forms 940, 941, 943, 944 and 945 for tax years 2023 and later are now available electronically through your IRS business tax account. The page points to IRS.gov/BusinessTranscript, and to IRS.gov/BusinessAccount for the business tax account.

**Related:** 7. Supplemental Wages — wage payments to an employee that are not regular wages, and the kinds of payment they include (p. 23)

## Note
**Forms for prior-period adjustments (pp. 41–42).** After an error is discovered on a previously filed Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944, the correction is made with Form 941-X, Form 943-X or Form 944-X. Form 945-X and Form CT-1 X report corrections on the corresponding returns. Form 843 is used to request a refund or abatement of assessed interest or penalties. The page refers to Revenue Ruling 2009-39 for examples of how the interest-free adjustment and claim for refund rules apply in 10 different situations.

**Background (p. 42).** Treasury Decision 9405 changed how interest-free adjustments to employment taxes on Form 941, Form 943 and Form 944 are made, and how a claim for refund of employment taxes is filed. The adjustment process is used if employment taxes were underreported and a payment is being made, or if they were overreported and the credit will be applied to the Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 period in which Form 941-X, Form 943-X or Form 944-X is filed. The claim process is used if employment taxes were overreported and a refund or abatement of the overreported amount is requested. The page says that "correct" and "corrections" cover interest-free adjustments under sections 6205 and 6413 and claims for refund and abatement under sections 6402, 6414 and 6404.

**Correcting employment taxes (p. 42).** On discovering an error on a previously filed Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944, an employer must:
- correct the error with Form 941-X, Form 943-X or Form 944-X;
- file a separate correction form of that kind for each return being corrected; and
- send each correction form on its own and not with Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944.

Current quarter adjustments for fractions of cents, third-party sick pay, tips and group-term life insurance are reported on Form 941 using lines 7–9, on Form 943 using line 10 and on Form 944 using line 6; the page points to Current Period Adjustments, earlier in the section. Corrections of underreported and overreported amounts for the same tax period go on a single Form 941-X, Form 943-X or Form 944-X, unless a refund is requested. If a refund is requested and both underreported and overreported amounts are being corrected, file one form correcting only the underreported amounts and a second form correcting only the overreported amounts. The chart on the last page of Form 941-X, Form 943-X or Form 944-X helps in choosing between the adjustment process and the claim process, and the instructions for each form give the details for making an adjustment or claim.

**E-file (p. 42).** The IRS e-file program lets a taxpayer file Form 941-X, Form 943-X and Form 945-X electronically.

**Income tax withholding adjustments (p. 42).** In a current calendar year, an error in income tax withholding for a prior quarter is corrected on Form 941-X when it is discovered. An adjustment may be made only for income tax withholding errors discovered in the same calendar year in which the wages were paid, because the employee claims the amount shown on Form W-2 (or, if applicable, Form W-2c) as a credit on their income tax return. Amounts reported as income tax withheld in a prior calendar year cannot be adjusted unless the adjustment corrects an administrative error or section 3509 applies. An administrative error occurs if the amount entered on Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 is not the amount actually withheld, for example because of a mathematical or transposition error. The administrative error adjustment corrects the amount on the return to agree with the amount actually withheld from employees and reported on their Forms W-2.

**Additional Medicare Tax withholding adjustments (p. 42).** Generally, the rules for income tax withholding adjustments apply to Additional Medicare Tax withholding adjustments. An adjustment may be made for errors discovered in the same calendar year in which the wages were paid, and amounts reported in a prior calendar year cannot be adjusted unless the adjustment corrects an administrative error or section 3509 applies. An employer that overpaid Additional Medicare Tax cannot claim a refund of the overpayment unless the amount was not actually withheld from the employee's wages (which would be an administrative error). If a prior-year error was a nonadministrative error, the employer may correct only the wages and tips subject to Additional Medicare Tax withholding.

**Collecting underwithheld taxes from employees (p. 42).** If no income, social security or Medicare tax, or less than the correct amount, was withheld from an employee's wages, the employer can make it up from later pay to that employee. The employer still owes the underpayment, and reimbursement is a matter for settlement between the employer and the employee. Underwithheld income tax and Additional Medicare Tax must be collected from the employee no later than the last day of the calendar year. The page points to special rules for tax on tips (section 6) and for fringe benefits (section 5).

**Refunding amounts incorrectly withheld from employees (pp. 42–43).** If more than the correct amount of income, social security or Medicare tax was withheld from wages, the employer repays or reimburses the employee the excess. Any excess income tax or Additional Medicare Tax withholding must be repaid or reimbursed before the end of the calendar year in which it was withheld. The employer keeps in its records the employee's written receipt showing the date and amount of the repayment, or a record of the reimbursement. If the employer did not repay or reimburse the employee, it must report and pay each excess amount when it files Form 941 for the quarter (or Form 943 or Form 944 for the year) in which too much tax was withheld.

**Correcting filed Forms W-2 and W-3 (p. 43).** When adjustments correct wages and social security and Medicare taxes because of a change in the wage totals reported for a previous year, Form W-2c and Form W-3c must also be filed with the SSA. Up to 25 Forms W-2c per Form W-3c may be filed per online session, with no limit on the number of sessions. The page refers to the SSA's Employer W-2 Filing Instructions & Information webpage.

**Exceptions to interest-free corrections of employment taxes (p. 43).** A correction is not eligible for interest-free treatment if:
- the failure to report concerns an issue raised during an IRS examination of a prior return, or
- the employer underreported its employment tax liability knowingly.

A correction is also not eligible for interest-free treatment after the earlier of receipt of an IRS notice and demand for payment after assessment, and receipt of an IRS notice of determination under section 7436.

**Related:** Wage Repayments — what to do when an employee repays wages received in error (p. 43)
