text:
## Note
**Redesigned Form W-4 (pp. 25–26).** The IRS redesigned Form W-4 for 2020 and later years. Until 2020 the value of a withholding allowance was tied to the amount of the personal exemption. Since changes in the law mean taxpayers can no longer claim personal exemptions or dependency exemptions, Form W-4 no longer has the employee report a number of withholding allowances. The revised form has five steps:
- Steps 1 and 5 apply to all employees: in Step 1 employees give personal information such as name and filing status, and in Step 5 they sign. An employee who completes only those two steps gets withholding figured on the standard deduction and tax rates for their filing status, with no other adjustments.
- Step 2, where applicable, raises withholding to account for higher tax rates caused by income from other jobs in the household. Employees can either enter an additional amount to withhold per payroll period in Step 4(c) or tick the box in Step 2(c) so that higher withholding rate tables apply to their wages.
- Step 3 lowers withholding by the annual amount of any credits the employee will claim on their income tax return.
- Step 4 lets employees raise or lower withholding according to the annual amount of other income or deductions they will report on their income tax return, and also to request any additional federal income tax they want withheld each pay period.

An employee who submitted a Form W-4 in any year before 2020 need not submit a new one just because of the redesign, and employers keep figuring withholding from the information on the employee's most recently submitted Form W-4. The Pub. 15-T withholding tables let employers figure withholding from a Form W-4 for 2019 or earlier as well as from the redesigned form. An employee first paid wages before 2020 who hasn't yet submitted a redesigned form may be asked to submit one, but you should explain that submitting it is not required and that, without a new Form W-4, withholding continues on a valid Form W-4 submitted earlier. All newly hired employees must use the redesigned form, and so must any other employees who want to adjust their withholding (p. 26).

Pub. 15-T offers an optional computational bridge for treating 2019 and earlier Forms W-4 as if they were 2020 or later Forms W-4 when figuring federal income tax withholding. With the bridge you apply the computational procedures and data fields of a 2020 and later Form W-4 to reach the withholding that the procedures and data fields of a 2019 or earlier Form W-4 would have produced. The page refers to How To Treat 2019 and Earlier Forms W-4 as if They Were 2020 or Later Forms W-4 under Introduction in Pub. 15-T (p. 26).

**More information (p. 26).** On the redesigned Form W-4 and on regulations guiding employers on income tax withholding from employees' wages, the page refers to Treasury Decision 9924. It points to IRS.gov/FormW4 for information about Form W-4. Pub. 15-T, available at IRS.gov/Pub15T, holds the employer instructions on figuring employee withholding.

**Tip (p. 26).** Farm operators and crew leaders must withhold federal income tax from farmworkers' wages if those wages are subject to social security and Medicare taxes.

**Using Form W-4 to figure withholding (p. 26).** You should hold a Form W-4 for each employee in order to know how much federal income tax to withhold. Encourage employees to file an updated Form W-4 for 2026; this matters most for those who owed taxes, or got a large refund, on their 2025 tax return. New employees should be asked for a signed Form W-4 when they start work, and the form takes effect with the first wage payment. A new employee who doesn't give you a completed Form W-4 in 2026 (a rehired employee who fails to furnish one is included) is treated as though they had checked the box for Single or Married filing separately in Step 1(c) and made no entries in Steps 2, 3 or 4 of the 2026 Form W-4. An employee paid wages before 2020 who failed to furnish a Form W-4 continues to be treated as single and claiming zero allowances on a 2019 Form W-4. With the optional computational bridge, described earlier under Redesigned Form W-4, you may instead treat this employee as having checked the box for Single or Married filing separately in Step 1(c), made no entries in Steps 2 and 3, entered $8,600 in Step 4(a) and entered zero in Step 4(b) of the 2026 Form W-4.

**Electronic system to receive Form W-4 (p. 26).** You may set up a system for receiving Forms W-4 electronically from employees. The page refers to Regulations section 31.3402(f)(5)-1(c) and Pub. 15-T for more information.

**Effective date of Form W-4 (p. 26).** A Form W-4 for 2025 or an earlier year stays in effect for 2026 unless the employee gives you a 2026 Form W-4. Withholding for pay periods before the effective date of a new Form W-4 is not adjusted. A Form W-4 that replaces an existing one must be put into effect no later than the start of the first payroll period ending on or after the 30th day from the date you received the replacement. For exceptions the page refers to Exemption from federal income tax withholding, IRS review of requested Forms W-4 and Invalid Forms W-4, later in the section. A Form W-4 making a change for the next calendar year does not take effect in the current calendar year.

**Successor employer (p. 26).** A successor employer (the page refers to Successor employer, later in the section) should secure new Forms W-4 from the transferred employees, unless the "Alternative Procedure" in section 5 of Revenue Procedure 2004-53 applies. The page refers to Revenue Procedure 2004-53, 2004-34 I.R.B. 320.

**IRS Tax Withholding Estimator for employees (p. 26).** You may advise employees to use the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator at IRS.gov/W4App to help decide how to complete their Forms W-4. An employee who changes their withholding mid-year after using the Estimator may be underwithheld or overwithheld once the Form W-4 applies to the next full calendar year. You should therefore remind such employees to return to the Estimator in early January and submit a new Form W-4 for the year.

**Completing Form W-4 (pp. 26–27).** Any federal income tax withholding has to rest on filing status, income (income from other jobs included), deductions and credits; employees may not base withholding on a fixed dollar amount or percentage. An employee may, however, specify a dollar amount to be withheld each pay period on top of the withholding based on filing status and the other information reported on Form W-4 (p. 26). Employees who are married filing jointly and whose spouses also currently work, and employees who hold more than one job at the same time, should account for their higher tax rate by completing Step 2 of the 2026 Form W-4. Employees can also report on their 2026 Form W-4 other income not subject to withholding and other deductions they will claim, which makes federal income tax withholding more accurate. The page refers to Pub. 505 for more on completing Form W-4 and says you may wish to order Pub. 505 for employees along with Form W-4. Accept no withholding or estimated tax payments from employees beyond the withholding based on their Form W-4. An employee needing additional withholding should submit a new Form W-4 and, if necessary, pay estimated tax by filing Form 1040-ES or making an electronic payment of estimated taxes. Employees who receive tips may provide funds to their employer for withholding on tips; the page refers to Collecting taxes on tips in section 6 (p. 27).

**Exemption from federal income tax withholding (p. 27).** Generally, an employee may claim exemption from federal income tax withholding on the ground of having had no income tax liability last year and expecting none this year; the page refers to the Form W-4 instructions. Social security and Medicare taxes still apply to the wages. The page also refers to Invalid Forms W-4, later in the section. A Form W-4 claiming exemption takes effect when the employer receives it and lasts only for that calendar year. To stay exempt, the employee must give a new Form W-4 by February 15. Without one by February 15, begin withholding as though the employee had checked the box for Single or Married filing separately in Step 1(c) and made no entries in Steps 2, 3 or 4 of the 2026 Form W-4. A new exemption Form W-4 given on February 16 or later may be applied to future wages, but taxes withheld while the exempt status wasn't in place are not refunded.

**Withholding federal income taxes on the wages of nonresident alien employees (p. 27).** In general, you must withhold federal income taxes on nonresident alien employees' wages. The page refers to Pub. 515 for exceptions, and to section 5 for more guidance on H-2A visa workers.

**Withholding adjustment for nonresident alien employees (p. 27).** Nonresident aliens may not claim the standard deduction on their tax returns, so for nonresident alien employees performing services within the United States the employer must add an amount to wages when figuring the federal income tax to withhold. The addition is made solely to calculate federal income tax withholding. It appears in no box of the employee's Form W-2 and doesn't raise the employee's income tax liability. Nor does it raise the social security or Medicare tax liability of the employer or the employee, or the employer's FUTA tax liability. For the amount to add to wages for the payroll period, the page refers to Withholding Adjustment for Nonresident Alien Employees under Introduction in Pub. 15-T.

**Supplemental wage payment (p. 27).** The adjustment for nonresident alien employees is not applied to a supplemental wage payment (the page refers to section 7) when the 37% mandatory flat rate withholding applies, or when the 22% optional flat rate withholding is being used to calculate income tax withholding on that payment.

**Nonresident alien employee's Form W-4 (p. 27).** On Form W-4, nonresident aliens are required to:
- Not claim exemption from income tax withholding, even if they meet both of the conditions for exemption listed in the Form W-4 instructions.
- Request withholding as if single, whatever their actual filing status.
- Not claim the child tax credit or credit for other dependents in Step 3. A nonresident alien who is a resident of Canada, Mexico or South Korea, a student from India or a business apprentice from India may claim them under certain circumstances; the page refers to Pub. 519, U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens.
- Write "Nonresident Alien" or "NRA" in the space below Step 4(c).

An employer that maintains an electronic Form W-4 system should provide a field in which nonresident aliens enter their nonresident alien status instead of writing it below Step 4(c). Nonresident aliens should be told to see Notice 1392, Supplemental Form W-4 Instructions for Nonresident Aliens, before completing Form W-4.

**Form 8233 (p. 27).** A nonresident alien employee claiming a tax treaty exemption from withholding must submit Form 8233, rather than Form W-4, for the income exempt under the treaty. The page refers to the Instructions for Form 8233 and to Pay for Personal Services Performed under Withholding on Specific Income in Pub. 515.

**IRS review of requested Forms W-4 (pp. 27–28).** On the IRS's request you must make original Forms W-4 available for inspection by an IRS employee. You may be directed to send certain Forms W-4 to the IRS, and a notice may require you to submit a copy of Form W-4 for one or more named employees; send the copy or copies to the address given, in the manner the notice directs. The IRS may also require you to submit copies of Form W-4 as directed by a revenue procedure or notice published in the Internal Revenue Bulletin. After sending a requested copy, keep withholding federal income tax on that Form W-4 if it is valid (the page refers to Invalid Forms W-4, later in the section). Should the IRS afterwards inform you in writing that the employee may not claim an exemption from withholding, or the amount of deductions or credits claimed, withhold federal income tax on the basis of the effective date, the employee's permitted filing status and the withholding instructions in the IRS notice (commonly referred to as a "lock-in letter").

**Initial lock-in letter (p. 28).** Information reported on Form W-2 is what the IRS uses to identify employees with withholding compliance problems. Where a serious underwithholding problem exists for a particular employee, the IRS may in some cases issue the employer a lock-in letter stating the employee's permitted filing status and giving withholding instructions for that employee. The employer also receives a copy for the employee, which identifies the permitted filing status, describes the withholding instructions the employer must follow, and describes how the employee can give the IRS additional information so that it can determine the appropriate withholding and/or modify the filing status. The employee copy must be furnished to an employee employed by you on the notice date within 10 business days of receipt, and any reasonable business practice may be used to furnish it. Begin withholding on the basis of the notice on the date the notice specifies.

**Implementation of lock-in letter (p. 28).** On receiving the notice, you may not start withholding on its basis immediately. You must begin withholding on the basis of the notice for any wages paid after the date the notice specifies. The gap between receiving the notice and that date gives the employee time to contact the IRS.

**Seasonal employees and employees not currently performing services (p. 28).** A notice for an employee who isn't currently performing services for you still requires you to furnish the employee copy and to withhold on the basis of the notice if any of these apply:
- Wages you are paying for the employee's prior services are subject to income tax withholding on or after the date specified in the notice.
- Within 12 months of the date of the notice, you reasonably expect the employee to resume services.
- The employee is on a leave of absence not exceeding 12 months, or has a right to reemployment after the leave.

**Termination and rehire of employees (p. 28).** Where you must furnish and withhold on the basis of the notice and the employment relationship ends after the notice date, you must keep withholding on that basis for as long as you continue to pay any wages subject to income tax withholding. You must also withhold on the basis of the notice or the modification notice (explained next) if the employee resumes the employment relationship with you within 12 months after it ended.

**Modification notice (p. 28).** After the original notice, the IRS may issue a later notice (a modification notice) changing it. The modification notice may alter the permitted filing status and the withholding instructions, and you must withhold federal income tax on the basis of the effective date it specifies.

**New Form W-4 after IRS notice (p. 28).** After a notice or modification notice, disregard a new Form W-4 from the employee that claims complete exemption from withholding or that results in less withholding than the notice or modification notice would. Withhold on the basis of the notice or modification notice unless the IRS tells you to withhold on the basis of the new Form W-4. An employee who wants a new Form W-4 resulting in less withholding than required to be put into effect must contact the IRS. If, though, the employee gives you a new completed Form W-4 resulting in more withholding than the notice or modification notice would, withhold on the basis of the new Form W-4. Disregard any other later Forms W-4 from the employee and withhold on the basis of the IRS notice or modification notice.

**Caution: lock-in letters from before 2020 (p. 28).** A lock-in letter received for an employee in a year before 2020 should still be followed for 2026. The withholding methods in Pub. 15-T for an employee with a Form W-4 from 2019 or earlier apply, or you may use the optional computational bridge for treating 2019 and earlier Forms W-4 as 2020 or later Forms W-4 when figuring federal income tax withholding; the page refers to How To Treat 2019 and Earlier Forms W-4 as if They Were 2020 or Later Forms W-4 under Introduction in Pub. 15-T. Keep following the pre-2020 lock-in letter until you receive a letter releasing the employee from the lock-in procedures, you receive a modification notice, or the employee gives you a new Form W-4 resulting in more withholding than the notice would. The page points to IRS.gov/WHC for additional information about employer withholding compliance.

**Substitute Forms W-4 (p. 28).** Employees are encouraged to use the official Form W-4, though you may use a substitute version to meet your business needs. A substitute must contain language identical to the official Form W-4 and meet all current IRS rules for substitute forms. When you give the employee your substitute form, you must also provide all tables, instructions and worksheets from the current Form W-4. The page refers to Pub. 15-T for more information. You can't accept substitute Forms W-4 that employees developed. An employee who submits an employee-developed substitute after October 10, 2007, is treated as failing to furnish a Form W-4, but valid employee-developed Forms W-4 you accepted before October 11, 2007, are still to be honored.

**Invalid Forms W-4 (pp. 28–29).** An unauthorized change or addition to Form W-4 makes it invalid, and that includes removing any language by which the employee certifies that the form is correct. A Form W-4 is also invalid if, by the date the employee gives it to you, the employee clearly indicates it is false. An employee submitting a false Form W-4 may be subject to a $500 penalty. You may treat a Form W-4 as invalid when the employee has written "exempt" below Step 4(c) and has also checked the box in Step 2(c) or entered numbers for Steps 3 and 4. An invalid Form W-4 must not be used to figure federal income tax withholding; tell the employee it is invalid and ask for another one. If no valid one is given and you hold an earlier valid Form W-4 for the employee, withhold as before. Without an earlier valid Form W-4, withhold as though the employee had checked the box for Single or Married filing separately in Step 1(c) and made no entries in Steps 2, 3 or 4 of the 2026 Form W-4. An employee who was paid wages in 2019, never submitted a valid Form W-4 and submits an invalid one in 2026 continues, however, to be treated as single and claiming zero allowances on a 2019 Form W-4. With the optional computational bridge, described earlier under Redesigned Form W-4, you may treat this employee as having checked the box for Single or Married filing separately in Step 1(c), made no entries in Steps 2 and 3, entered $8,600 in Step 4(a) and entered zero in Step 4(b) of the 2026 Form W-4.

**Amounts exempt from levy on wages, salary and other income (p. 29).** On receiving a Notice of Levy on Wages, Salary, and Other Income (a notice in the Form 668 series), you must withhold amounts as the instructions for these forms describe. Pub. 1494 has tables for figuring the amount exempt from levy. Where a levy issued in a prior year is still in effect and the taxpayer submits a new Statement of Exemptions and Filing Status, the current year Pub. 1494 is used to figure the exempt amount.

**Related:** 7. Supplemental Wages — wage payments to an employee that are not regular wages, and the withholding methods for them (pp. 23–25)

## Note
**Who needs an EIN (p. 13).** You need an EIN if you are required to report employment taxes or to give tax statements to employees or annuitants. The EIN is a nine-digit number that the IRS issues, arranged as 00-0000000. It identifies the tax accounts of employers and of certain others who have no employees. Use your EIN on all of the items you send to the IRS and the SSA. The page points to Pub. 1635 for more information.

**Applying for an EIN (p. 13).** If you don't have an EIN, you may apply for one online at IRS.gov/EIN. You may also apply by faxing or mailing Form SS-4 to the IRS. If the principal business was created or organized outside the United States or U.S. territories, you may also apply by calling 267-941-1099 (a toll call). Don't use an SSN in place of an EIN.

**Only one EIN (p. 13).** You should have only one EIN. Should you hold more than one and be unsure which applies, call 800-829-4933, or 800-829-4059 (TDD/TTY, for persons who are deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech disability). Give each number you hold, the name and address tied to each, and the address of your main place of business, and the IRS will say which number to use. The page points to Pub. 1635 for more information.

**Successor employers and a pending EIN (p. 13).** If you took over another employer's business (the page refers to Successor employer in section 9), don't use that employer's EIN. If you have applied for an EIN but don't have it by the time a return is due, file a paper return and enter "Applied For" and the date you applied in the space shown for the number.

**Caution: the EIN must match (pp. 13–14).** The EIN on any form you file has to be identical to the EIN the IRS assigned to your business. An SSN or ITIN must not be used on forms that ask for an EIN. Suppose the EIN you used on Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 (a prior owner's EIN included) differs from the one reported on Form W-3: the page then refers to Box h—Other EIN used this year in the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3. For Puerto Rico's Form W-3 (PR), "Other EIN used this year" is reported in box f. Form 945 must show the same name and EIN as your information returns that report federal income tax withholding (for example, backup withholding reported on Form 1099-NEC). A Form 945 filed with an incorrect EIN, or with another business's EIN, may bring penalties and delays in processing the return.

**Agricultural employers that have crew leaders (p. 14).** An agricultural employer must record the crew leader's name, address and EIN. The page refers to sections 2 and 14.

**Related:** 2. Who Are Employees? — how employees are defined under common law and under statutes for certain situations (p. 14)

## Note
The Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) is an independent organization within the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) (p. 58). TAS helps taxpayers resolve problems with the IRS, makes administrative and legislative recommendations to prevent or correct the problems, and protects taxpayer rights (p. 58). It works to ensure that every taxpayer is treated fairly and that taxpayers know and understand their rights under the Taxpayer Bill of Rights (p. 58). The page adds the line "We are Your Voice at the IRS" (p. 58).

**Related:** How Can TAS Help Me? — who TAS helps, when you may be eligible for its help, and the TAS website (p. 58)

## Note
- If an employee submits an updated Form W-4, the employer has to use it, together with the Pub. 15-T withholding procedures, so the employee can reflect the expected qualified tips or qualified overtime deduction and get more pay in each paycheck (F03, p. 2).
- On new hire reporting, the page says that many states take a copy of Form W-4 with employer information added (F07, p. 7).
- Each new employee is asked to complete the 2026 Form W-4 (F07, p. 7).
- Federal income tax is withheld from each wage payment or supplemental unemployment compensation plan benefit payment according to the employee’s Form W-4 and the right withholding table in Pub. 15-T (F09, pp. 7–8).
- The Employer Responsibilities list includes asking new employees for Form W-4, withholding on each payday based on each employee’s Form W-4, reminding employees to turn in a new Form W-4 when they need to change their withholding, and asking for a new Form W-4 from employees who claim exemption (F09, p. 8).
- The records you keep should include copies of employees’ and recipients’ withholding certificates: Forms W-4, W-4P, W-4R, W-4S and W-4V (F11, p. 9).
- By February 15, the Calendar says to ask each employee who claimed exemption from withholding last year for a new Form W-4 (F21, p. 11).
- On February 16, an exemption Form W-4 for the previous year has expired. If the employee has not given a new Form W-4 for the current year, you start withholding as though the employee had checked Single or Married filing separately in Step 1(c) and left Steps 2, 3 and 4 of the 2026 Form W-4 blank (F21, p. 11).
- A new Form W-4 claiming exemption that arrives after February 15 may be applied to future wages, but taxes withheld while the exempt status was not in place are not refunded (F21, p. 11).
- Before December 1, the Calendar says to remind employees to send a new Form W-4 when their filing status, other income, deductions or credits have changed or will change for the next year, and also when they made a mid-year change using the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator (F21, p. 12).
- An employee who made a mid-year change may be underwithheld or overwithheld once the Form W-4 applies for the next full calendar year (F21, p. 12).
- An employer need not withhold federal income tax on pay to an H-2A worker for agricultural labor under the visa, but may if the worker asks and the employer agrees; the worker then has to give the employer a completed Form W-4 (S05, p. 19).
- The part of an employee’s supplemental wages above $1 million in a calendar year is withheld at 37% (or the highest income tax rate for the year), without regard to the employee’s Form W-4 (S07, p. 24).
- The IRS redesigned Form W-4 for 2020 and later years. Because personal and dependency exemptions can no longer be claimed, the form no longer asks for a number of withholding allowances (S09.01, p. 25).
- The redesigned form has five steps. Steps 1 and 5 apply to every employee: Step 1 asks for personal information such as name and filing status, and Step 5 is the signature (S09.01, p. 25).
- An employee who completes only Steps 1 and 5 has withholding figured from the standard deduction and tax rates for the filing status, with no other adjustments (S09.01, p. 25).
- Step 2 lets an employee with other jobs in the household raise withholding for higher tax rates, either with an extra amount per payroll period in Step 4(c) or by checking the Step 2(c) box for higher withholding rate tables (S09.01, p. 25).
- Step 3 lowers withholding by the annual amount of credits the employee will claim, and Step 4 raises or lowers it based on the annual amount of other income or deductions and lets the employee request extra withholding per pay period (S09.01, pp. 25–26).
- An employee who gave you a Form W-4 before 2020 does not have to submit a new one merely because of the redesign; you keep figuring withholding from the most recent form (S09.01, p. 26).
- Newly hired employees have to use the redesigned form, and so do other employees who want to change their withholding (S09.01, p. 26).
- You should have a Form W-4 on file for every employee; ask new employees for a signed Form W-4 when they start work, and make it effective with the first wage payment (S09.01, p. 26).
- Where a new employee, including a rehired one, doesn’t give you a completed Form W-4 in 2026, you treat that employee as having checked Single or Married filing separately in Step 1(c) and made no entries in Steps 2, 3 and 4 of the 2026 Form W-4 (S09.01, p. 26).
- You may set up a system for receiving Forms W-4 electronically from employees (S09.01, p. 26).
- A Form W-4 from 2025 or earlier stays in effect for 2026 unless the employee gives you a 2026 form, and when a new form arrives you do not change withholding for earlier pay periods (S09.01, p. 26).
- When a replacement Form W-4 comes in, withholding on it starts no later than the start of the first payroll period ending on or after the 30th day from the date you received it (for exceptions, the page points to Exemption from federal income tax withholding, IRS review of requested Forms W-4, and Invalid Forms W-4), and a form that changes things for the next calendar year takes no effect in the current year (S09.01, p. 26).
- You may suggest that employees use the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator to help fill in their Forms W-4 (S09.01, p. 26).
- Withholding must rest on filing status, income (including income from other jobs), deductions and credits; employees can’t choose a fixed dollar amount or percentage, but may name an extra dollar amount to withhold each pay period (S09.01, p. 26).
- Married employees filing jointly whose spouses also work, and employees with more than one job, should allow for the higher tax rate by completing Step 2 of their 2026 Form W-4 (S09.01, pp. 26–27).
- Don’t accept withholding or estimated tax payments from employees on top of the withholding based on their Form W-4; an employee who needs more withholding should submit a new Form W-4 (S09.01, p. 27).
- In general, an employee may claim exemption from withholding having had no income tax liability last year and expecting none this year; the wages remain subject to social security and Medicare taxes (S09.01, p. 27).
- An exemption Form W-4 takes effect when given to the employer and lasts only for that calendar year, and the employee must give a new Form W-4 by February 15 to stay exempt (S09.01, p. 27).
- Nonresident aliens completing Form W-4 must ask for withholding as if single, write “Nonresident Alien” or “NRA” below Step 4(c), and may not claim exemption from withholding (S09.01, p. 27).
- A nonresident alien employee claiming a tax treaty exemption submits Form 8233 for the treaty-exempt income rather than Form W-4 (S09.01, p. 27).
- On request, you must let an IRS employee inspect original Forms W-4, and you may be told to send certain Forms W-4 to the IRS (S09.01, p. 27).
- After an IRS notice or modification notice, a new Form W-4 that claims complete exemption or leads to less withholding than the notice is disregarded unless the IRS tells you to use it, while a new form leading to more withholding is used (S09.01, p. 28).
- You are encouraged to have employees use the official Form W-4. A substitute must contain language identical to the official form, must meet all current IRS rules for substitute forms, and must be accompanied by all the current form’s tables, instructions and worksheets (S09.01, p. 28).
- Substitutes developed by employees are not accepted; one handed in after October 10, 2007 counts as no Form W-4 at all, but valid employee-developed forms accepted before October 11, 2007 stay honored (S09.01, p. 28).
- Any unauthorized change or addition makes a Form W-4 invalid, as does removing the language by which the employee certifies it is correct (S09.01, pp. 28–29).
- A Form W-4 is also invalid if the employee clearly indicates by the date they give it to you that it is false, and a false form may bring the employee a $500 penalty (S09.01, p. 29).
- You may treat a Form W-4 as invalid if the employee wrote “exempt” below Step 4(c) and also checked the Step 2(c) box or entered numbers for Steps 3 and 4 (S09.01, p. 29).
- On receiving an invalid Form W-4, don’t use it for withholding; tell the employee and ask for another. If none valid comes back, withhold as before when you hold an earlier valid form; otherwise withhold as for Single or Married filing separately in Step 1(c) with no entries in Steps 2 to 4 of the 2026 form, except for an employee paid wages in 2019 who never submitted a valid Form W-4, who is still treated as single with zero allowances on a 2019 Form W-4 (S09.01, p. 29).
- Employers needn’t tell employees who claim exemption from withholding on Form W-4 about the EIC (S10, p. 31).

### Where it is used
- What’s New — says employers must use an employee’s updated Form W-4, if submitted, with the Pub. 15-T procedures for the qualified tips and qualified overtime deductions (p. 2)
- Hiring New Employees — says to ask each new employee to complete the 2026 Form W-4, and that many states accept a copy of Form W-4 with employer information added for new hire reporting (p. 7)
- Federal Income Tax Withholding — says withholding is according to the employee’s Form W-4, and lists asking for, withholding on and renewing Forms W-4 among the employer responsibilities (pp. 7–8)
- Recordkeeping — lists copies of employees’ and recipients’ withholding certificates, Forms W-4, W-4P, W-4R, W-4S and W-4V, among the records to keep (p. 9)
- Calendar — lists asking exempt employees for a new Form W-4 by February 15, the expiry of exemption Forms W-4 on February 16, and reminding employees to submit new Forms W-4 before December 1 (pp. 11–12)
- 5. Wages and Other Compensation — says an H-2A worker who asks for withholding, and whose employer agrees, must give the employer a completed Form W-4, and repeats that employers must use an employee’s updated Form W-4 for the qualified overtime deduction (pp. 19, 22)
- 6. Tips — says employers must use an employee’s updated Form W-4, if submitted, with the Pub. 15-T procedures for the qualified tips deduction (p. 23)
- 7. Supplemental Wages — says the 37% rate on supplemental wages over $1 million is withheld without regard to the employee’s Form W-4, and uses Form W-4 in its examples (p. 24)
- Federal Income Tax Withholding — covers the redesigned Form W-4, using Form W-4 to figure withholding, its effective date, exemption, nonresident aliens, IRS review and lock-in letters, substitute forms and invalid forms (pp. 25–29)
- 10. Required Notice to Employees About the Earned Income Credit (EIC) — says employers don’t have to notify employees who claim exemption from withholding on Form W-4 about the EIC (p. 31)

## Note
Section 17 of the publication covers the certifying requirements of federal agencies for federal income taxes withheld from U.S. Government employees working in, or federal pension recipients residing in, American Samoa, the CNMI and Guam. It has three parts, Special Certifying Requirements for Federal Agencies (with a part for each territory it names), "Federal Income Taxes" From American Samoa, the CNMI, or Guam, and Certification Procedures, which follow in the clusters below. The chapter's own text is its heading alone, so nothing further is summarised here.

## Parts of Federal Agency Certifying Requirements
- Special Certifying Requirements for Federal Agencies — the legal authorities requiring federal agencies to certify federal income taxes withheld, and the note that these requirements do not apply to federal agencies with employees working in Puerto Rico or the USVI (p. 54)
- Federal Income Taxes From American Samoa, the CNMI, or Guam — which federal income taxes the certification procedures cover, listed by the group of employees, pensioners or military personnel they were withheld from (p. 55)
- Certification Procedures — the quarterly certification to the IRS, the contents of the letter, the annual certification by an agency that certifies for other agencies, the data required for certain servicemembers, the quarterly due dates and the mailing address (pp. 55–56)

## Parts of Special Certifying Requirements for Federal Agencies
- American Samoa — the Code sections requiring the U.S. Government to cover over federal income taxes withheld for residents of American Samoa to its Treasury (p. 54)
- Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands — the cover over requirement for the CNMI, and the Caution on the 2006 agreement under which federal employers withhold CNMI income taxes for certain employees (pp. 54–55)
- Guam — the cover over requirement for Guam (p. 55)
- Puerto Rico — the note that the special certifying requirements do not apply to federal agencies with employees working in Puerto Rico, and the Caution on the 1988 agreement (p. 55)
- U.S. Virgin Islands — the note that the special certifying requirements do not apply to federal agencies with employees working in the USVI (p. 55)

text:
## Note
**What the publication covers (p. 12).** The publication sets out an employer’s tax responsibilities. It speaks to agricultural employers, and to employers whose principal place of business is in American Samoa, Guam, the CNMI, the USVI or Puerto Rico. It covers the requirements for withholding, depositing, reporting, paying and correcting employment taxes, and the forms that employers give to employees, that employees give to employers, and that employers send to the IRS and the SSA. “Income tax,” as used in the guide, means federal income tax only, and state or local rules must be checked with your state or local tax department. The term “United States” in the publication includes American Samoa, Guam, the CNMI, the USVI and Puerto Rico, unless otherwise noted.

**Trust fund taxes (p. 12).** Employees are not paid everything they earned, because the employer withholds taxes from their paychecks. The federal income tax and the employees’ share of social security and Medicare taxes withheld form part of the employees’ wages, and they go to the U.S. Treasury rather than to the employees. Employees trust the employer to get the withheld taxes to the U.S. Treasury through federal tax deposits, and that is why the withheld taxes are called trust fund taxes. The trust fund recovery penalty may apply if federal income, social security or Medicare tax that must be withheld is not withheld, or is not deposited or paid to the U.S. Treasury. The page refers to section 11 for more information.

**FUTA tax (p. 12).** The publication also gives employers (employers in the USVI and Puerto Rico included) a summary of their responsibilities under the Federal Unemployment Tax Act, known as FUTA tax. The page refers to section 14.

**Other publications on employment tax (p. 12).** More employment tax information is in Pubs. 15-A, 15-B and 15-T. Pub. 15-A supplements the basic employment tax information of this publication with specialized information. Pub. 15-B, Employer’s Tax Guide to Fringe Benefits, covers the employment tax treatment and valuation of various types of noncash compensation. Pub. 15-T has the federal income tax withholding tables and the instructions for using them.

**The employment taxes (p. 12).** Most employers must withhold (except FUTA), deposit, report and pay four employment taxes: income tax, social security tax, Medicare tax and FUTA tax. The requirements have exceptions, and the page refers to section 15 for guidance. The Instructions for Form CT-1 explain railroad retirement taxes.

**Comments and suggestions (pp. 12–13).** The IRS welcomes comments on the publication and suggestions for future editions. They can be sent through IRS.gov/FormComments, or by mail to Internal Revenue Service, Tax Forms and Publications, 1111 Constitution Ave. NW, IR-6526, Washington, DC 20224. The IRS can’t respond individually to each comment received, but it appreciates the feedback and will weigh the comments and suggestions in revising its tax forms, instructions and publications. Tax questions, tax returns and payments must not be sent to that address.

**Getting answers to your tax questions (p. 13).** For a tax question the publication doesn’t answer, check IRS.gov and How To Get Tax Help at the end of the publication.

**Getting and ordering tax forms, instructions and publications (p. 13).** IRS.gov/Forms has current and prior-year forms, instructions and publications to download. To order current ones, go to IRS.gov/OrderForms; for prior-year forms and instructions, call 800-829-3676. The IRS will process an order as soon as possible; requests already sent should not be resubmitted. Forms and publications can be had faster online.

**Federal government employers (p. 13).** The publication’s information, including the rules for making federal tax deposits, applies to federal agencies.

**State and local government employers (p. 13).** Payments for services in the employ of state and local governments are generally subject to federal income tax withholding but not FUTA tax. Under common-law rules, most elected and appointed public officials of a state or local government are employees; the page refers to chapter 3 of Pub. 963, Federal-State Reference Guide. With certain exceptions, wages are subject to social security and Medicare taxes as well, and the page refers to section 15 for the exceptions. For an election worker employed in another capacity with the same government entity, it refers to Revenue Ruling 2000-6 on page 512 of Internal Revenue Bulletin 2000-6. Information on reporting and social security coverage is available from your local IRS office. A question about coverage under a section 218 (Social Security Act) agreement goes to the appropriate state official; the National Conference of State Social Security Administrators website, NCSSSA.org, is where to find your State Social Security Administrator.

**Indian tribal governments (p. 13).** The page refers to Pub. 4268 for employment tax information for Indian tribal governments.

**Disregarded entities and qualified subchapter S subsidiaries (QSubs) (p. 13).** For employment tax purposes, eligible single-owner disregarded entities and QSubs count as separate entities. An eligible single-member entity reports and pays employment taxes on wages paid to its employees under the entity’s own name and EIN. The page refers to Regulations sections 1.1361-4(a)(7) and 301.7701-2(c)(2)(iv).

**Useful Items (p. 13).** Under this printed heading, “You may want to see,” the page lists these publications: 15-A, Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide; 15-B, Employer’s Tax Guide to Fringe Benefits; 15-T, Federal Income Tax Withholding Methods; 225, Farmer’s Tax Guide; 583, Starting a Business and Keeping Records; and 1635, Employer Identification Number: Understanding Your EIN.

**Related:** 11. Depositing Taxes — depositing federal employment taxes: when deposits are due, how to make them and the penalties for not depositing properly (p. 31)

## Note
**What the list is (pp. 10–11).** The Calendar lists important dates and responsibilities. Its dates are not adjusted for Saturdays, Sundays or legal holidays; Pub. 509, Tax Calendars (for use in 2026), makes that adjustment. For depositing taxes reported on Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 and Form 945, the page refers to section 11, and for depositing FUTA tax it refers to section 14. Due dates for forms required for health coverage reporting are not listed, and the page refers to Pub. 509 for those dates.

**Weekends and holidays (p. 11).** When a date for filing a return, furnishing a form or depositing taxes lands on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, the due date becomes the next business day. A “legal holiday” is any legal holiday in the District of Columbia. A statewide legal holiday pushes back a filing due date only when the IRS office where you must file is in that state, but it does not delay the due date of federal tax deposits; the page refers to Deposits Due on Business Days Only in section 11. For any filing due date, the “file” or “furnish” requirement is met if the envelope is properly addressed, carries sufficient postage and is postmarked by the USPS on or before the due date, or if an IRS-designated private delivery service (PDS) sends it on or before that date. The page refers to Private Delivery Services (PDSs) under Reminders, earlier.

**Fiscal-year taxpayers (p. 11).** The due dates listed apply whether you use a calendar year or a fiscal year.

**By January 31 (p. 11)**
- **File Form 941 or Form 944.** Form 941 for the fourth quarter of the previous calendar year is filed, and any undeposited income, social security and Medicare taxes are deposited. Those taxes may instead be paid with Form 941 if total tax liability for the quarter (Form 941, line 12) is under $2,500. Where the IRS has notified you in writing to file Form 944, you file that form for the previous calendar year in place of Form 941 and pay any undeposited taxes with it. Those taxes may be paid with Form 944 if total tax liability for the year (Form 944, line 9) is under $2,500. For further rules on paying with a return, the page refers to Payment with return in section 11. If you timely deposited all taxes when due, you may file by February 10.
- **File Form 943.** This is the agricultural employer’s return for the previous calendar year. Income, social security and Medicare taxes still undeposited are deposited, or may be paid with the form if total tax liability for the year (Form 943, line 13) is under $2,500. If you timely deposited all taxes when due, you may file by February 10.
- **File Form 945.** This form reports any nonpayroll federal income tax withheld. A filer that deposited all taxes when due may file by February 10. The page refers to Nonpayroll Federal Income Tax Withholding under Reminders, earlier.
- **File Form 940.** This form reports any FUTA tax. A filer that deposited all the FUTA tax when due may file by February 10. The page refers to section 14.
- **Furnish Forms 1099 and W-2.** Each employee gets a completed 2025 Form W-2, and payees of nonemployee compensation get a 2025 Form 1099-NEC. Most Forms 1099 must go to payees by January 31, although some may go by February 15, and the page refers to the Guide to Information Returns chart in the General Instructions for Certain Information Returns.
- **File Form W-2.** Copy A of all 2025 paper and electronic Forms W-2 goes to the SSA with Form W-3, Transmittal of Wage and Tax Statements. Forms W-2AS, W-2CM, W-2GU and W-2VI travel with Form W-3SS, and Forms 499R-2/W-2PR with Form W-3 (PR). On reporting Form W-2 information to the SSA electronically, the page points to the SSA’s Employer W-2 Filing Instructions & Information webpage at SSA.gov/employer. Filing through the SSA’s Form W-2 Online service means the SSA generates the Form W-3 data from the Form W-2 submission. Copy 1 of Forms W-2AS, W-2CM, W-2GU and W-2VI, plus Form W-3SS, is sent to your local tax department at the address on Form W-3SS; for more on Copy 1, contact that department. CNMI employers should ask their local tax department how to file Copy 1. For filing Forms 499R-2/W-2PR with the Puerto Rico Department of Treasury, the page gives Hacienda.pr.gov and 787-622-0123.
- **File Form 1099-NEC reporting nonemployee compensation.** Copy A of all 2025 paper and electronic Forms 1099-NEC is filed with the IRS, and paper forms go in with Form 1096, Annual Summary and Transmittal of U.S. Information Returns. For electronic filing of information returns with the IRS, the page refers to Pub. 1220.

**By February 15 (p. 11)**
- **Request a new Form W-4 from exempt employees.** Ask every employee who claimed exemption from federal income tax withholding last year for a new Form W-4.

**On February 16 (p. 11)**
- **Forms W-4 claiming exemption from withholding expire.** A Form W-4 that claimed exemption for the previous year has expired. Withholding must start for an employee who claimed exemption before but has not given you a new Form W-4 for the current year. Without a new Form W-4, withhold as though the employee had checked Single or Married filing separately in Step 1(c) of the 2026 Form W-4 and left Steps 2, 3 and 4 blank; the page refers to section 9. If an employee gives you a new Form W-4 claiming exemption after February 15, you may apply the exemption to future wages, but you do not refund taxes withheld while the exempt status was not in place.

**By February 28 (p. 12)**
- **File paper 2025 Forms 1099 and 1096.** Copy A of all paper 2025 Forms 1099 other than Forms 1099-NEC is filed with the IRS together with Form 1096. For returns filed electronically, the page refers to By March 31, later.
- **File paper Form 8027.** Form 8027, Employer’s Annual Information Return of Tip Income and Allocated Tips, is filed on paper with the IRS. The page refers to section 6, and to By March 31 for electronically filed returns.

**By March 31 (p. 12)**
- **File electronic 2025 Forms 1099 and 8027.** Electronic 2025 Forms 1099 other than Forms 1099-NEC go to the IRS, and so does electronic Form 8027. For filing information returns electronically with the IRS, the page refers to Pub. 1220 and to Pub. 1239, Specifications for Electronic Filing of Form 8027.

**By April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31 (p. 12)**
- **Deposit FUTA tax.** The quarter’s FUTA tax, including any amount carried over from other quarters, is deposited if it is over $500; at $500 or less it is carried over to the next quarter. The page refers to section 14.
- **File Form 941.** Form 941 is filed and any undeposited income, social security and Medicare taxes are deposited. These taxes may be paid with the form if total tax liability for the quarter (Form 941, line 12) is under $2,500. Where all taxes were timely deposited when due, filing may wait until May 10, August 10, November 10 or February 10, respectively. A business that has been notified to file Form 944, and did not ask for and receive written IRS notice to file quarterly Forms 941, does not file Form 941 for these quarters.

**Before December 1 (p. 12)**
- **New Forms W-4.** Employees should be reminded to send in a new Form W-4 when their filing status, other income, deductions or credits have changed, or will change, for the next year. They should also be reminded to do so if they made a mid-year change to their Form W-4 using the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator, available at IRS.gov/W4App. An employee who made a mid-year change may be underwithheld or overwithheld once the Form W-4 applies to the next full calendar year.

**Related:** Deposits Due on Business Days Only — when a deposit due on a day that is not a business day is timely, legal holidays and the 2026 list of them (p. 34)

text:
## Note
- Return transcripts for Forms 940, 941, 943, 944 and 945 for tax years 2023 and later are now available through your IRS business tax account (F03, p. 3).
- The COVID-19 related sick and family leave wage credit applies only to leave taken after March 31, 2020, and before October 1, 2021, and Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 can’t any longer be used to claim it (F04, p. 3).
- For tax periods beginning after 2023 the claim lines were removed from Form 944, Employer’s ANNUAL Federal Tax Return, and from Forms 941 and 943. An employer entitled to the credit for wages paid after 2023 for an earlier applicable leave period claims it on Form 944-X (or Form 941-X or Form 943-X) (F04, pp. 3–4).
- A Form 944-X filed before the Form 944 for the year may cause errors or processing delays (F04, p. 4).
- The amount from Form 8974, line 12 or, if applicable, line 17, is reported on Form 944 (or Form 941 or Form 943); for reducing your record of tax liability for the payroll tax credit, the page points to the line 13 instructions in the Instructions for Form 944 (F04, p. 4).
- Written notice from the IRS is required before you may file Form 944 (F04, p. 5).
- An employer that has filed quarterly Forms 941 and expects calendar-year employment taxes of $1,000 or less, and wants Form 944 instead, must contact the IRS in the first calendar quarter of the tax year and must receive written IRS notice before filing Form 944 in place of quarterly Forms 941 (F04, p. 5).
- Employers may also ask to file quarterly Forms 941 instead of an annual Form 944: an employer that got IRS notice to file Form 944 but prefers Forms 941 contacts the IRS in the first calendar quarter of the tax year, and may file quarterly only after receiving written IRS notice (F04, p. 5).
- For the methods and deadlines of either request, the page points to the Instructions for Form 944 (F04, p. 5).
- A mistake on a filed Form 944 is corrected with Form 944-X, which is filed on its own and separately from Form 944 (F04, p. 5).
- Unless you have filed a “final” Form 940 and a “final” Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944, you continue to file Form 944 for periods with no wages paid (the “seasonal” employer condition is for Form 941 only); the IRS encourages filing “zero wage” returns electronically (F04, p. 6).
- The Employer Responsibilities list includes filing Form 944 if required, with payment of the tax with the return when no deposit is required, among the items under Annually (see Calendar for due dates) (F09, p. 8).
- Payroll withholding (Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944) and nonpayroll withholding (Form 945) are deposited separately (F10, p. 8).
- Income tax withheld on distributions to participants from some nonqualified pension and deferred compensation plans goes on Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944, not on Form 945; distributions from such plans to a beneficiary or estate of a deceased employee aren't wages, and the income tax withheld on them goes on Form 945 (F10, pp. 8–9).
- The filing address for Form 944 generally turns on where your residence or principal place of business is located and on whether a payment goes with the return; tax-exempt organizations and government entities have separate addresses, found in the separate instructions for Form 944 (F14, pp. 9–10).
- For depositing taxes reported on Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 and Form 945, the Calendar refers to section 11 (F21, p. 10).
- Under the Calendar’s By January 31 date, an employer the IRS has notified in writing files Form 944 for the previous calendar year in place of Form 941, and pays any income, social security and Medicare taxes not yet deposited with it (F21, p. 11).
- Those taxes may be paid with Form 944 when the year’s total tax liability (Form 944, line 9) is under $2,500; for further rules on paying with the return, the page points to Payment with return in section 11 (F21, p. 11).
- A business notified to file Form 944 that did not ask for, and receive, written IRS notice to file quarterly Forms 941 does not file Form 941 for the quarterly dates listed (F21, p. 12).
- If an EIN you used on Form 944 (or Form 941 or Form 943) differs from the EIN reported on Form W-3, the page refers to Box h—Other EIN used this year in the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 (S01, p. 13).
- Form 941 or Form 944 is filed to report withholding and employment taxes on tips (S06, p. 23).
- Tips and the collected and uncollected social security and Medicare taxes go on Form 944, lines 4b and 4c and, if applicable, 4d, and a negative adjustment for the uncollected taxes goes on Form 944, line 6 (S06, p. 23).
- The deposit schedule depends on the total tax liability reported on Form 944, line 9 (and on the other forms the page lists) during a lookback period (S11.01, p. 32).
- For a Form 944 filer in the current year or either of the 2 years before, the schedule comes from the taxes reported in the second preceding calendar year; for 2026 the lookback period for a Form 943 or Form 944 filer is calendar year 2024 (S11.01, p. 32).
- A Form 944 filer whose lookback taxes (Form 944, line 9) were $50,000 or less is a monthly schedule depositor for the calendar year, and one whose taxes were more than $50,000 is a semiweekly schedule depositor (S11.01.01, p. 33; S11.01.02, p. 33).
- Monthly schedule depositors shouldn’t file Form 944 monthly (S11.01.01, p. 33).
- For Form 944 filers, liability from before the business began or was acquired counts as zero in the lookback period, so a new filer is a monthly schedule depositor in its first and second calendar years; however, the page points to the $100,000 Next-Day Deposit Rule (S11.01.01, p. 33).
- A semiweekly schedule depositor filing Form 944 completes Form 945-A, Annual Record of Federal Tax Liability, and submits it with the return (S11.01.02, p. 33).
- For annual Form 944 the return period is a calendar year (S11.01.02, p. 33).
- When you deposited too much, you choose on Form 944 for that year whether the overpayment is refunded or credited to your next return (S11.02, p. 36).
- The deposit penalty information is written about Form 941 but applies to Form 944 as well (S11.03, p. 36).
- An employer that filed Form 944 for the prior year and files Forms 941 for the current year owes no FTD penalty for a late January deposit of the current year’s employment taxes if the taxes are fully deposited by March 15 of the current year (S11.03, p. 36).
- To avoid an “averaged” FTD penalty, a monthly schedule depositor lists tax liabilities (not deposits) in the monthly entry spaces on Form 944, line 13, and a semiweekly schedule depositor lists them on Form 945-A; check that the total liability on Form 944, line 13, or Form 945-A, line M, equals the liability on Form 944, line 9 (S11.03, p. 37).
- With written notification that you qualify for the Form 944 program, you file Form 944 rather than Forms 941, even if you have no taxes to report (or have more than $1,000 to report), unless you filed a final return for the prior year (S12, p. 38).
- An employer notified to file Form 944 who prefers Forms 941 may ask, during the first calendar quarter of the tax year, to have the filing requirement changed back to Forms 941; the page points to the Instructions for Form 944 (S12, p. 38).
- Your 2025 Form 944 is due by February 2, 2026, or by February 10, 2026 if timely deposits fully paid the year’s taxes (S12, p. 38).
- An employer required to file Forms 941 that expects calendar-year employment taxes of $1,000 or less must contact the IRS in the first calendar quarter of the tax year to ask to file Form 944, and needs written IRS notice before filing it (S12, p. 38).
- Seasonal employers, household employers and agricultural employers are exceptions to the filing requirements for Form 941 and Form 944; an employer that files Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 for business employees may add the taxes of household employees to that return (S12, p. 38).
- Railroad employers report RRTA taxes on Form CT-1, and report federal income taxes withheld from their employees’ wages on Form 941 or Form 944 (S12, p. 38).
- Form 944 can be filed through the IRS e-file program, and reporting agents filing it for groups of taxpayers can file electronically (S12, p. 38).
- An employer with multiple locations or divisions files only one Form 944 per year (S12, p. 39).
- Name and EIN on Form 944 should read exactly as on earlier returns, and the Instructions for Form 944 explain how to prepare the form (S12, p. 39).
- A business that closes files a final return for the last year in which wages are paid (S12, p. 39).
- A late Form 944 for a previous year is filed on a copy of the form (with separate instructions) with a revision date showing that year; the page gives IRS.gov/Form944 for prior year forms (S12, p. 39).
- Social security and Medicare wages and taxes are reported separately on Forms W-2 and W-3 and on Forms 941, 943 or 944, and Form W-3 is reconciled with the annual Form 944 (S12, p. 40).
- Only taxes and withholding that appear on Form W-2 belong on Forms 941, 943 or 944 (S12, p. 40).
- Where Additional Medicare Tax was withheld, the Medicare tax on Form 944, line 4c, column 2, will not be double the Medicare tax withheld in box 6 of Form W-3, because that tax falls on the employee alone (S12, p. 40).
- Certain social security and Medicare amounts reported on Form 944, lines 4a–4d, column 2, have to be adjusted to reach the correct tax liability, and current period adjustments are reported on Form 944, line 6 (S13, p. 40).
- Fractions-of-cents adjustments go on Form 944, line 6, and an employer paying with Form 944 rather than depositing, because the year’s total taxes are under $2,500, may also report one (S13.01, pp. 40–41).
- Under the adjustment of tax on third-party sick pay, the employer share and the employee share of social security and Medicare taxes on sick pay are reported on Form 944, lines 4a and 4c; the Additional Medicare Tax goes on line 4d when the employer’s and third-party payer’s combined wages for an employee exceed $200,000 for the calendar year; and the taxes a third-party payer withheld on sick pay are a negative adjustment on line 6 (S13.01, p. 41).
- If, by the 10th of the month after an employee’s tip report was received, the employer lacks the employee funds to withhold the employee’s social security and Medicare share, it no longer has to collect it. The entire amount of those tips still goes on Form 944, lines 4b and 4c; the Additional Medicare Tax goes on line 4d if the employee’s wages and tips exceed $200,000 for the calendar year; and the total uncollected employee share is a negative adjustment on line 6 (S13.01, p. 41).
- For group-term life insurance premiums over $50,000 paid for a former employee, the former employee pays the employee share of the taxes with their own return and the employer does not collect it, yet all social security and Medicare taxes for the coverage go on Form 944, lines 4a and 4c; if the premium amount combined with other wages exceeds $200,000 for the calendar year, the Additional Medicare Tax goes on line 4d, and the employee share is backed out as a negative adjustment on line 6 (S13.01, p. 41).
- The supporting statement for these adjustments is not attached to Form 944 (S13.01, p. 41).
- For current period adjustments you make no change to your record of federal tax liability on Form 944, line 13, or Form 945-A (S13.01, p. 41).
- An error found on a filed Form 944 is corrected on a separate Form 944-X for each Form 944 corrected, and Form 944-X is filed on its own, not with Form 944 (S13.02, p. 42).
- Treasury Decision 9405 changed how interest-free adjustments to employment taxes reported on Form 944 are made and how a refund claim is filed (S13.02, p. 42).
- Income tax withheld in a prior calendar year can’t be adjusted unless the adjustment corrects an administrative error or section 3509 applies; an administrative error is an amount entered on Form 941, 943 or 944 that differs from the amount actually withheld (S13.02, p. 42).
- Where you did not repay or reimburse the employee, you report and pay the excess when you file the Form 944 for the year in which too much tax was withheld (S13.02, p. 43).
- FUTA tax for household employees need not be deposited unless their wages are reported on Form 941, 943 or 944; where they weren’t reported there, FUTA tax for them goes on Schedule H (Form 1040) (S14, pp. 44–45).
- A footnote to the section’s table says wages for services not considered farmwork are reported on Forms 941 or Form 944, and that other exemptions may apply (S15, p. 46).
- Return transcripts for Form 944 for tax years 2023 and later can be accessed through your IRS business tax account (B04, p. 57).

text:
## Note
The labels monthly schedule depositor and semiweekly schedule depositor say nothing about how often a business pays its employees or even how often it must deposit. They name the set of deposit rules to follow when an employment tax liability arises. Those rules look at the dates wages are paid (the cash basis), not at when liabilities accrue for accounting purposes.

**Monthly schedule example.** Spruce Co., a monthly schedule depositor with seasonal employees, paid wages every Friday in March and none in April. Under the monthly schedule it must deposit the combined liabilities for the March paydays by April 15. It has no deposit requirement for April (which would be due by May 15), since it paid no wages and so had no tax liability for April.

**Semiweekly schedule example.** Green, Inc., a semiweekly schedule depositor, pays wages once a month, on the last Friday. It deposits only once a month, since it has wages only once a month, but the deposit follows the semiweekly schedule: the liability for the Friday, May 29, 2026 payday must be deposited by Wednesday, June 3, 2026. Under that schedule, liabilities for wages paid Wednesday through Friday are deposited by the following Wednesday.

**Related:** $100,000 Next-Day Deposit Rule — the deposit due by the next business day when $100,000 or more in taxes accumulates on any day of a deposit period (p. 34)

text:
## Note
Section 11 of the publication covers depositing federal employment taxes: when deposits are due, how to make them and the penalties for not depositing properly. The chapter's own opening text, summarised below, sets the general deposit rule, the cases where a payment may go with a return in place of a deposit, and the separate-deposit requirements; its parts follow in the clusters.

**General rule (p. 31).** Generally, withheld federal income tax and both the employer's and the employee's social security and Medicare taxes have to be deposited. Every federal tax deposit must be made by EFT, and the electronic deposit requirements are covered later in the section, under How To Deposit.

**Payment with return (p. 31).** A payment may go with a timely filed Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 or Form 945 in place of a deposit, with no penalty, in any of these cases:
- You are a monthly schedule depositor (a term defined later) and your payment follows the accuracy of deposits rule, discussed later in the section; such a payment may be $2,500 or more.
- On Form 941, the total tax liability (line 12) for the current quarter or for the prior quarter is less than $2,500, and no $100,000 next-day deposit obligation arose during the current quarter. If you are unsure that the current quarter's liability will be under $2,500 (and the prior quarter's liability was not under $2,500), the publication advises depositing under the semiweekly or monthly rules, to avoid an FTD penalty.
- On Form 943, the total tax liability for the year (line 13) is less than $2,500. If you are unsure that you will report under $2,500, the publication advises depositing under the section's rules, to avoid an FTD penalty.
- On Form 944, the total tax liability for the year (line 9) is less than $2,500; or it is $2,500 or more, you have already deposited the taxes owed for the first three quarters, the net tax for the fourth quarter is less than $2,500, and you pay that fourth-quarter tax in full with a timely filed return.
- On Form 945, the total tax liability for the year (line 3) is less than $2,500. If you are unsure that you will report under $2,500, the publication advises depositing under the section's rules, to avoid an FTD penalty.

**Nonpayroll (Form 945) tax liabilities (pp. 31–32).** Nonpayroll income tax withholding is deposited separately from payroll withholding, so liabilities for Form 945 are not combined with those for Form 941 (or Form 943 or Form 944) in one deposit. Generally, the nonpayroll deposit rules match the ones described next in the publication, except that the return period is a year, not a quarter. When the year's total tax reported on Form 945 is less than $2,500, no deposits are required during the year; the separate Instructions for Form 945 give more information.

**Employers of both farm and nonfarm workers (p. 32).** Employment taxes for farmworkers (Form 943 taxes) and for nonfarm workers (Form 941/944 taxes) must be treated separately. They are not combined when any of the deposit schedule rules is applied, and when a deposit is due each group is deposited on its own. For example, a monthly schedule depositor for both groups with an end-of-April liability of $1,500 reportable on Form 941/944 and $1,200 reportable on Form 943 deposits both amounts by May 15, in two transactions: one for the $1,500 and one for the $1,200.

## When To Deposit
- When To Deposit — the two deposit schedules, monthly and semiweekly, the lookback period that decides which one applies, and the term deposit period (p. 32)

## Parts of When To Deposit
- Monthly Deposit Schedule — who is a monthly schedule depositor, deposits by the 15th of the following month, and how new employers are treated (p. 33)
- Semiweekly Deposit Schedule — who is a semiweekly schedule depositor, the deposit days for each payday, and deposit periods that span two quarters or two return periods (p. 33)
- Example of Monthly and Semiweekly Schedules — examples of Rose Co. (Form 941 taxes) and Red Co. (Form 943 taxes) and their deposit schedules (pp. 33–34)
- Deposits Due on Business Days Only — deposits due on a day that is not a business day, legal holidays and the 2026 list of them (p. 34)
- Application of Monthly and Semiweekly Schedules — what the terms monthly and semiweekly schedule depositor mean, with an example of each (p. 34)
- $100,000 Next-Day Deposit Rule — the deposit due by the next business day once $100,000 or more in taxes accumulates, with examples (pp. 34–35)
- Accuracy of Deposits Rule — the 100% deposit requirement, when a shortfall draws no penalty, and the makeup dates (p. 35)

## How To Deposit and Deposit Penalties
- How To Deposit — the EFT requirement, ways to make electronic deposits, same-day payment and wire options, and claiming credit for overpayments (pp. 35–36)
- Deposit Penalties — penalty rates, reasonable cause and waivers, the averaged FTD penalty, the trust fund recovery penalty, separate accounting and criminal prosecution (pp. 36–37)

## Note
Code section 7654 and 48 U.S.C. section 1421(h) require the U.S. Government to cover over federal income taxes to the Treasury of Guam. These are the taxes withheld on payments to military and civilian employees and to pensioners who are residents of Guam (p. 55). The federal government transfers the federal income taxes withheld or collected from its employees and pensioners who are residents of Guam to the Guam Treasury at least once a year (p. 55).

To let the federal government cover over these taxes as the law requires, federal agencies must certify the federal income taxes withheld or collected from their employees, following the procedures under Certification Procedures, later in the section (p. 55).

**Related:** Certification Procedures — the procedures federal agencies follow to certify to the IRS the federal income taxes paid to and deposited into the U.S. Treasury (p. 55)
