text:
## Note
Section 12 covers who files Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 and Form 945, when each is due, how they may be filed electronically, the penalties for filing or paying late, and how to reconcile Forms W-2 and W-3 with the quarterly and annual returns.

**Form 941 (p. 38).** An employer who paid wages subject to federal income tax withholding (including withholding on sick pay and supplemental unemployment benefits) or social security and Medicare taxes must file Form 941 each quarter, even with no taxes to report. The exceptions are a final return, an IRS notification that the employer may file Form 944, and the exceptions discussed later in the section. An employer required to file Forms 941 who expects employment taxes for the calendar year to be $1,000 or less, and would like to file Form 944 instead, must contact the IRS during the first calendar quarter of the tax year to ask for it. Form 944 may be filed in place of Forms 941 only after written notice from the IRS; the Instructions for Form 944 give the methods and deadlines for a request. Form 941 is due by the last day of the month after the quarter ends. An employer who made timely deposits in full payment of the quarter's taxes may file by the 10th day of the 2nd month after the quarter ends. The page points to the Calendar, earlier in the publication.

**Form 943 (p. 38).** Form 943 must be filed for each calendar year, starting with the first year in which you pay $2,500 or more for farmwork or employ a farmworker who meets the $150 test explained under Social Security and Medicare Taxes in section 9. These wages are not reported on Form 941, Form 944 or Form 945. The 2025 Form 943 is due February 2, 2026; with timely deposits in full payment of the year's taxes, it may be filed by February 10, 2026.

**Form 944 (p. 38).** An employer who receives written notification that it qualifies for the Form 944 program must file Form 944 instead of Forms 941. It must be filed even with no taxes to report (or with taxes over $1,000 to report), unless a final return was filed for the prior year. An employer notified to file Form 944 who prefers Forms 941 can request, during the first calendar quarter of the tax year, to have its filing requirement changed to Forms 941; the Instructions for Form 944 give the methods and deadlines. The 2025 Form 944 is due February 2, 2026; with timely deposits in full payment of the year's taxes, it may be filed by February 10, 2026.

**Form 945 (p. 38).** An employer who withholds, or is required to withhold, federal income tax (including backup withholding) from nonpayroll payments must file Form 945. All federal income tax withholding from nonpayroll payments reported on Forms 1099 or Form W-2G must go on Form 945 and not on another form such as Form 1040-ES. Withholding that must be reported on Form 1042 is not reported on Form 945. Form 945 need not be filed for years with no nonpayroll tax liability. The 2025 Form 945 is due February 2, 2026; with timely deposits in full payment of the year's taxes, it may be filed by February 10, 2026.

**Exceptions (p. 38).** These exceptions apply to the filing requirements for Form 941 and Form 944.
- Seasonal employers need not file Forms 941 for quarters with no tax liability because they paid no wages. To alert the IRS that no return will be filed for 1 or more quarters during the year, check the "Seasonal employer" box on Form 941, line 18, and check the box at the top of the form for the quarter reported. Generally, the IRS won't inquire about unfiled returns if at least one taxable return is filed each year, but the "Seasonal employer" box must be checked on every Form 941 filed; otherwise the IRS expects a return for each quarter.
- Household employers reporting social security and Medicare taxes and/or withheld income tax: an employer filing Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 for business employees may include the taxes for household employees on that return. Otherwise those taxes and the income tax withholding are reported on Schedule H (Form 1040). The page refers to Pub. 926.
- Agricultural employers report social security, Medicare and withheld income taxes on Form 943.

**Railroad employers (p. 38).** Employers that pay Railroad Retirement Tax Act (RRTA) taxes use Form CT-1 for the employment taxes the RRTA imposes. They use Form 941 or Form 944 for federal income taxes withheld from their employees' wages and other compensation.

**E-file (p. 38).** The IRS e-file program lets a taxpayer file Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 and Form 945 electronically. The page gives a web address and a telephone number for more information.

**Electronic filing by reporting agents (p. 38).** Reporting agents who file Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 or Form 945 for groups of taxpayers can file them electronically. The page refers to Pub. 3112 for details, to Revenue Procedure 2007-40 for information on electronic filing, and to section 16 for the different types of third-party payer arrangements.

**Electronic filing by CPEOs (pp. 38–39).** Except for the first quarter (Form 941 only) for which a CPEO is certified, CPEOs must file Form 941 electronically with Schedule R (Form 941) or, if applicable, Form 943 with Schedule R (Form 943). In certain circumstances the IRS may waive the electronic filing requirement. To ask for a waiver, the CPEO must send a written request through the IRS Online Registration System for Professional Employer Organizations at least 45 days before the due date of the return it cannot file electronically. The page refers to Revenue Procedure 2023-18.

**Penalties (p. 39).** For each whole or part month a return is not filed when required, the failure-to-file (FTF) penalty is 5% of the unpaid tax due with that return, generally up to a maximum of 25% of the tax due. For each whole or part month the tax is paid late, the failure-to-pay (FTP) penalty is 0.5% per month of the amount of tax, also up to a maximum of 25%. For individual filers only, the FTP penalty falls to 0.25% per month if an installment agreement is in effect, and only if the return was filed on or before its due date. If both penalties apply in a month, the FTF penalty is reduced by the amount of the FTP penalty. The penalties are not charged if there is reasonable cause for failing to file or pay, and a person who receives a penalty notice can explain why reasonable cause exists. Interest accrues from the due date of the tax on any unpaid balance, in addition to any penalties.

**Trust fund recovery penalty (p. 39).** A person may be personally liable for the trust fund recovery penalty if income, social security or Medicare tax that must be withheld is not withheld or is not paid. The page points to Trust fund recovery penalty in section 11.

**Third-party payers (p. 39).** Generally, using a third-party payer such as a PSP or reporting agent does not relieve an employer of responsibility for ensuring that returns are filed and taxes are paid or deposited correctly and on time. The page points to Certified professional employer organization (CPEO) in section 16 for an exception.

**One return per return period (p. 39).** Do not file more than one return per return period. An employer with multiple locations or divisions files only one Form 941 per quarter or one Form 944 per year. An agricultural employer files only one Form 943 per year. A payer of nonpayroll payments that withheld federal income tax or backup withholding files only one Form 945 per year. Filing more than one return may cause processing delays and may require correspondence with the IRS. For adjustments to previously filed returns, the page points to section 13.

**Reminders about filing (p. 39).**
- Don't report more than 1 calendar quarter on a Form 941.
- A needed Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 or Form 945 is available at IRS.gov/Forms; the page also points to Ordering Employer Tax Forms, Instructions, and Publications, earlier.
- Enter your name and EIN on the form exactly as they appeared on earlier returns.
- The Instructions for each of the four forms give information on preparing it.

**Final return (p. 39).** An employer who goes out of business must file a final return for the final period in which it pays wages: the last quarter, or the last year for Form 943, Form 944 or Form 945, where Form 945 looks to nonpayroll payments rather than wages. An employer who keeps paying wages or other compensation for periods after the business ends must file returns for those periods. The Instructions for each form give details on filing a final return. An employer required to file a final return must also furnish Forms W-2 to its employees and file Forms W-2 and W-3 with the SSA by the due date of the final return. An original or copy of Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 is not sent to the SSA. The page refers to the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3, and employers in Puerto Rico to the General Instructions for Forms W-3 (PR) and W-3C (PR).

**Filing late returns for previous years (p. 39).** To file a delinquent return, get a copy of Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 or Form 945 (and its separate instructions) with a revision date that shows the year and, if applicable, the quarter being filed. Prior year and quarterly versions are available at the IRS.gov addresses the page gives for each form (select the link for "All form revisions"). The page also points to Ordering Employer Tax Forms, Instructions, and Publications, earlier, and gives a telephone number to call the IRS about late returns.

Table 3. Social Security and Medicare Tax Rates (for 3 Prior Years) (p. 39)

| Calendar year and tax | Wage base limit per employee | Tax rate on wages and tips |
|---|---|---|
| 2025—social security | $176,100 | 12.4% |
| 2025—Medicare | All wages | 2.9% |
| 2024—social security | $168,600 | 12.4% |
| 2024—Medicare | All wages | 2.9% |
| 2023—social security | $160,200 | 12.4%* |
| 2023—Medicare | All wages | 2.9% |
| * Qualified sick leave wages and qualified family leave wages for leave taken after March 31, 2020, and before April 1, 2021, aren’t subject to the employer share of social security tax; therefore, the tax rate on these wages is 6.2% (0.062). |  |  |

**Reconciling Forms W-2 and W-3 with Forms 941, Form 943, or Form 944 (pp. 39–40).** When Forms 941, 943 or 944 filed with the IRS differ from Forms W-2 and W-3 filed with the SSA, the IRS or the SSA may contact the employer to resolve the differences. The page lists these steps to help reduce them:
1. Report bonuses as wages and as social security and Medicare wages on Forms W-2 and on Forms 941, 943 or 944.
2. Report social security and Medicare wages and taxes separately on Forms W-2 and W-3 and on Forms 941, 943 or 944.
3. Put the employee share of social security taxes in the Form W-2 box for social security tax withheld (box 4) and not in social security wages; on Form 499R-2/W-2PR that tax goes in box 21.
4. Put the employee share of Medicare taxes in the Form W-2 box for Medicare tax withheld (box 6) and not in Medicare wages; on Form 499R-2/W-2PR that tax goes in box 23.
5. Make sure each employee's social security wages do not exceed the annual social security wage base limit ($184,500 for 2026).
6. Noncash wages not subject to social security or Medicare tax, covered earlier under Wages not paid in money in section 5, must not be reported as social security or Medicare wages.
7. When the EIN used on any Forms 941, 943 or 944 for the year is not the one on Form W-3, the other EIN goes in the Form W-3 box labelled "Other EIN used this year" (box h, or box f on Form W-3 (PR)).
8. Make sure the amounts on Form W-3 are the total of the amounts from Forms W-2.
9. Reconcile Form W-3 with the four quarterly Forms 941, the annual Form 943 or the annual Form 944 by comparing federal income tax withheld, social security and Medicare wages, and social security and Medicare taxes. Generally the taxes shown on Forms 941, 943 or 944, with current year adjustments, should be approximately twice the amounts on Form W-3, because those returns report both the employer and employee social security and Medicare taxes while Form W-3 reports only the employee taxes.

Backup withholding and withholding on nonpayroll payments, such as pensions, annuities and gambling winnings, are not reported on Forms 941, 943 or 944. Withholding on nonpayroll payments goes on Forms 1099 or Form W-2G, and the employer must report it on Form 945. Forms 941, 943 and 944 carry only the taxes and withholding that are reported on Form W-2.

Amounts on Forms W-2, W-3 and Forms 941, 943 or 944 may fail to match for valid reasons. For example, where Additional Medicare Tax was withheld from an employee's wages, the Medicare tax on Form 941 (line 5c, column 2), Form 943 (line 5) or Form 944 (line 4c, column 2) will not be twice the Medicare tax withheld in box 6 of Form W-3 (box 13 of Form W-3 (PR)), because Additional Medicare Tax is imposed only on the employee and has no employer share. The employer should make sure there are valid reasons for any mismatch and keep the reconciliation as a record of why amounts did not match, in case the IRS or the SSA inquires. The page points to the Instructions for Schedule D (Form 941) for explaining discrepancies caused by an acquisition, statutory merger or consolidation.

**Related:** 16. Third-Party Payer Arrangements — payroll service providers, reporting agents, agents with an approved Form 2678, payers designated under section 3504 and CPEOs (p. 53)

text:
## Note
- For payments made after calendar year 2025, the page raises to $2,000 the threshold for wage reporting on Forms W-2, Wage and Tax Statement, when no federal income, social security or Medicare tax was withheld; the threshold will be inflation-adjusted for each year after 2026, and the page points to the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 and for Certain Information Returns (F03, p. 2).
- In its items on qualified tips and qualified overtime compensation, the page says employers and other payers file information returns (Forms W-2, 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC are examples) with the SSA or IRS as applicable and furnish statements to the recipients, and that the IRS has given transition relief for the 2025 tax year reporting requirements (F03, p. 2).
- Unless the text says otherwise, “Form W-2” in the publication takes in Forms W-2AS, W-2CM, W-2GU and W-2VI as well as Form 499R-2/W-2PR (F04, p. 3).
- For CNMI federal employers, the page points to IRS.gov/5517Agreements for more information, details on completing Form W-2 included (F04, p. 6).
- For electronic filing of Forms W-2 (the territorial forms included), the page directs you to SSA.gov/employer; you may be required to file Forms W-2 electronically, and the page points to the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 (F05, p. 6).
- You must file Forms W-2 to report wages paid to employees (F08, p. 7).
- Wages and other pay to employees go on Form W-2 rather than on Forms 1099, as a rule, and the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 cover filing details and electronic filing (F08, p. 7).
- The IRS runs the TSO to answer questions about reporting on Forms W-2, W-3 and 1099 and on other information returns (F08, p. 7).
- The Employer Responsibilities list, under Annually (see Calendar for due dates), includes furnishing each employee a Form W-2, filing Copy A of Forms W-2 with the SSA along with Form W-3, and reconciling Forms 941 (or 943 or 944) with Forms W-2 and W-3 (F09, p. 8).
- Some nonqualified pension plan and deferred compensation plan distributions (those of section 457(b) plans of tax-exempt organizations included) count as wages and are reported on Form W-2 (F10, p. 8).
- Your records should include employee copies of Forms W-2 and W-2c that were returned to you undeliverable (F11, p. 9).
- In place of ordering paper Forms W-2 and W-3, the page suggests the SSA’s free e-file service, where you can create Forms W-2 online by typing wage information into fill-in fields and submit them to the SSA (F19, p. 10).
- That service also lets you print finished copies of Forms W-2 for state or local governments, for your employees and for your own records (F19, p. 10).
- Under the Calendar’s Furnish Forms 1099 and W-2 item, each employee receives a completed 2025 Form W-2 (F21, p. 11).
- Under the Calendar’s File Form W-2 item, Copy A of all 2025 Forms W-2, paper or electronic, goes to the SSA with Form W-3, Transmittal of Wage and Tax Statements (F21, p. 11).
- Forms W-2AS, W-2CM, W-2GU and W-2VI go with Form W-3SS, and Forms 499R-2/W-2PR go with Form W-3 (PR); for filing electronically with the SSA the page names the SSA’s Employer W-2 Filing Instructions & Information webpage at SSA.gov/employer, and notes that the SSA’s Form W-2 Online service generates the Form W-3 data (F21, p. 11).
- Copy 1 of Forms W-2AS, W-2CM, W-2GU and W-2VI, with Form W-3SS, goes to your local tax department at the address printed on Form W-3SS; CNMI employers should ask their local tax department how to file Copy 1 (F21, p. 11).
- For filing Forms 499R-2/W-2PR with the Puerto Rico Department of Treasury, the page gives Hacienda.pr.gov and 787-622-0123 (F21, p. 11).
- H-2A workers are not statutory employees, so box 13 (Statutory employee) of Form W-2 is not checked for them (S02, p. 15).
- Employers have to obtain each employee’s name and SSN and enter them on Form W-2, resident and nonresident alien employees included (S04, p. 17).
- A wrong employee name or SSN on Form W-2 can bring a penalty unless there is reasonable cause (S04, p. 17).
- For a paper Form W-2 where the employee has applied for an SSN but has none yet, “Applied For” is entered; for an electronic filing, the SSN field gets all zeros (S04, p. 17).
- Once the employee receives the SSN, Copy A of Form W-2c is filed with the SSA to show it, Copies B, C and 2 of Form W-2c go to the employee, and the employee should be advised to correct the SSN on the original Form W-2 (S04, p. 17).
- After the SSA issues an updated card following a name change, or a new card with a different SSN following a change in alien work status, a Form W-2c corrects the name and SSN on the most recently filed Form W-2; earlier years need no correction if the previous name and number were used for them (S04, p. 17).
- An ITIN is not used in place of an SSN on Form W-2 (S04, p. 18).
- Noncash wages paid to farmworkers go in box 1 of Form W-2 (box 7 of Form 499R-2/W-2PR) with the cash wages, and stay out of box 3 or 5 (box 20 or 22 of Form 499R-2/W-2PR) unless the transaction is in substance a cash payment (S05, p. 18).
- Pay of $600 or more in 2025 ($2,000 or more in 2026) to foreign agricultural workers on H-2A visas is reported in box 1 of Form W-2 (box 7 of Form 499R-2/W-2PR), not as social security wages (box 3) or Medicare wages (box 5), since agricultural labor under that visa isn’t subject to social security and Medicare taxes (S05, p. 19).
- For H-2A workers, box 13 (Statutory employee) is left unchecked and any federal income tax withheld goes in box 2 of Form W-2; these rules hold when the worker gives the employer a TIN (S05, p. 19).
- When a per diem or allowance exceeds the substantiated amount, the excess is wages; the substantiated (nontaxable) amount is shown in box 12 of Form W-2 with code “L,” and employers in Puerto Rico use box 12 without a code (S05, p. 20).
- Differential wage payments are wages for income tax withholding but not for social security, Medicare or FUTA tax, and they are reported in box 1 of Form W-2 (box 7 of Form 499R-2/W-2PR) (S05, p. 21).
- Where you deposited the right amount but withheld less from the employee, you may recover the social security, Medicare or income tax deposited on their behalf and included on their Form W-2, though the income tax must be recovered before April 1 of the following year (S05, p. 22).
- Identity protection services an employer provides, including those given before a data breach, are outside the employee’s gross income and need not be reported on an information return such as Form W-2 (S05, p. 22).
- Tips, and the collected and uncollected social security and Medicare taxes on them, are reported on Form W-2 (Form 499R-2/W-2PR for employers in Puerto Rico) (S06, p. 23).
- Uncollected social security tax goes in box 12 of Form W-2 with code “A” and uncollected Medicare tax with code “B”; on Form 499R-2/W-2PR they go in boxes 25 and 26 (S06, p. 23).
- Uncollected Additional Medicare Tax is kept out of box 12 of Form W-2 (S06, p. 23).
- For more on reporting tips, the page points to section 13 and to the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 (S06, p. 23).
- The amount added to a nonresident alien employee’s wages only for figuring income tax withholding appears in no box of the employee’s Form W-2 and does not raise the employee’s income tax liability (S09.01, p. 27).
- The IRS relies on information reported on Form W-2 to spot employees with withholding compliance problems (S09.01, p. 28).
- A household or agricultural employer that pays the employee’s share of social security and Medicare taxes instead of withholding it adds that amount to box 1 of the employee’s Form W-2 (box 7 of Form 499R-2/W-2PR), and leaves it out of social security and Medicare wages and out of boxes 3 and 5 (S09.02, p. 30).
- In the example, Gavrielle puts $1,076.50 in box 1 of Dan’s Form W-2 ($1,000 of wages plus $76.50 of taxes paid for Dan) and $1,000.00 in boxes 3 and 5 (S09.02, p. 30).
- You meet the EIC notification requirement by issuing a Form W-2 that has the EIC notice printed on the back of Copy B, or a substitute Form W-2 containing the same statement (S10, p. 31).
- Where a substitute Form W-2 was given on time but lacks the required statement, the employee must be notified within 1 week of the date the substitute was given (S10, p. 31).
- Where Form W-2 is required but wasn’t given on time, Notice 797 or your own written statement goes to the employee by the date Form W-2 is required to be given; where no Form W-2 is required, the employee is notified by February 9, 2026 (S10, p. 31).
- In addition to civil penalties, you may face criminal prosecution for willfully furnishing false or fraudulent Forms W-2 to employees or failing to furnish Forms W-2, among other acts the page lists (S11.03, p. 37).
- An employer that must file a final return also furnishes Forms W-2 to its employees and files Forms W-2 and W-3 with the SSA, by the final return’s due date (S12, p. 39).
- Discrepancies between Forms 941, 943 or 944 filed with the IRS and Forms W-2 and W-3 filed with the SSA may lead the IRS or the SSA to contact you (S12, p. 39).
- To reduce discrepancies, bonuses are reported as wages and as social security and Medicare wages on Forms W-2 and on Forms 941, 943 or 944 (S12, p. 40).
- Social security and Medicare wages and taxes are reported separately on Forms W-2 and W-3 and on Forms 941, 943 or 944 (S12, p. 40).
- The employee share of social security tax belongs in the Form W-2 box for social security tax withheld (box 4), not in social security wages, and the employee share of Medicare tax in the box for Medicare tax withheld (box 6), not in Medicare wages (S12, p. 40).
- On Form 499R-2/W-2PR, social security tax withheld is in box 21 and Medicare tax withheld in box 23 (S12, p. 40).
- No employee’s social security wages may exceed the annual social security wage base limit ($184,500 for 2026) (S12, p. 40).
- Noncash wages that are not subject to social security or Medicare tax are not reported as social security or Medicare wages (S12, p. 40).
- The amounts on Form W-3 must total the amounts from the Forms W-2 (S12, p. 40).
- Only taxes and withholding that appear on Form W-2 belong on Forms 941, 943 or 944, while nonpayroll withholding on Forms 1099 or Form W-2G goes on Form 945 (S12, p. 40).
- Amounts on Forms W-2, W-3 and Forms 941, 943 or 944 can differ for valid reasons (S12, p. 40).
- For how Form W-2 reports the employee’s share of social security and Medicare taxes left uncollected on tips and on group-term life insurance, the page points to the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 (S13.01, p. 41).
- An income tax withholding error can be adjusted only if found in the same calendar year the wages were paid, since the employee takes the amount on Form W-2 (or Form W-2c) as a credit on the income tax return (S13.02, p. 42).
- An administrative error adjustment brings the amount on Form 941, 943 or 944 into line with what was actually withheld and shown on the employees’ Forms W-2 (S13.02, p. 42).
- Under the heading Correcting filed Forms W-2 and W-3, the page says a changed wage total for a previous year, which leads to adjusting wages and social security and Medicare taxes, also means filing Form W-2c and Form W-3c with the SSA; online sessions may include up to 25 Forms W-2c per Form W-3c, with no limit on sessions (S13.02, p. 43).
- In the section’s table, the row on wages paid to a beneficiary or estate in the same calendar year as the worker’s death points to the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 for details (S15, p. 47).
- In the table’s row on election workers for state and local governments, a note says Form W-2 is to be filed on payments of $600 or more in 2025 ($2,000 or more in 2026), whether or not social security or Medicare tax was withheld (S15, p. 49).
- A payroll service provider (PSP) may prepare Forms W-2, and so may an agent authorized under section 3504 (S16, p. 53).
- Where an employer and a section 3504 authorized agent (or CPEO or other third-party payer) both paid wages to an employee in a quarter, each should issue Forms W-2 for the wages it paid that employee during the year (S16, p. 54).
- For CNMI and Puerto Rico federal employers under the 5517 agreement, the page points to IRS.gov/5517Agreements for more information, details on completing Form W-2 included (B01.02, p. 55; B01.04, p. 55).
- The SSA offers an online service at SSA.gov/employer, described as fast, free and secure, with W-2 filing options for CPAs, accountants, enrolled agents and individuals who process Form W-2 and Form W-2c (B04, p. 57).

## Sources & References
- Source: Publication 15 (2026) — forms.csv W-2

### Where it is used
- What’s New — gives the $2,000 wage reporting threshold for Forms W-2, and says employers and other payers file information returns such as Forms W-2 for qualified tips and qualified overtime (p. 2)
- Reminders — says that “Form W-2” takes in Forms W-2AS, W-2CM, W-2GU, W-2VI and Form 499R-2/W-2PR unless noted otherwise, and refers to IRS.gov/5517Agreements for details on completing Form W-2 for CNMI federal employers (pp. 3, 6)
- Electronic Filing and Payment — says Forms W-2 are filed electronically at SSA.gov/employer, that electronic filing may be required, and refers to the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 (p. 6)
- Information Returns — says you must file Forms W-2 to report wages paid to employees, and that wages aren’t reported on Forms 1099 (p. 7)
- Federal Income Tax Withholding — lists furnishing Form W-2, filing Copy A with Form W-3 and reconciling Forms 941, 943 and 944 with Forms W-2 and W-3 among the employer responsibilities (p. 8)
- Nonpayroll Federal Income Tax Withholding — says distributions from some nonqualified pension plans and deferred compensation plans are treated as wages and reported on Form W-2 (p. 8)
- Recordkeeping — lists employee copies of Forms W-2 and W-2c returned as undeliverable among the records to keep (p. 9)

text:
## Note
**Spouses as partners (p. 15).** When spouses jointly own and run a business and split its profits and losses, they may be partners in a partnership. This can be so with or without a formal partnership agreement. The page points to Pub. 541 for more details. The partnership counts as the employer of any employees and is liable for employment taxes due on the wages it pays them.

**Exception—qualified joint venture (pp. 15–16).** For tax years beginning after 2006, the Small Business and Work Opportunity Tax Act of 2007 (P.L. 110-28) lets a "qualified joint venture" elect out of partnership treatment for federal tax purposes; its only members must be spouses filing a joint income tax return. A qualified joint venture carries on a trade or business in which:
- Spouses who file a joint income tax return are the venture's only members.
- Each spouse materially participates in the trade or business (the page refers to Material participation in the instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040), line G); owning property jointly is not enough.
- Each spouse elects not to be treated as a partnership.
- The two spouses co-own the business, and it is not held in the name of a state law entity such as a partnership or limited liability company (LLC).

To make the election, every item of income, gain, loss, deduction and credit must be split between the spouses according to each one's interest in the venture, and each spouse reports their share as a sole proprietor on a separate Schedule C (Form 1040) or Schedule F (Form 1040) (p. 16). Each spouse must in addition file a separate Schedule SE (Form 1040) to pay self-employment taxes, as applicable. For American Samoa, Guam, the CNMI, the USVI and Puerto Rico, the page refers to the Instructions for Form 1040-SS.

Spouses under the qualified joint venture rules are treated as sole proprietors for federal tax purposes, and generally need no EIN. When the venture owes employment taxes, either spouse may report and pay them, on the wages paid to the employees, under the EIN of that spouse's sole proprietorship. Generally, filing as a qualified joint venture will not raise the spouses' total tax on their joint income tax return. It does give each spouse credit for the social security earnings that retirement benefits are based on, and for Medicare coverage, without a partnership return being filed (p. 16).

If your spouse is your employee rather than your partner, the page refers to One spouse employed by another in section 3. For more on qualified joint ventures it points to IRS.gov/QJV (p. 16).

**Exception—community income (p. 16).** Spouses who wholly own an unincorporated business as community property under the community property laws of a state, foreign country or U.S. territory can treat it as a sole proprietorship (of the spouse who carried on the business), or as a partnership. They may still elect to be taxed as a qualified joint venture rather than as a partnership.

**Related:** 3. Family Employees — payments for the services of a child employed by parents, one spouse employed by another and a parent employed by their child (p. 16)

## Note
**Eligibility for employment (p. 7).** The legal eligibility of every new employee to work in the United States (American Samoa, Guam, the CNMI, the USVI and Puerto Rico included) must be verified. That involves completing U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) Form I-9, Employment Eligibility Verification, which is available at USCIS.gov/Forms. For more information the page points to USCIS.gov/I-9-Central, or to 800-375-5283 or 800-767-1833 (TTY).

**Verifying a name and an SSN (p. 7).** The Social Security Number Verification Service (SSNVS), at SSA.gov/employer/ssnv.htm, may be used to check that an employee name matches a social security number (SSN). A person can hold a valid SSN without being authorized to work in the United States. E-Verify, at E-Verify.gov, may be used to confirm the employment eligibility of newly hired employees.

**New hire reporting (p. 7).** All 50 states and most of the territories have a new hire registry, and each new employee must be reported to a designated state new hire registry. A new employee is someone not previously employed by you, or previously employed by you but separated from that employment for at least 60 consecutive days. Many states accept a copy of Form W-4 with employer information added, and the page points to acf.gov/css/employers for more. Employers in American Samoa, Guam, the CNMI, the USVI and Puerto Rico should contact their local government about their new hire registry.

**W-4 request (p. 7).** Ask each new employee to complete the 2026 Form W-4. The page refers to section 9.

**Name and SSN (p. 7).** Record each new employee’s name and SSN as shown on the social security card, if it is available. Where the employee can’t provide the card, you should verify the SSN and the employee’s eligibility for employment as discussed under Verification of SSNs in section 4. An employee with no social security card should apply for one, and the page refers to section 4.

**Related:** 4. Employee’s Social Security Number (SSN) — the requirement to obtain each employee’s name and SSN and to put them on Form W-2 (p. 17)

text:
## Note
**Payroll period (p. 25).** A payroll period is a period of service for which you usually pay wages. With a regular payroll period, income tax is withheld for that period even when the employee doesn't work all of it.

**No regular payroll period (p. 25).** Without a regular payroll period, withhold as though the wages were paid for a daily or miscellaneous payroll period. Count the days (Sundays and holidays included) in the period that the wage payment covers. When the wages are unrelated to a specific length of time (commissions paid on completion of a sale, for example), count back the number of days from the payment period to the latest of:
- The last wage payment made during the same calendar year.
- The date employment began, if during the same calendar year.
- January 1 of the same year.

**Employee paid for a period of less than 1 week (p. 25).** Suppose you pay an employee for less than 1 week, and the employee signs a statement under penalties of perjury saying that they are not working for any other employer during the same week for wages subject to withholding. Withholding is then figured on a weekly payroll period. If the employee later starts work for another employer for wages subject to withholding, the employee must tell you within 10 days, and withholding is then figured on the daily or miscellaneous period.

**Related:** Federal Income Tax Withholding — federal income tax withholding, starting with the redesigned Form W-4 (p. 25)

source.attribution: Internal Revenue Service, Publication 15 (2026), Catalog Number 10000W
source.title: Publication 15 (Circular E), Employer’s Tax Guide

text:
## Note
The requirement is to deposit the whole, 100%, of the tax liability on or before the deposit due date. No penalty is applied for depositing less than 100% provided both of these conditions are met:
- The shortfall is no more than the greater of $100 or 2% of the taxes otherwise required to be deposited.
- The shortfall is paid or deposited by the shortfall makeup date described below.

**Shortfall makeup date.**
1. Monthly schedule depositor: deposit the shortfall, or pay it with the return, by the due date of the return for the return period in which the shortfall occurred. The shortfall may be paid with the return even when the amount is $2,500 or more.
2. Semiweekly schedule depositor: the shortfall is deposited by the earlier of two dates. One (a) is the first Wednesday or Friday, whichever comes first, on or after the 15th day of the month following the month of the shortfall; the other (b) is the due date of the return for the return period of the tax liability.

**Example.** For a semiweekly schedule depositor with a deposit shortfall during April 2026, the makeup date is Friday, May 15, 2026. If instead the shortfall occurred on the required deposit due date of Wednesday, July 1, 2026, for the pay date of Friday, June 26, 2026, the return due date for that pay date, July 31, 2026, comes before the makeup date of Wednesday, August 19, 2026, so the shortfall must be deposited by July 31, 2026.

**Related:** How To Deposit — the requirement to deposit employment taxes by EFT and the ways to make electronic deposits (p. 35)

**Timely mailing as timely filing (p. 10).** Certain private delivery services (PDSs) designated by the IRS can be used to meet the “timely mailing as timely filing” rule for tax returns. IRS.gov/PDS, the page says, has the current list of PDSs, and the PDS itself can explain how to get written proof of the mailing date.

text:
## Note
**Rose Co. (Form 941 taxes) (pp. 33–34).** The example gives Rose Co.'s Form 941 taxes for two lookback periods:
- 2025 lookback period, 3rd quarter 2023 through 2nd quarter 2024: $12,000 in each of the 4 quarters, $48,000 in all.
- 2026 lookback period, 3rd quarter 2024 through 2nd quarter 2025: $12,000 in each of 3rd quarter 2024, 4th quarter 2024 and 1st quarter 2025, and $15,000 in 2nd quarter 2025, $51,000 in all.

For 2025, Rose Co. is a monthly schedule depositor: its liability for the 4 quarters of that lookback period was not more than $50,000. For 2026 it will be a semiweekly schedule depositor, since the taxes for the 4 quarters of its lookback period exceeded $50,000 (p. 34).

**Example for employers of farmworkers (p. 34).** Red Co. reported $48,000 on line 13 of its 2024 Form 943 and $60,000 on line 13 of its 2025 Form 943. For 2026 it is a monthly schedule depositor, because its lookback period is calendar year 2024, with taxes of $48,000, which were not more than $50,000. For 2027 it will be a semiweekly schedule depositor, because its lookback period is calendar year 2025, with taxes of $60,000, which exceeded $50,000.

**Related:** Deposits Due on Business Days Only — how deposits due on a day that is not a business day are treated, and the 2026 legal holidays (p. 34)

## Note
TAS can help with problems that you have not been able to resolve with the IRS on your own (p. 58). The page says to always try to resolve the problem with the IRS first and, if that fails, to come to TAS. Its services are free (p. 58).
- TAS serves all taxpayers and their representatives, whether individuals, businesses or exempt organizations. Eligibility for TAS help may arise if an IRS problem is causing you financial difficulty, if you tried to resolve your issue with the IRS and could not, or if you believe an IRS system, process or procedure just is not working as it should (p. 58).
- For help any time with general tax topics, the page gives the TAS website, www.TaxpayerAdvocate.IRS.gov. The site can help with common tax issues and situations, such as what to do if you make a mistake on your return or get a notice from the IRS (p. 58).
- TAS works to resolve large-scale (systemic) problems that affect many taxpayers. Systemic issues can be reported at www.IRS.gov/SAMS, and the page asks that no personal identifiable information be included (p. 58).

**Related:** How Do I Contact TAS? — where TAS has offices and how to find a local advocate's number (p. 58)

text:
## Note
**What it is and where it is reported (p. 8).** Nonpayroll federal income tax withholding (reported on Forms 1099 and Form W-2G, Certain Gambling Winnings) has to be reported on Form 945 (Annual Return of Withheld Federal Income Tax). Payroll withholding (Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944) and nonpayroll withholding (Form 945) require separate deposits.

**Nonpayroll items (p. 8).** The items include:
- military retirement;
- gambling winnings;
- Indian gaming profits;
- pensions, annuities and IRA distributions, the pensions including distributions from tax-favored retirement plans such as section 401(k), section 403(b) and governmental section 457(b) plans;
- certain government payments for which the recipient elected voluntary federal income tax withholding;
- dividends and other distributions by an ANC for which the recipient elected voluntary federal income tax withholding;
- payments subject to backup withholding.

On depositing and reporting nonpayroll federal income tax withholding, the page refers to the Instructions for Form 945.

**Distributions from nonqualified pension plans and deferred compensation plans (pp. 8–9).** Some nonqualified pension plans and deferred compensation plans (section 457(b) plans of tax-exempt organizations included) pay distributions to participants that are treated as wages and reported on Form W-2. The federal income tax withheld from them is reported on Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944, not on Form 945. A distribution from such a plan to a beneficiary or to the estate of a deceased employee is not wages and is reported on Forms 1099-R, and the federal income tax withheld from it is reported on Form 945.

**Backup withholding (p. 9).** Generally, 24% must be withheld from certain taxable payments when the payee does not give you their correct TIN; this is called “backup withholding.” It applies to interest, dividends, patronage dividends, rents, royalties, commissions, nonemployee compensation, payments in settlement of payment card or third-party network transactions, and certain other payments made in your trade or business. Transactions by brokers and barter exchanges, and certain payments by fishing boat operators, are subject to it too.

**Form W-9 (p. 9).** Form W-9 can be used to ask payees for their TINs. It must be used when payees need to certify that the number given is correct, or need to certify that they are not subject to backup withholding or are exempt from it. The Instructions for the Requester of Form W-9 list the types of payees exempt from backup withholding, and the page refers to Pub. 1281, Backup Withholding for Missing and Incorrect Name/TIN(s), for more.

**Caution: where backup withholding doesn’t apply (p. 9).** The following are outside backup withholding: real estate transactions, long-term-care benefits, health savings accounts (HSAs), medical savings accounts (MSAs), section 404(k) distributions from an employee stock ownership plan (ESOP), IRAs (simplified employee pension (SEP) and SIMPLE retirement plans included), annuities, pensions and wages.

**Related:** Federal Income Tax Withholding — withholding federal income tax from each wage payment or supplemental unemployment compensation plan benefit payment, and the list of employer responsibilities (pp. 7–8)

## Note
In certain cases the amounts reported as social security and Medicare taxes must be adjusted to arrive at the correct tax liability, for example by excluding amounts withheld by a third-party payer or amounts the employer was not required to withhold (p. 40). The amounts concerned are those in column 2 of Form 941, lines 5a–5d; on Form 943, lines 3, 5 and 7; and in column 2 of Form 944, lines 4a–4d. Current period adjustments are reported on Form 941, lines 7–9; Form 943, line 10; or Form 944, line 6 (p. 40). The page lists four types.

**Fractions-of-cents adjustment (pp. 40–41).** A small difference between total taxes after adjustments and nonrefundable credits (Form 941, line 12; Form 943, line 13; Form 944, line 9) and total deposits (Form 941, line 13; Form 943, line 14; Form 944, line 10) may be caused, in whole or in part, by rounding to the nearest cent each time payroll is figured. The rounding occurs when the social security and Medicare taxes to be withheld and deposited are figured from each employee's wages, and the IRS calls such differences "fractions-of-cents" adjustments. An employer that pays its taxes with Form 941 (or Form 943 or Form 944) instead of depositing, because total taxes for the quarter (the year for Form 943 or Form 944) are under $2,500, may also report a fractions-of-cents adjustment. To find out whether there is one for 2026, multiply the total wages and tips for the quarter that are subject to each of these taxes by the rate shown:
- social security tax reported on Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944: 6.2% (0.062);
- Medicare tax reported on Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944: 1.45% (0.0145);
- Additional Medicare Tax reported on Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944: 0.9% (0.009).

Compare the results (the employee share of social security and Medicare taxes) with the total social security and Medicare taxes actually withheld from employees and shown in the payroll records for the quarter (Form 941) or the year (Form 943 or Form 944). A small difference, positive or negative, may be a fractions-of-cents adjustment. It is reported on Form 941, line 7; Form 943, line 10; or Form 944, line 6. If the amount actually withheld is less, report a negative adjustment with a minus sign if possible (otherwise in parentheses); if it is more, report a positive adjustment (p. 41).

**Adjustment of tax on third-party sick pay (p. 41).** Report both the employer share and the employee share of social security and Medicare taxes for sick pay on Form 941, lines 5a and 5c (Form 943, lines 2 and 4; Form 944, lines 4a and 4c). When the wages that the employer and the third-party payer paid to an employee together exceed $200,000 for the calendar year, the Additional Medicare Tax is reported on Form 941, line 5d (Form 943, line 7; Form 944, line 4d). Show the social security and Medicare taxes that a third-party payer withheld on sick pay as a negative adjustment on Form 941, line 8 (Form 943, line 10; Form 944, line 6). The page refers to section 6 of Pub. 15-A.

**Adjustment of tax on tips (p. 41).** If, by the 10th of the month after the month the employer received an employee's report on tips, there are not enough employee funds available to withhold the employee's share of social security and Medicare taxes, the employer no longer has to collect it. The entire amount of these tips is still reported on Form 941, lines 5b and 5c (Form 944, lines 4b and 4c). If the aggregate wages and tips paid to an employee exceed $200,000 for the calendar year, report the Additional Medicare Tax on Form 941, line 5d (Form 944, line 4d). The total uncollected employee share of social security and Medicare taxes goes in as a negative adjustment on Form 941, line 9 (Form 944, line 6).

**Adjustment of tax on group-term life insurance premiums paid for former employees (p. 41).** For premiums on group-term life insurance over $50,000 for a former employee, the former employee pays the employee share of social security and Medicare taxes with their own tax return, and the employer does not collect it. All social security and Medicare taxes for such coverage are still included on Form 941, lines 5a and 5c (Form 944, lines 4a and 4c). For Form 943, the social security wages and Medicare wages go on lines 2 and 4, and the social security tax and Medicare tax on lines 3 and 5. If the premium amount combined with other wages exceeds $200,000 for the calendar year, report the Additional Medicare Tax on Form 941, line 5d (Form 944, line 4d); for Form 943, the Additional Medicare Tax wages go on line 6 and the tax on line 7. The employee share of these taxes is backed out as a negative adjustment on Form 941, line 9 (Form 943, line 10; Form 944, line 6). The page refers to Pub. 15-B for more on group-term life insurance.

**Supporting statement (p. 41).** For these adjustments, the employer prepares and keeps a brief supporting statement explaining the nature and amount of each. The statement is not attached to Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944. The page refers to the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 for reporting on Form W-2 the uncollected employee share of social security and Medicare taxes on tips and group-term life insurance.

**Example (p. 41).** Cedar, Inc., filed Form 941 and was entitled to these current period adjustments:
- Fractions of cents: over the quarter, Cedar, Inc. withheld and deposited a net $1.44 more in social security and Medicare taxes than the employee share of the column 2 amount on Form 941, lines 5a–5d. Adding or dropping fractions of cents on each wage payment caused the difference. Cedar, Inc. reports a positive $1.44 fractions-of-cents adjustment on Form 941, line 7.
- Third-party sick pay: Cedar, Inc. included $2,000 of taxes for sick pay in column 2 of Form 941, lines 5a and 5c. The third-party payer of the sick pay withheld and paid the employee share ($1,000) of these taxes, so Cedar, Inc. is entitled to a negative $1,000 sick pay adjustment on Form 941, line 8.
- Life insurance premiums: Cedar, Inc. paid group-term life insurance premiums for policies over $50,000 for former employees. The former employees owe the employee share ($200) of the social security and Medicare taxes on those policies, yet Cedar, Inc. includes that share in the column 2 taxes on Form 941, lines 5a and 5c. It is therefore entitled to a negative $200 adjustment on Form 941, line 9.

**No change to the record of federal tax liability (p. 41).** Current period adjustments leave the employer's record of federal tax liability as it is: Form 941, line 16, or Schedule B (Form 941); for Form 943 filers, Form 943, line 17, or Form 943-A; for Form 944 filers, Form 944, line 13, or Form 945-A. The record shows the actual amounts withheld from employees' wages for social security and Medicare taxes. The current period adjustments bring the amounts reported on Form 941, lines 5a–5d, column 2 (Form 943, lines 3, 5 and 7; Form 944, lines 4a–4d, column 2) into line with the actual amounts withheld, which are the amounts on the record, so no further change to the record is needed for these adjustments.

**Related:** Prior-Period Adjustments — correcting an error found on a previously filed Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 (p. 41)

## Note
This part of section 17 describes which "federal income taxes" are subject to the certification procedures (p. 55). For the purposes of the cover over certification requirements, the term "federal income taxes" includes federal income taxes that were withheld from compensation and other amounts paid to any of the following groups and deposited into the U.S. Treasury (p. 55):
- Federal government civilian employees who are residents of American Samoa, the CNMI or Guam.
- Recipients (including survivors) of federal pensions, civilian or military, who are residents of American Samoa, the CNMI or Guam.
- Military personnel stationed in American Samoa, the CNMI or Guam.
- Military personnel not stationed in American Samoa, the CNMI or Guam who have a state of legal residence in any of these territories.
- Employees of a service or social organization associated with a military or civilian agency in American Samoa, the CNMI or Guam.

**Related:** Certification Procedures — the procedures federal agencies follow to certify to the IRS the federal income taxes paid to and deposited into the U.S. Treasury (p. 55)

## Note
**Outsourcing payroll (p. 53).** An employer may hand some or all of its federal employment tax withholding, reporting and payment obligations to someone else. An employer that outsources these payroll and related tax duties (withholding, reporting and paying over social security, Medicare, FUTA and income taxes) to a third-party payer generally stays responsible for them, liability for the taxes included. The page points to Certified professional employer organization (CPEO), later in the section, for an exception.

**What an employer that outsources should consider (p. 53).**
- The employer stays responsible for federal tax deposits and other federal tax payments, even if it forwards the tax amounts to the third-party payer to make them. When the third party fails to make them, the IRS may assess penalties and interest on the employer's account, and the employer may be liable for all taxes, penalties and interest due. Personal liability for certain unpaid federal taxes is also possible.
- When there are issues with the employer's account, the IRS sends correspondence to the address of record. The page strongly recommends that the employer keep its own address as the address of record, because correspondence going to the third-party payer's address may significantly limit the employer's ability to learn of tax matters involving its business. Form 8822-B is used to update the business address.
- When a third party enrolls an employer in EFTPS for federal tax deposits, the employer receives an Inquiry PIN. The employer should activate and use that PIN to monitor its account and to check that the third party is making the required deposits.

**Common third-party payers (p. 53).** The page lists five that an employer may contract with for payroll and related tax duties: a payroll service provider (PSP), a reporting agent, an agent with an approved Form 2678, a payer designated under section 3504, and a certified professional employer organization (CPEO).

**Payroll service provider (PSP) (p. 53).** A PSP helps run payroll and payroll-related tax duties for the employer, working under the employer's EIN. It may prepare paychecks, prepare and file employment tax returns, prepare Forms W-2, and make federal tax deposits and other federal tax payments. A PSP is not liable, as an employer or as the employer's agent, for the employer's employment taxes. An employer using a PSP remains liable for its employment tax obligations, including liability for employment taxes. The employer should make sure that the PSP uses EFTPS for the federal tax deposits it makes for the employer, so that the employer can confirm payments are being made on its behalf.

**Reporting agent (p. 53).** A reporting agent is a type of PSP. It helps run payroll and payroll-related tax duties for the employer, including authority to sign and file electronically the forms listed on Form 8655, which an employer uses to authorize a reporting agent to act for it. It works under the employer's EIN. A reporting agent is not liable, as an employer or as the employer's agent, for the employer's employment taxes. An employer using one remains liable for its employment obligations, including liability for employment taxes. A reporting agent must use EFTPS for the federal tax deposits it makes for an employer, and the employer has access to EFTPS to confirm those deposits. The page refers to Revenue Procedure 2012-32 and to Pub. 1474 for more on reporting agents.

**Agent with an approved Form 2678 (p. 53).** Such an agent helps run payroll and related tax duties for the employer. An agent authorized under section 3504 may pay wages or compensation to some or all of an employer's employees, prepare and file employment tax returns as Form 2678 sets out, prepare Forms W-2, and make federal tax deposits and other federal tax payments. The employer asks for authority to appoint the agent by using Form 2678. The agent acts under its own EIN. It files Schedule R (Form 941) or, if applicable, Schedule R (Form 943), which spreads wages, taxes and credits claimed among the employers it represents. The agent and an employer that uses it are jointly liable for the employment taxes and related tax duties the agent is authorized to perform. Form 2678 does not reach FUTA taxes reportable on Form 940, except where the employer is a home care service recipient who receives home care services through a program run by a federal, state or local government agency. The page refers to Revenue Procedure 2013-39 for more on such an agent.

**Payer designated under section 3504 (p. 54).** In certain circumstances the IRS may designate a third-party payer to perform the acts of an employer, and it will do so for an employer if the third party has a service agreement with that employer. In a service agreement the third-party payer (1) asserts that it is the employer of the individuals performing services for the employer, (2) pays wages to those individuals, and (3) takes on responsibility for withholding, reporting and paying federal employment taxes on the wages it pays them. The designated payer performs its tax duties under the service agreement using its own EIN. Where the IRS designates a payer under section 3504, the payer and the employer are jointly liable for the employment taxes and related tax duties for which the payer is designated. The page refers to Regulations section 31.3504-2.

**Certified professional employer organization (CPEO) (p. 54).** The Stephen Beck, Jr., ABLE Act of 2014 required the IRS to set up a voluntary certification program for professional employer organizations (PEOs). PEOs take on various payroll administration and tax reporting duties for business clients and are typically paid a fee based on payroll costs. A CPEO must meet various requirements, set out in sections 3511 and 7705 and related published guidance, to become and stay certified. Certification may affect the employment tax liabilities of the CPEO and of its customers. For employment tax purposes a CPEO is generally treated as the employer of an individual who does work for one of its customers under a contract between the CPEO and that customer that section 7705(e)(2) describes (a CPEO contract). This treatment covers only wages and other compensation the CPEO pays that individual. For certain employees covered by a CPEO contract, the page says the reader ("you") may also be treated as an employer of those employees and may be liable for federal employment taxes on wages and other compensation the CPEO pays to them. When filing an aggregate Form 940, Form 941 or Form 943, a CPEO completes Schedule R (Form 940), Schedule R (Form 941) or Schedule R (Form 943), respectively. A CPEO files Form 8973 to notify the IRS when it starts or ends a service contract with a customer. An organization becomes a CPEO by applying through the IRS Online Registration System. The page refers to IRS.gov/CPEO and to Revenue Procedure 2023-18.

**Tip (p. 54).** When an employer and a section 3504 authorized agent (or CPEO or other third-party payer) each paid wages to an employee during a quarter, each should file Form 941 for the wages it paid to the employee in that quarter and should issue Forms W-2 for the wages it paid to the employee during the year.

**Related:** 15. Special Rules for Various Types of Services and Payments — a table of special classes of employment and special types of payments and their treatment under employment taxes (p. 46)

text:
## Note
- Return transcripts for Forms 940, 941, 943, 944 and 945 for tax years 2023 and later are now available through your IRS business tax account (F03, p. 3).
- The COVID-19 related sick and family leave wage credit applies only to leave taken after March 31, 2020, and before October 1, 2021, and Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 can’t any longer be used to claim it (F04, p. 3).
- For tax periods beginning after 2023 the claim lines were removed from Form 941, Employer’s QUARTERLY Federal Tax Return, and from Forms 943 and 944. An employer entitled to the credit for wages paid after 2023 for an earlier applicable leave period claims it on Form 941-X (or Form 943-X or Form 944-X) (F04, pp. 3–4).
- A Form 941-X filed before the Form 941 for the quarter may cause errors or processing delays (F04, p. 4).
- The amount from Form 8974, line 12 or, if applicable, line 17, is reported on Form 941 (or Form 943 or Form 944); for reducing your record of tax liability for the payroll tax credit, the page points to the line 16 instructions in the Instructions for Form 941 (F04, p. 4).
- Approved section 3504 agents and CPEOs must complete Schedule R (Form 941), Allocation Schedule for Aggregate Form 941 Filers, for an aggregate Form 941 (F04, p. 4).
- An aggregate quarterly Form 941 is filed by an agent the IRS approved under section 3504, and also by CPEOs approved under section 7705 (F04, p. 4).
- CPEOs generally must file Form 941 or Form 943, with the applicable Schedule R, electronically (F04, p. 5).
- Other third-party payers filing an aggregate quarterly Form 941 or annual Form 943, non-certified PEOs for example, file the applicable Schedule R when their clients claim an employment tax credit (F04, p. 5).
- An employer that has filed quarterly Forms 941 and expects calendar-year employment taxes of $1,000 or less, and wants Form 944 instead, must contact the IRS in the first calendar quarter of the tax year and must receive written IRS notice before filing Form 944 in place of quarterly Forms 941 (F04, p. 5).
- Employers may also ask to file quarterly Forms 941 instead of an annual Form 944: an employer that got IRS notice to file Form 944 but prefers Forms 941 contacts the IRS in the first calendar quarter of the tax year, and may file quarterly only after receiving written IRS notice (F04, p. 5).
- A mistake on a filed Form 941 is corrected with Form 941-X, which is filed on its own and separately from Form 941 (F04, p. 5).
- Unless you have filed a “final” Form 940 and a “final” Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944, or are a “seasonal” employer (Form 941 only), you continue to file Forms 941 for periods with no wages paid; the IRS encourages filing “zero wage” returns electronically (F04, p. 6).
- The Employer Responsibilities list includes filing Form 941, with payment of the tax with the return when no deposit is required, among the items under Quarterly (by April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31) (F09, p. 8).
- Payroll withholding (Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944) and nonpayroll withholding (Form 945) are deposited separately (F10, p. 8).
- Income tax withheld on distributions to participants from some nonqualified pension and deferred compensation plans goes on Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944, not on Form 945; distributions from such plans to a beneficiary or estate of a deceased employee aren't wages, and the income tax withheld on them goes on Form 945 (F10, pp. 8–9).
- The filing address for Form 941 generally turns on where your residence or principal place of business is located and on whether a payment goes with the return; tax-exempt organizations and government entities have separate addresses, found in the separate instructions for Form 941 (F14, pp. 9–10).
- For depositing taxes reported on Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 and Form 945, the Calendar refers to section 11 (F21, p. 10).
- Under the Calendar’s By January 31 date, Form 941 for the previous calendar year’s fourth quarter is filed and any income, social security and Medicare taxes not yet deposited are deposited; they may be paid with Form 941 when the quarter’s total tax liability (Form 941, line 12) is under $2,500 (F21, p. 11).
- Timely depositors of all taxes may file by February 10; for further rules on paying with the return, the page points to Payment with return in section 11 (F21, p. 11).
- Under the Calendar’s April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31 dates, Form 941 is filed and undeposited taxes are deposited; they may be paid with the form when the quarter’s total tax liability (Form 941, line 12) is under $2,500, and timely depositors of all taxes may file by May 10, August 10, November 10 or February 10, respectively (F21, p. 12).
- A business notified to file Form 944 that did not ask for, and receive, written IRS notice to file quarterly Forms 941 does not file Form 941 for those quarters (F21, p. 12).
- If an EIN you used on Form 941 (or Form 943 or Form 944) differs from the EIN reported on Form W-3, the page refers to Box h—Other EIN used this year in the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 (S01, p. 13).
- Form 941 or Form 944 is filed to report withholding and employment taxes on tips (S06, p. 23).
- Tips and the collected and uncollected social security and Medicare taxes go on Form 941, lines 5b and 5c and, if applicable, 5d, and a negative adjustment for the uncollected taxes goes on Form 941, line 9 (S06, p. 23).
- A payment may accompany a timely filed Form 941 in place of a deposit, without penalty, when the Form 941 total tax liability (line 12) for the current or the prior quarter is under $2,500 and no $100,000 next-day deposit obligation arose in the current quarter (S11, p. 31).
- If you can’t be sure the current quarter’s liability will be under $2,500 (and the prior quarter’s was not), deposit under the semiweekly or monthly rules to avoid an FTD penalty (S11, p. 31).
- Deposits for Forms 941 (or 943 or 944) and for Form 945 are kept apart and never combined (S11, pp. 31–32).
- An employer of both farm and nonfarm workers treats Form 943 taxes for farmworkers separately from Form 941/944 taxes for nonfarm workers and makes separate deposits (S11, p. 32).
- The deposit schedule depends on the total tax liability reported on Form 941, line 12 (and on the other forms the page lists) during a lookback period (S11.01, p. 32).
- A Form 941 filer’s schedule for a calendar year comes from the taxes on Forms 941, line 12, over a 4-quarter lookback period running from July 1 to June 30: $50,000 or less makes a monthly schedule depositor, and more than $50,000 a semiweekly schedule depositor (S11.01, p. 32).
- The 2026 lookback period for a Form 941 filer that filed Form 944 in 2024 or 2025 is calendar year 2024 (S11.01, p. 32).
- Corrections made on Form 941-X do not change the tax liability counted for earlier periods under the lookback rule (S11.01, p. 32).
- A Form 941 filer whose lookback taxes (Forms 941, line 12, for the 4 quarters) were $50,000 or less is a monthly schedule depositor for the calendar year, and one whose taxes were more than $50,000 is a semiweekly schedule depositor (S11.01.01, p. 33; S11.01.02, p. 33).
- Monthly schedule depositors shouldn’t file Form 941 monthly (S11.01.01, p. 33).
- For Form 941 filers, liability for any lookback quarter before the business began or was acquired counts as zero, so a new filer is a monthly schedule depositor in its first calendar year; however, the page points to the $100,000 Next-Day Deposit Rule (S11.01.01, p. 33).
- A semiweekly schedule depositor completes Schedule B (Form 941), Report of Tax Liability for Semiweekly Schedule Depositors, and submits it with Form 941 (S11.01.02, p. 33).
- A Form 941 filer with several pay dates in one semiweekly period that fall in different calendar quarters makes separate deposits for the separate liabilities (S11.01.02, p. 33).
- Determining your schedule includes adding the taxes reported on Forms 941, line 12 (and on the other forms’ lines the page lists) for the lookback period (S11.01.02, p. 33).
- In the example, Rose Co. reported Form 941 taxes totalling $48,000 for its 2025 lookback period, so it is a monthly schedule depositor for 2025, and $51,000 for its 2026 lookback period (third quarter 2024 through second quarter 2025), so it will be a semiweekly schedule depositor for 2026 (S11.01.03, pp. 33–34).
- When you deposited too much for a quarter, you choose on Form 941 for that quarter whether the overpayment is refunded or credited to your next return (S11.02, p. 36).
- The deposit penalty information is written about Form 941 but applies to Forms 943, 944 and 945 as well (S11.03, p. 36).
- An employer that filed Form 944 for the prior year and files Forms 941 for the current year owes no FTD penalty for a late January deposit of the current year’s employment taxes if the taxes are fully deposited by March 15 of the current year (S11.03, p. 36).
- To avoid an “averaged” FTD penalty, a monthly schedule depositor lists tax liabilities (not deposits) in the monthly entry spaces on Form 941, line 16, and a semiweekly schedule depositor lists them on Schedule B (Form 941); check that the total liability on Form 941, line 16, or at the bottom of Schedule B (Form 941), equals the liability on Form 941, line 12 (S11.03, p. 37).
- An employer that paid wages subject to federal income tax withholding (sick pay and supplemental unemployment benefit withholding included) or social security and Medicare taxes files Form 941 every quarter, even with no taxes to report, unless it filed a final return, was notified it may file Form 944, or the exceptions on the page apply (S12, p. 38).
- An employer required to file Forms 941 that expects calendar-year employment taxes of $1,000 or less must contact the IRS in the first calendar quarter of the tax year to ask to file Form 944, and needs written IRS notice before filing it (S12, p. 38).
- Form 941 is due by the last day of the month after the quarter ends; with timely deposits fully paying the quarter’s taxes, it may be filed by the 10th day of the 2nd month after the quarter ends (S12, p. 38).
- Seasonal employers, household employers and agricultural employers are exceptions to the filing requirements for Form 941 and Form 944 (S12, p. 38).
- Seasonal employers needn’t file Forms 941 for quarters without tax liability because no wages were paid; they check the “Seasonal employer” box on Form 941, line 18, and the box at the top of the form for the quarter reported (S12, p. 38).
- The IRS generally won’t ask about unfiled returns when at least one taxable return is filed each year, but the “Seasonal employer” box must be checked on every Form 941 filed, or the IRS expects a return for each quarter (S12, p. 38).
- An employer that files Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 for business employees may add the taxes of household employees to that return, and agricultural employers report their social security, Medicare and withheld income taxes on Form 943 (S12, p. 38).
- Railroad employers report RRTA taxes on Form CT-1, and report federal income taxes withheld from their employees’ wages on Form 941 or Form 944 (S12, p. 38).
- Form 941 can be filed through the IRS e-file program, and reporting agents filing it for groups of taxpayers can file electronically (S12, p. 38).
- CPEOs, apart from the first quarter (Form 941 only) for which a CPEO is certified, must file Form 941 with Schedule R (Form 941) electronically (S12, p. 38).
- An employer with multiple locations or divisions files only one Form 941 per quarter, and a Form 941 should not report more than 1 calendar quarter (S12, p. 39).
- Name and EIN on Form 941 should read exactly as on earlier returns, and the Instructions for Form 941 explain how to prepare the form (S12, p. 39).
- A business that closes files a final return for the last quarter in which wages are paid (S12, p. 39).
- An employer required to file a final return also furnishes Forms W-2 to its employees and files Forms W-2 and W-3 with the SSA by the final return’s due date, and sends no original or copy of Form 941, 943 or 944 to the SSA (S12, p. 39).
- A late Form 941 for a previous year is filed on a copy of the form (with separate instructions) with a revision date showing the year and, if applicable, the quarter; the page gives IRS.gov/Form941 for prior year and quarterly forms (S12, p. 39).
- Bonuses are reported as wages and as social security and Medicare wages on Forms W-2 and on Forms 941, 943 or 944 (S12, p. 40).
- Social security and Medicare wages and taxes are reported separately on Forms W-2 and W-3 and on Forms 941, 943 or 944, and Form W-3 is reconciled with your four quarterly Forms 941 (S12, p. 40).
- Backup withholding and withholding on nonpayroll payments such as pensions, annuities and gambling winnings are not reported on Forms 941, 943 or 944, and only taxes and withholding that appear on Form W-2 belong on them (S12, p. 40).
- Where Additional Medicare Tax was withheld, the Medicare tax on Form 941, line 5c, column 2, will not be double the Medicare tax withheld in box 6 of Form W-3, because that tax falls on the employee alone (S12, p. 40).
- Certain social security and Medicare amounts reported on Form 941, lines 5a–5d, column 2, have to be adjusted to reach the correct tax liability, and current period adjustments are reported on Form 941, lines 7–9 (S13, p. 40).
- Fractions-of-cents adjustments go on Form 941, line 7, and an employer paying with Form 941 rather than depositing, because the quarter’s total taxes are under $2,500, may also report one (S13.01, pp. 40–41).
- Under the adjustment of tax on third-party sick pay, the employer share and the employee share of social security and Medicare taxes on sick pay are reported on Form 941, lines 5a and 5c; the Additional Medicare Tax goes on line 5d when the employer’s and third-party payer’s combined wages for an employee exceed $200,000 for the calendar year; and the taxes a third-party payer withheld on sick pay are a negative adjustment on line 8 (S13.01, p. 41).
- If, by the 10th of the month after an employee’s tip report was received, the employer lacks the employee funds to withhold the employee’s social security and Medicare share, it no longer has to collect it. The entire amount of those tips still goes on Form 941, lines 5b and 5c; the Additional Medicare Tax goes on line 5d if the employee’s wages and tips exceed $200,000 for the calendar year; and the total uncollected employee share is a negative adjustment on line 9 (S13.01, p. 41).
- For group-term life insurance premiums over $50,000 paid for a former employee, the former employee pays the employee share of the taxes with their own return and the employer does not collect it, yet all social security and Medicare taxes for the coverage go on Form 941, lines 5a and 5c; if the premium amount combined with other wages exceeds $200,000 for the calendar year, the Additional Medicare Tax goes on line 5d, and the employee share is backed out as a negative adjustment on line 9 (S13.01, p. 41).
- The supporting statement for these adjustments is not attached to Form 941 (S13.01, p. 41).
- In the example, Cedar, Inc., filed Form 941 and reports a positive $1.44 fractions-of-cents adjustment on line 7, a negative $1,000 sick pay adjustment on line 8, and a negative $200 adjustment on line 9 for the former employees’ share of taxes on group-term life insurance premiums (S13.01, p. 41).
- For current period adjustments you make no change to your record of federal tax liability on Form 941, line 16, or Schedule B (Form 941) (S13.01, p. 41).
- An error found on a filed Form 941 is corrected on a separate Form 941-X for each Form 941 corrected, and Form 941-X is filed on its own, not with Form 941 (S13.02, p. 42).
- Treasury Decision 9405 changed how interest-free adjustments to employment taxes reported on Form 941 are made and how a refund claim is filed (S13.02, p. 42).
- Income tax withheld in a prior calendar year can’t be adjusted unless the adjustment corrects an administrative error or section 3509 applies; an administrative error is an amount entered on Form 941, 943 or 944 that differs from the amount actually withheld (S13.02, p. 42).
- Where you did not repay or reimburse the employee, you report and pay the excess when you file the Form 941 for the quarter in which too much tax was withheld (S13.02, p. 43).
- FUTA tax for household employees need not be deposited unless their wages are reported on Form 941, 943 or 944; where they weren’t reported there, FUTA tax for them goes on Schedule H (Form 1040) (S14, pp. 44–45).
- A footnote to the section’s table says wages for services not considered farmwork are reported on Forms 941 or Form 944, and that other exemptions may apply (S15, p. 46).
- Where an employer and a section 3504 authorized agent (or CPEO or other third-party payer) both paid wages to an employee in a quarter, each should file Form 941 for the wages it paid that employee in the quarter (S16, p. 54).
- A CPEO files Schedule R (Form 940), Schedule R (Form 941) or Schedule R (Form 943), matching the aggregate return it files, which is Form 940, Form 941 or Form 943 respectively (S16, p. 54).
- A certification’s amounts must agree with the federal income tax withheld and reported on the agency’s quarterly federal tax return(s) (Form 941) (B03, p. 56).
- Return transcripts for Form 941 for tax years 2023 and later can be accessed through your IRS business tax account (B04, p. 57).

## Note
**The penalty (p. 10).** A payment in any form that a financial institution dishonors and returns draws a penalty of $25 or 2% of the payment, whichever is more.

**Small payments (p. 10).** For a dishonored payment of $24.99 or less, though, the penalty equals the amount of the payment. A dishonored payment of $18, for example, is charged a penalty of $18.

Every section note cites its section and pages.
