text:
## Note
**FICA (p. 29).** The Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) sets up a federal system of old-age, survivors, disability and hospital insurance. The social security tax finances the old-age, survivors and disability part, and the Medicare tax finances the hospital insurance part. The two taxes are reported separately. Generally, you must withhold social security and Medicare taxes from employees' wages and pay the employer share. Certain types of wages and compensation are not subject to these taxes, and the page refers to section 5 and section 15 for details. Generally, employee wages are subject to them whatever the employee's age and whether or not the employee receives social security benefits. For an employee who reported tips, the page refers to section 6.

**The $150 test or the $2,500 test for farmwork (p. 29).** All cash wages you pay an employee during the year for farmwork are subject to social security and Medicare taxes and to federal income tax withholding if either of two tests is met:
- You pay the employee cash wages of $150 or more in a year for farmwork (all cash wages count, whether paid on a time, piecework or other basis). The $150 test applies separately to each farmworker you employ, each member of a family of workers being treated separately. Wages paid by other employers are not counted.
- Your total payments for farmwork (cash and noncash) to all your employees are $2,500 or more during the year.

**Exceptions (p. 29).** A seasonal farmworker's annual cash wages of less than $150 from you are not subject to social security and Medicare taxes or federal income tax withholding, even if you pay $2,500 or more to all your farmworkers. These wages do count toward the $2,500 test when determining whether other farmworkers' wages are subject to social security and Medicare taxes. A seasonal farmworker meets all four of these descriptions:
- They are employed in agriculture as a hand-harvest laborer.
- They are paid piece rates in an operation that is usually paid on a piece-rate basis in the region of employment.
- They commute daily from a permanent home to the farm.
- They had been employed in agriculture less than 13 weeks in the preceding calendar year.

Social security and Medicare taxes also don't apply to wages paid to a child under 18 who works on a farm that is a sole proprietorship, or a partnership in which each partner is a parent of a child. Those wages likewise count toward the $2,500 test when determining whether other farmworkers' wages are subject to those taxes.

**Deducting the tax (p. 29).** The employee tax is deducted from each wage payment. If you are unsure whether a farmworker's wages for the year will be taxable, you may either deduct the tax as you make payments or wait until the $2,500 test or the $150 test has been met.

**Tax rates and the social security wage base limit (p. 29).** Social security and Medicare taxes have different rates, and only social security tax has a wage base limit, the maximum wage subject to the tax for the year. Withholding for each tax is figured by multiplying each payment by the employee tax rate. For 2026 the social security tax rate is 6.2% (the amount withheld) for the employer and 6.2% for the employee (12.4% total), and the social security wage base limit is $184,500. The Medicare tax rate is 1.45% (the amount withheld) for the employee and 1.45% for the employer (2.9% total). Medicare tax has no wage base limit, so all covered wages are subject to it.

**Additional Medicare Tax withholding (pp. 29–30).** On top of withholding Medicare tax at 1.45%, you must withhold a 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax from wages you pay an employee in excess of $200,000 in a calendar year. Withholding must begin in the pay period in which you pay wages over $200,000 to the employee and continue each pay period until the end of the calendar year. Only the employee bears Additional Medicare Tax, and there is no employer share. All wages subject to Medicare tax are subject to Additional Medicare Tax withholding when paid in excess of the $200,000 withholding threshold (p. 30). For what wages are subject to Medicare tax the page refers to section 15, and it points to IRS.gov/ADMTfaqs for more on Additional Medicare Tax (p. 30).

**Successor employer (p. 30).** If corporate acquisitions meet certain requirements, wages the predecessor paid are treated as paid by the successor for applying the social security wage base limit and the Additional Medicare Tax withholding threshold ($200,000 in a calendar year). Whether you should file Schedule D (Form 941) is determined by reviewing the Instructions for Schedule D (Form 941). The page refers to Regulations section 31.3121(a)(1)-1(b) and to Revenue Procedure 2004-53, 2004-34 I.R.B. 320.

Example: Early in 2026 you bought all the assets of a plumbing business from Adam Black. Julian Gold had been employed by Adam and had received $2,000 in wages before the purchase date, and he continued working for you. Social security tax applies to the first $182,500 ($184,500 minus $2,000) of the wages you pay Julian. Medicare tax is due on all the wages you pay him in the calendar year. The $2,000 he received while employed by Adam should be counted in determining whether his wages exceed the $200,000 threshold for Additional Medicare Tax withholding.

**Employee's portion of taxes paid by employer (p. 30).** When you pay an employee's social security and Medicare taxes instead of deducting them from the employee's pay, the amount of those payments must be included in the employee's wages for social security and Medicare taxes. That increase in the wage payment is itself subject to employee social security and Medicare taxes, which again increases the additional taxes you must pay. The page refers to Revenue Ruling 86-14 and Pub. 15-A.

**Household and agricultural employers (p. 30).** For a household or agricultural employee, you may pay the employee's share of social security and Medicare taxes without withholding it from the employee's wages. If you don't withhold the taxes, you must still pay them on the employee's behalf. The employee social security and Medicare taxes you pay count as additional income to the employee. Put that income in box 1 of the employee's Form W-2 (box 7 of Form 499R-2/W-2PR), but leave it out of social security and Medicare wages and out of boxes 3 and 5 (boxes 20 and 22 of Form 499R-2/W-2PR). It is not wages for FUTA tax purposes either. For non-household and non-agricultural employees different rules apply to an employer's payment of these taxes; the page refers to section 7 of Pub. 15-A.

Example: Gavrielle runs a small family fruit farm and hires day laborers in the picking season. Instead of deducting the employees' share of social security and Medicare taxes from their pay, Gavrielle pays it on their behalf. When preparing the employees' Forms W-2, Gavrielle adds each employee's share of the taxes paid to the employee's wage income in box 1, and leaves it out of box 3 (social security wages) and box 5 (Medicare wages and tips). For 2026, Dan was paid $1,000 during the year. Gavrielle enters $1,076.50 in box 1 of Dan's Form W-2 ($1,000 wages plus $76.50 of social security and Medicare taxes paid for him) and $1,000.00 in boxes 3 and 5.

**Sick pay payments (p. 30).** Most sick pay payments, those made by third parties such as insurance companies included, are subject to social security and Medicare taxes. For details on third-party payers of sick pay the page refers to Pub. 15-A.

**Motion picture project employers (p. 30).** A motion picture project employer's payments to a motion picture project worker during a calendar year are all subject to one social security tax wage base limit ($184,500 for 2026) and one FUTA tax wage base limit ($7,000 for 2026), whether or not the worker is a common-law employee of multiple clients of the employer. The page refers to section 3512 for more information, including the definitions of a "motion picture project employer" and a "motion picture project worker."

**Withholding social security and Medicare taxes on nonresident alien employees (p. 30).** In general, wages paid to nonresident alien employees are treated for social security and Medicare tax withholding as they would be for a U.S. citizen or resident alien. The page refers to Pub. 515 for exceptions. One exception covers foreign agricultural workers on H-2A visas, who are exempt from social security and Medicare taxes; the page refers to Compensation paid to H-2A visa holders in section 5.

**International social security agreements (p. 30).** The United States has social security agreements, also called totalization agreements, with many countries; they eliminate dual social security coverage and taxation. Compensation subject to social security and Medicare taxes may be exempt under one of them. More information and a list of agreement countries are available from the SSA at SSA.gov/international, and the page refers to Pub. 519.

**Religious exemption (pp. 30–31).** Members of a recognized religious sect opposed to insurance can claim an exemption from social security and Medicare taxes. It is available only if the employee and the employer are both members of the sect. The page refers to Pub. 517, Social Security and Other Information for Members of the Clergy and Religious Workers (p. 31).

**Foreign persons treated as American employers (p. 31).** Under section 3121(z), a foreign person is generally treated as an American employer when paying FICA taxes on wages to an employee who is a U.S. citizen or resident, if both of these conditions are met:
1. The foreign person is a member of a domestically controlled group of entities.
2. The foreign person's employee performs services in connection with a contract between the U.S. Government (or one of its instrumentalities) and any member of the domestically controlled group of entities.

Ownership of more than 50% constitutes control.

**Related:** 5. Wages and Other Compensation — the pay that counts as wages subject to federal employment taxes, in cash or in other forms (p. 18)

## Note
The penalty information is written about Form 941 but applies equally to Form 943, Form 944 and Form 945. It does not apply when the employer qualifies for the exceptions discussed under Payment with return, earlier in section 11 (p. 36).

**When penalties apply (p. 36).** A penalty may apply to deposits that are late or for less than the amount required. None applies when the failure to deposit properly and on time was due to reasonable cause and not to willful neglect, and a taxpayer who receives a penalty notice can explain why reasonable cause exists.

**Waivers (p. 36).** For a timely filed employment tax return, the IRS may also waive deposit penalties where the failure was inadvertent and either it was the first quarter in which any employment tax deposit was required, or it was the first deposit after the deposit frequency changed. The net worth and size limitations that apply to awards of administrative and litigation costs under section 7430 must also be met: an individual’s net worth can’t exceed $2 million, and a business’s net worth can’t exceed $7 million with no more than 500 employees. The IRS may also waive the penalty for the first time a deposit is required if the payment was inadvertently sent to the IRS instead of being deposited by EFT.

**Penalty rates (p. 36).** For amounts not properly or timely deposited:
- 2% for deposits made 1 to 5 days late.
- 5% for deposits made 6 to 15 days late.
- 10% for deposits made at least 16 days late, provided they are made before 10 days have passed from the date of the IRS’s first notice asking for the tax due.
- 10% for amounts that should have been deposited but were instead paid directly to the IRS or paid with the tax return; the page points to Payment with return, earlier in section 11, for exceptions.
- 15% for amounts still unpaid more than 10 days after the date of the first IRS notice asking for the tax due, or the day on which notice and demand for immediate payment was received, whichever is earlier.

Late deposit penalty amounts are worked out in calendar days, counted from the due date of the liability (p. 36).

**Former Form 944 filers (p. 36).** Where Form 944 was filed for the prior year and Forms 941 are filed for the current year, the FTD penalty doesn’t apply to a late deposit of the current year’s January employment taxes, provided the taxes are deposited in full by March 15 of that year.

**Order in which deposits are applied (p. 36).** Deposits generally go against the most recent tax liability within the quarter. After an FTD penalty notice, you may designate how your deposits are applied so as to minimize the penalty, provided you do so within 90 days of the notice’s date and follow the instructions on the notice; the page refers to Revenue Procedure 2001-58 for more on designating deposits. Example: Cedar, Inc., owes deposits of $1,000 on April 15 and $1,500 on May 15, skips the April 15 deposit and deposits $2,000 on May 15. Applying deposits to the most recent liability puts $1,500 against the May 15 deposit and the remaining $500 against April, which leaves $500 of the April 15 liability undeposited, and the penalty on that underdeposit applies as explained earlier.

**Trust fund recovery penalty (pp. 36–37).** The trust fund recovery penalty may apply when federal income, social security or Medicare tax that must be withheld (trust fund taxes) is not withheld, or is not deposited or paid to the U.S. Treasury. It equals 100% of the unpaid trust fund tax. When those taxes can’t be collected immediately from the employer or business, the penalty may be imposed on every person the IRS determines to be responsible for collecting, accounting for or paying them over and who acted willfully in not doing so. It doesn’t apply to trust fund taxes an employer holds back in anticipation of credits it is entitled to.

A responsible person can be any of the following: an officer or employee of a corporation; a partner or employee of a partnership; an accountant; a volunteer director or trustee; an employee of a sole proprietorship; or another person or entity responsible for collecting, accounting for or paying over trust fund taxes. The term may also cover someone who signs the business’s checks or otherwise has authority to cause business funds to be spent (pp. 36–37).

Willfully means voluntarily, consciously and intentionally. A responsible person acts willfully by knowing that the collecting, accounting for or paying over of trust fund taxes isn’t happening, or by recklessly disregarding obvious and known risks to the government’s right to receive them (p. 37).

**Separate accounting (p. 37).** Separate accounting may be required where withheld employee social security, Medicare or income tax isn’t paid over, or required taxes aren’t deposited, required payments aren’t made, or tax returns aren’t filed. The IRS would then give written notice requiring deposits into a special trust account for the U.S. Government, and failing to meet the special bank deposit requirements for that account may bring criminal penalties.

**“Averaged” FTD penalty (p. 37).** The page pairs each return’s tax liability line with the line on which liabilities are reported: Form 941, liability on line 12, reported on line 16 (or on Schedule B (Form 941)); Form 943, liability on line 13, reported on line 17 (or on Form 943-A); Form 944, liability on line 9, reported on line 13 (or on Form 945-A); Form 945, liability on line 3, reported on line 7 (or on Form 945-A). The IRS may assess an “averaged” FTD penalty of 2% to 10% in two cases:
- A monthly schedule depositor didn’t properly complete the reporting line (16, 17, 13 or 7) when the liability line (12, 13, 9 or 3) equaled or exceeded $2,500.
- A semiweekly schedule depositor’s liability on that line equaled or exceeded $2,500 and the depositor completed the reporting line (Form 941 line 16, Form 943 line 17, Form 944 line 13 or Form 945 line 7) in place of Schedule B (Form 941), Form 943-A or Form 945-A (Form 945-A for Forms 944 and 945), failed to attach a properly completed Schedule B (Form 941), Form 943-A or Form 945-A as applicable, or completed that schedule improperly, for example by entering tax deposits instead of tax liabilities in the numbered spaces.

The penalty is figured by spreading the total tax liability from the liability line evenly across the tax period. Deposits and payments are then applied to those averaged liabilities in the date order the IRS received them, and the penalty is figured on any tax not deposited, deposited late or not deposited in the correct amounts. Deposits and payments may not be counted as timely, because the actual dates of the liabilities can’t be accurately determined.

**Avoiding an “averaged” FTD penalty (p. 37).** The penalty can be avoided by reviewing the return before filing it. Before submitting Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 or Form 945, take these steps:
- A monthly schedule depositor reports tax liabilities (not deposits) in the monthly entry spaces of the reporting line (Form 941 line 16, Form 943 line 17, Form 944 line 13 or Form 945 line 7).
- A semiweekly schedule depositor reports tax liabilities (not deposits) on Schedule B (Form 941), Form 943-A or Form 945-A, as applicable, on the lines for the dates employees were paid.
- Check that the total liability on the reporting line, or at the bottom of Schedule B (Form 941) or on line M of Form 943-A or Form 945-A, equals the liability on the liability line: Form 941 line 16 (or the bottom of Schedule B) against line 12; Form 943 line 17 (or Form 943-A line M) against line 13; Form 944 line 13 (or Form 945-A line M) against line 9; Form 945 line 7 (or Form 945-A line M) against line 3.
- Don’t show negative amounts on the reporting lines or on Schedule B (Form 941), Form 943-A or Form 945-A.
- For prior-period errors, don’t adjust the liabilities reported on those lines or schedules; file an adjusted return (Form 941-X, 943-X, 944-X or 945-X) if you are also adjusting your tax liability. If you are only adjusting deposits in response to an FTD penalty notice, the page refers to the Instructions for Schedule B (Form 941), for Form 943-A (for Form 943) or for Form 945-A (for Forms 944 and 945).

**Criminal prosecution (p. 37).** On top of civil penalties, you may face criminal prosecution (a trial) for willful acts of these kinds: evading tax; failing to collect tax, or to account for and pay it over truthfully; failing to file a return, supply information or pay tax due; furnishing false or fraudulent Forms W-2 to employees, or not furnishing Forms W-2; committing fraud and giving false statements; preparing and filing a fraudulent return; and identity theft.

**Related:** When To Deposit — the two deposit schedules, monthly and semiweekly, and the lookback period (p. 32)

## Note
**Who must be notified (p. 31).** You must notify employees who have no federal income tax withheld that they may be able to claim a tax refund because of the EIC. This does not apply to employees in American Samoa, Guam, Puerto Rico, the CNMI and the USVI. Notifying employees who claim exemption from withholding on Form W-4 about the EIC is not required. Notifying any employee whose wages for 2025 were less than $61,555 ($68,675 if married filing jointly) is encouraged, so that they know they may be eligible to claim the credit for 2025; the page gives the reason that eligible employees may get a refund of the amount of the EIC that exceeds the tax they owe.

**How to meet the requirement (p. 31).** Issuing the employee a Form W-2 with the EIC notice printed on the back of Copy B meets the notification requirement, as does a substitute Form W-2 carrying the same statement. Providing Notice 797, Possible Federal Tax Refund Due to the Earned Income Credit (EIC), or a statement of your own with the same wording, also meets it.

**Timing (p. 31).**
- A substitute for Form W-2 may be given on time without the required statement. You must then notify the employee within 1 week of the date the substitute was given.
- Form W-2 may be required but not given on time. You must then give the employee Notice 797 or your written statement by the date Form W-2 is required to be given.
- Form W-2 may not be required. You must then notify the employee by February 9, 2026.

**Related:** Federal Income Tax Withholding — the Form W-4 and its use in figuring federal income tax withholding, including exemption from withholding (p. 27)

## Note
- Unless otherwise noted, the publication’s references to Form W-3 also cover Form W-3SS and Form W-3 (PR) (F04, p. 3).
- Form W-3 is printed as Transmittal of Wage and Tax Statements; under the Calendar’s By January 31 date, you send the SSA Copy A of every 2025 Form W-2, paper or electronic, together with Form W-3 (F21, p. 11).
- Forms W-2AS, W-2CM, W-2GU and W-2VI go with Form W-3SS, and Forms 499R-2/W-2PR go with Form W-3 (PR) (F21, p. 11).
- When you file through the SSA’s Form W-2 Online service, the SSA produces the Form W-3 data itself from the Form(s) W-2 you submit electronically (F21, p. 11).
- Copy 1 of Forms W-2AS, W-2CM, W-2GU and W-2VI, together with Form W-3SS, goes to your local tax department at the address printed on Form W-3SS (F21, p. 11).
- In place of ordering paper Forms W-2 and W-3, the page suggests considering the SSA’s free e-file service, and says Form W-3 is created for you from your Forms W-2 (F19, p. 10).
- The IRS runs the TSO to answer questions about reporting on Forms W-2, W-3 and 1099 and on other information returns (F08, p. 7).
- The Employer Responsibilities list, under Annually (see Calendar for due dates), includes filing Copy A of Forms W-2 with the transmittal Form W-3 to the SSA, and reconciling Forms 941 (or Form 943 or Form 944) with Forms W-2 and W-3 (F09, p. 8).
- An employer that must file a final return must also file Forms W-2 and W-3 with the SSA, by the final return’s due date (S12, p. 39).
- Discrepancies between Forms 941, 943 or 944 filed with the IRS and Forms W-2 and W-3 filed with the SSA may lead the IRS or the SSA to contact you (S12, p. 39).
- To reduce discrepancies, report social security and Medicare wages and taxes separately, both on Forms W-2 and W-3 and on Forms 941, 943 or 944 (S12, p. 40).
- If an EIN you used on a Form 941, 943 or 944 during the year differs from the EIN reported on Form W-3, put the other EIN in the Form W-3 box “Other EIN used this year” (box h); the matching box on Form W-3 (PR) is box f (S12, p. 40).
- The amounts on Form W-3 must add up to the amounts from your Forms W-2 (S12, p. 40).
- Form W-3 is reconciled with your four quarterly Forms 941, or your annual Form 943 or Form 944, by comparing federal income tax withheld, social security and Medicare wages, and social security and Medicare taxes (S12, p. 40).
- Generally the social security and Medicare taxes on Forms 941, 943 or 944 (current year adjustments included) come to roughly double those on Form W-3, since the returns count the employer share and the employee share while Form W-3 counts only the employee share (S12, p. 40).
- Amounts on Forms W-2, W-3 and Forms 941, 943 or 944 can differ for valid reasons (S12, p. 40).
- Where Additional Medicare Tax was withheld, the Medicare tax on Form 941 (line 5c, column 2), Form 943 (line 5) or Form 944 (line 4c, column 2) will not be double the Medicare tax withheld shown in box 6 of Form W-3 (box 13 of Form W-3 (PR)), because that tax falls on the employee alone (S12, p. 40).
- Under the heading Correcting filed Forms W-2 and W-3, the page says a changed wage total for a previous year, which leads to adjusting wages and social security and Medicare taxes, also means filing Form W-2c and Form W-3c with the SSA (S13.02, p. 43).

## Note
**What you must file (p. 7).** Wages paid to employees are reported by filing Forms W-2. Certain other payments made during the year may also require information returns. As an example, Form 1099-NEC, Nonemployee Compensation, must be filed for payments to persons not treated as employees (independent contractors, for instance) for services performed for your trade or business: $600 or more if paid in 2025, and $2,000 or more if paid in 2026.

**Where the details are (p. 7).** Details on filing Forms 1099 for payments made in 2025, and on required electronic filing, are in the General Instructions for Certain Information Returns and in the separate, specific instructions for each information return you file; the Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC are one example. The page says a new Pub. 1099 will replace those general instructions for payments made after 2025. Details on filing Form W-2, and on its required electronic filing, are in the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3.

**Forms 1099 and wages (p. 7).** Generally, wages and other compensation paid to employees are reported on Form W-2, not on Forms 1099.

**Technical Services Operation (TSO) (p. 7).** The IRS operates the TSO to answer questions on reporting on Forms W-2, W-3 and 1099 and other information returns. Questions can be put by phone to 866-455-7438 (toll free), 304-263-8700 (toll call) or 304-579-4827 (TDD), or by email to mccirp@irs.gov. Taxpayer identification numbers (TINs) and attachments should not go in an email, because email isn’t secure.

**Related:** Federal Income Tax Withholding — withholding federal income tax from each wage payment or supplemental unemployment compensation plan benefit payment (p. 7)

text:
## Note
Employment taxes, Form 945 taxes included, must be deposited by EFT. For the cases in which tax may be paid with the return in place of a deposit, the page points back to Payment with return (p. 35).

**Electronic deposit requirement (p. 35).** Every federal tax deposit must be made by EFT, which can be done through EFTPS, IRS Direct Pay or your IRS business tax account. If you prefer not to use one of these, you can arrange for your tax professional, financial institution, payroll service or another trusted third party to make the electronic deposits for you. EFTPS is a free service of the Department of the Treasury, and payments through IRS Direct Pay or the IRS business tax account are free as well. For more on IRS Direct Pay and on payments through the business tax account, the page gives IRS.gov/Pay; for more on EFTPS or to enroll, it gives EFTPS.gov and telephone numbers, among them numbers for reaching EFTPS through TRS. Pub. 966 has further information on EFTPS.

**When you receive your EIN (p. 35).** A new employer that indicated a federal tax obligation when requesting an EIN is pre-enrolled in EFTPS. The EIN Package carries information about Express Enrollment, and a further mailing brings the EFTPS personal identification number (PIN) with instructions for activating it. The enrollment is activated by calling the toll-free number in the “How to Activate Your Enrollment” brochure, after which payroll tax deposits can begin. An employer that outsources payroll and related tax duties to a third-party payer, such as a payroll service provider (PSP) or reporting agent, should tell that payer about the EFTPS enrollment.

**Deposit record (p. 35).** Each successful payment gets an EFT Trace Number, which can serve as a receipt or be used to trace the payment.

**Depositing on time (p. 36).** EFTPS accepts same-day payments of $1 million or less when they are submitted before 3:00 p.m. Eastern time on a business day. A payment above $1 million has to be submitted by 8:00 p.m. Eastern time on the day before the deposit is due. A third party making the deposit for you may set different cutoff times.

**Same-day wire payment option (p. 36).** If a timely deposit transaction wasn’t submitted on EFTPS, the Federal Tax Collection Service (FTCS) can still be used for a same-day wire payment that makes the deposit on time. This needs arrangements with your financial institution in advance; availability, deadlines and costs are to be checked with it, and it may charge a fee. The page gives IRS.gov/SameDayWire for the information to give your financial institution.

**Claiming credit for overpayments (p. 36).** Where more than the right amount of taxes was deposited for a quarter, the choice between a refund and a credit toward the next return is made on Form 941 for that quarter (or on Form 943, Form 944 or Form 945 for the year). EFTPS is not to be asked to request a refund from the IRS.

**Related:** Deposit Penalties — penalties for deposits that are late or for less than the required amount, and the penalty rates (p. 36)

text:
## Note
A deposit that falls due on a day that is not a business day is timely if it is made by the close of the next business day. Any day except a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday is a business day. For example, a deposit due on a Friday that is a legal holiday is timely if it is made the following Monday, provided that Monday is a business day.

A semiweekly schedule depositor has at least 3 business days after the close of the semiweekly period in which to deposit. Each legal holiday among the 3 weekdays after the end of a semiweekly period adds one more day for the required deposit. For example, with taxes accumulated on payments made on a Friday and the following Monday a legal holiday, the deposit normally due on Wednesday may be made on Thursday, which still leaves 3 business days.

**Legal holiday.** The term means any legal holiday in the District of Columbia; for the deposit rules it leaves out other statewide legal holidays. The 2026 legal holidays are:
- New Year’s Day, January 1
- Birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr., January 19
- Washington’s Birthday, February 16
- District of Columbia Emancipation Day, April 16
- Memorial Day, May 25
- Juneteenth National Independence Day, June 19
- Independence Day (observed), July 3
- Labor Day, September 7
- Indigenous Peoples’ Day (Columbus Day), October 12
- Veterans Day, November 11
- Thanksgiving Day, November 26
- Christmas Day, December 25

**Related:** Application of Monthly and Semiweekly Schedules — what the terms monthly and semiweekly schedule depositor mean, with an example of each (p. 34)

source.attribution: Internal Revenue Service, Publication 15 (2026), Catalog Number 10000W
source.title: Publication 15 (Circular E), Employer’s Tax Guide

text:
## Note
How To Get Tax Help lists IRS resources for answers to tax questions, forms and publications, tax return preparers, language and accessibility services, payments, and responding to notices, and it ends with a message from the Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS). The chapter's own text is summarised below. The message from TAS has four parts, which follow in the cluster.

**Where to start (p. 56).** For questions about a tax issue, help preparing a tax return, or free publications, forms and instructions, the page says to go to IRS.gov for resources that can help right away.

**Tax reform (p. 56).** Tax reform legislation affecting federal taxes, credits and deductions was enacted in P.L. 119-21. IRS.gov/OBBB has more information and updates on how it affects your taxes.

**Preparing and filing your tax return (p. 56).** IRS.gov/EmploymentEfile has more information on filing employment tax returns electronically.

**Getting answers to your tax questions (p. 56).** IRS.gov has up-to-date information on current events and changes in tax law. IRS.gov/Help offers a variety of tools for answers to some of the most common tax questions. IRS.gov/Forms has forms, instructions and publications, with details on the most recent tax changes and interactive links to help find answers. Tax information may also be accessible in your e-filing software.

**Need someone to prepare your tax return? (p. 56).** There are various types of tax return preparers, including enrolled agents, certified public accountants (CPAs), accountants, and many others without professional credentials, and the page says to choose a preparer wisely. A paid tax preparer is primarily responsible for the overall substantive accuracy of your return, is required to sign the return, and is required to include their preparer tax identification number (PTIN). The Caution says that although the preparer always signs the return, you are ultimately responsible for providing all the information the preparer needs to prepare it accurately and for the accuracy of every item reported on it. Anyone paid to prepare returns for others should have a thorough understanding of tax matters. The page refers to Tips for Choosing a Tax Preparer on IRS.gov.

**Business Services Online and W-2 filing (p. 57).** Employers can register to use Business Services Online. The SSA offers an online service at SSA.gov/employer, described as fast, free and secure, for W-2 filing by CPAs, accountants, enrolled agents and individuals who process Form W-2 and Form W-2c.

**Business tax account (p. 57).** A sole proprietor, partnership, S corporation, C corporation or single-member limited liability company (LLC) can view its tax information on record with the IRS and do more with a business tax account. IRS.gov/BusinessAccount has more information.

**IRS social media (p. 57).** IRS.gov/SocialMedia lists the social media tools the IRS uses to share the latest information on tax changes, scam alerts, initiatives, products and services. The page says that at the IRS, privacy and security are the highest priority, and that these tools are used to share public information. Do not post your identification number (EIN or SSN) or other confidential information on social media sites, and always protect your identity when using any social networking site. Three IRS YouTube channels offer short videos on various tax-related topics in English, Spanish and ASL: Youtube.com/irsvideos, Youtube.com/irsvideosmultilingua and Youtube.com/irsvideosASL.

**Online tax information in other languages (p. 57).** IRS.gov/MyLanguage has information for those whose native language is not English.

**Over-the-Phone Interpreter (OPI) Service (p. 57).** Taxpayers who need language interpretation can use the IRS's OPI Service. Its locations are Taxpayer Assistance Centers (TACs), most IRS offices, and each Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) and Tax Counseling for the Elderly (TCE) return site. The languages offered are Spanish, Mandarin, Cantonese, Korean, Vietnamese, Russian and Haitian Creole.

**Accessibility Helpline (p. 57).** Taxpayers with disabilities who need information about accessibility services can call 833-690-0598. The Helpline can answer questions about current and future accessibility products and services available in alternative media formats (for example, braille-ready, large print, audio, etc.). It does not have access to your IRS account. For help with tax law, refunds or account-related issues, the page refers to IRS.gov/LetUsHelp.

**Disasters (p. 57).** IRS.gov/DisasterRelief lists the available disaster tax relief.

**Getting tax forms and publications (p. 57).** IRS.gov/Forms is where most of the forms, instructions and publications needed can be viewed, downloaded or printed, and IRS.gov/OrderForms is where to place an order.

**Getting tax publications and instructions in eBook format (p. 57).** Most tax publications and instructions (including Pub. 15) can be downloaded and viewed on mobile devices as eBooks at IRS.gov/eBooks. The IRS eBooks have been tested using Apple's iBooks for iPad. They have not been tested on other dedicated eBook readers, and eBook functionality may not operate as intended.

**Get a transcript of your return (p. 57).** Return transcripts of Form 940, Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 and Form 945 for tax years 2023 and later can now be accessed through your IRS business tax account. The page refers to IRS.gov/BusinessTranscript and, for the business tax account, to IRS.gov/BusinessAccount.

**Using direct deposit (p. 57).** The page calls e-filing and choosing direct deposit the safest and easiest way to receive a tax refund; direct deposit securely and electronically transfers the refund into your financial account. Direct deposit also avoids the possibility that a check could be lost, stolen, destroyed or returned undeliverable to the IRS. Someone without a bank account can go to IRS.gov/DirectDeposit for where to find a bank or credit union that can open an account online.

**Reporting and resolving your tax-related identity theft issues (p. 57).**
- Tax-related identity theft means someone steals your personal information in order to commit tax fraud. If your EIN is used for a fraudulent return, or to claim a refund or credit, your taxes can be affected.
- The IRS does not start contact with taxpayers through email, text messages (shortened links included), telephone calls or social media channels to ask for or confirm personal or financial information. That covers requests for personal identification numbers (PINs), passwords or similar details for credit cards, banks or other financial accounts.
- IRS.gov/IdentityTheft, called the IRS Identity Theft Central webpage, carries information about identity theft and data security protection for taxpayers, tax professionals and businesses. A person whose EIN has been lost or stolen, or who suspects tax-related identity theft, can learn which steps to take.

**Making a tax payment (pp. 57–58).** The IRS recommends paying electronically whenever possible. Payments of U.S. tax must be remitted to the IRS in U.S. dollars, and digital assets are not accepted. IRS.gov/Pay has information on how to pay with any of these options (pp. 57–58):
- IRS Direct Pay: taxes are paid from your bank account. It is free and secure, needs no sign-in, and lets you change or cancel within 2 days of the scheduled payment.
- Debit Card, Credit Card or Digital Wallet: an approved payment processor takes the payment online or by phone.
- Electronic Funds Withdrawal: a payment is scheduled while you file your federal taxes, through tax return preparation software or a tax professional.
- Electronic Federal Tax Payment System: described as the best option for businesses; enrollment is required.
- Check or Money Order: the payment is mailed to the address on the notice or instructions.
- Cash: payment in cash may be possible at a participating retail store.
- Same-Day Wire: a same-day wire from your financial institution may be possible; ask the institution about availability, cost and time frames.

The page's Note says the IRS uses the latest encryption technology to ensure that electronic payments made online, by phone or from a mobile device using the IRS2Go app are safe and secure, and that paying electronically is quick and easy (p. 58).

**What if I can't pay now? (p. 58).** IRS.gov/Pay has more information about the options. A taxpayer who cannot pay in full today can apply for an online payment agreement (IRS.gov/OPA) to meet the tax obligation in monthly installments, and immediately learns whether the agreement has been approved once the online process is complete. The Offer in Compromise Pre-Qualifier shows whether a tax debt can be settled for less than the full amount owed; IRS.gov/OIC has more on the Offer in Compromise program.

**Understanding an IRS notice or letter (p. 58).** IRS.gov/Notices has additional information about responding to an IRS notice or letter.

**IRS Document Upload Tool (p. 58).** For eligible IRS notices and letters, a taxpayer may be able to reply digitally with the Document Upload Tool, which securely uploads the required documents online through IRS.gov. The page refers to IRS.gov/DUT.

**Contacting your local TAC (p. 58).** Many questions can be answered on IRS.gov without visiting a TAC, and IRS.gov/LetUsHelp covers the topics people ask about most. If you still need help, TACs provide tax help when a tax issue cannot be handled online or by phone. All TACs now provide service by appointment, so you know in advance that you can get the service you need without long wait times. Before visiting, go to IRS.gov/TAC to find the nearest TAC and to check hours, available services and appointment options. Alternatively, on the IRS2Go app, under the Stay Connected tab, choose the Contact Us option and click on "Local Offices."

**Message from the Taxpayer Advocate Service (p. 58).** The page introduces the message that follows as one from the Taxpayer Advocate Service, an independent organization established by Congress.

## The Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) Is Here To Help You
- What Is the Taxpayer Advocate Service? — what TAS is, what it does and the Taxpayer Bill of Rights (p. 58)
- How Can TAS Help Me? — who TAS helps, when you may be eligible, the TAS website for general tax topics and reporting systemic issues (p. 58)
- How Do I Contact TAS? — where TAS has offices and three ways to find a local advocate's number (p. 58)
- What Are My Rights as a Taxpayer? — the ten basic rights of the Taxpayer Bill of Rights and where to read more about them (p. 58)

## Note
**Caution (p. 7).** Employers in American Samoa, Guam, the CNMI, the USVI and Puerto Rico can disregard the references to federal income tax withholding, unless they have employees who are subject to U.S. income tax withholding. For information about income tax withholding they should contact their local tax department.

**What to withhold on (pp. 7–8).** Federal income tax is withheld from each wage payment or supplemental unemployment compensation plan benefit payment, based on the employee’s Form W-4 and on the correct table in Pub. 15-T. Farm operators and crew leaders must also withhold federal income tax from farmworkers’ wages when those wages are subject to social security and Medicare taxes. For supplemental wages paid to an employee, the page refers to section 7. For nonresident alien employees, it refers to Withholding federal income taxes on the wages of nonresident alien employees in section 9. For withholding on pensions (including distributions from tax-favored retirement plans), annuities and individual retirement arrangements (IRAs), it refers to section 8 of Pub. 15-A.

**Employer Responsibilities (p. 8).** The page gives a list that briefly summarises your basic responsibilities. Individual circumstances can vary greatly, so responsibilities for withholding, depositing and reporting employment taxes can differ. Each item carries a page reference to a more detailed discussion in the publication, and those pages are given below.

*New employees:*
- Verify work eligibility of new employees (page 7).
- Record employees’ names and SSNs from social security cards (page 7).
- Ask employees for Form W-4 (page 7).

*Each payday:*
- Withhold federal income tax based on each employee’s Form W-4 (page 25).
- Withhold the employee’s share of social security and Medicare taxes (page 29).
- Deposit the withheld federal income tax, the withheld and employer social security taxes, and the withheld and employer Medicare taxes (page 31). How soon a deposit is due generally depends on whether you follow the monthly or the semiweekly deposit schedule.

*Quarterly (by April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31):*
- Deposit FUTA tax if the undeposited amount is over $500 (page 44).
- File Form 941, paying the tax with the return if not required to deposit (page 38).

*Annually (see Calendar for due dates):*
- File Form 943 if required, paying the tax with the return if not required to deposit (page 38).
- File Form 944 if required, paying the tax with the return if not required to deposit (page 38).
- Remind employees to submit a new Form W-4 if they need to change their federal income tax withholding (page 25).
- Ask employees who claim exemption from federal income tax withholding for a new Form W-4 (page 27).
- Reconcile Forms 941 (or Form 943 or Form 944) with Forms W-2 and W-3 (page 39).
- Furnish each employee a Form W-2 (page 11).
- File Copy A of Forms W-2 and the transmittal Form W-3 with the SSA (page 11).
- Furnish each payee a Form 1099, for example Form 1099-NEC (page 11).
- File Forms 1099 and the transmittal Form 1096 (page 11).
- File Form 940 (page 11).
- File Form 945 for any nonpayroll income tax withholding (page 11).

**Related:** 7. Supplemental Wages — wage payments to an employee that are not regular wages, and the kinds of payment they include (p. 23)

text:
## Note
A Form 941 filer is a monthly schedule depositor for a calendar year when the Form 941 line 12 taxes of the 4 quarters in the lookback period add up to $50,000 or less. A filer of Form 943, Form 944 or Form 945 is a monthly schedule depositor for the calendar year when the lookback-period taxes, taken from line 13 of Form 943, line 9 of Form 944 or line 3 of Form 945, were $50,000 or less.

The monthly schedule calls for employment taxes on payments made in a month to be deposited by the 15th day of the next month. The page points ahead to Deposits Due on Business Days Only and to the $100,000 Next-Day Deposit Rule. A monthly schedule depositor should not file Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 or Form 945 every month.

**New employers.** For a Form 941 filer, tax liability for any lookback-period quarter that came before the business was started or acquired counts as zero, which makes the filer a monthly schedule depositor in the first calendar year of the business. For a filer of Form 943, Form 944 or Form 945, liability in the lookback period before the start or acquisition of the business likewise counts as zero, which gives monthly schedule depositor status in the first and second calendar years. The page then says to see the $100,000 Next-Day Deposit Rule, later in the section.

**Related:** Semiweekly Deposit Schedule — who is a semiweekly schedule depositor and the weekdays by which deposits are due (p. 33)

text:
## Note
**Caution (p. 43).** Employers in American Samoa, Guam and the CNMI do not owe FUTA tax, but employers in the USVI and Puerto Rico do. Work done for a federally recognized Indian tribal government is exempt from FUTA tax, as is work for any subdivision, subsidiary or wholly owned business of such a tribe, subject to the tribe's compliance with state law. The page refers to section 3309(d) and to Pub. 4268.

**The tax (p. 43).** The Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA) works with state unemployment systems to pay unemployment compensation to workers who have lost their jobs. Most employers pay a federal and also a state unemployment tax. The page refers to the U.S. Department of Labor's website for a list of state unemployment agencies. Only the employer pays FUTA tax; it is not withheld from the employee's wages. The page refers to the Instructions for Form 940.

**Who must pay (pp. 43–44).** Three tests decide whether FUTA tax must be paid. Each applies to a different category of employee and each is independent of the others. If a test describes the employer's situation, the employer is subject to FUTA tax on the wages it pays to employees in that category during the current calendar year.
1. General test: for wages paid to employees who are not farmworkers or household workers, the employer is subject to FUTA tax in 2026 if either (a) it paid wages of $1,500 or more in any calendar quarter of 2025 or 2026, or (b) it had at least one employee, for some part of a day, in each of 20 or more different weeks of 2025 or of 20 or more different weeks of 2026.
2. Household employees test: the employer is subject to FUTA tax in 2026 if it paid total cash wages of $1,000 or more to household employees in any calendar quarter of 2025 or 2026. A household employee does household work in a private home, a local college club, or a local fraternity or sorority chapter.
3. Farmworkers test: for wages paid to farmworkers, the employer is subject to FUTA tax in 2026 if either (a) it paid cash wages of $20,000 or more to farmworkers in any calendar quarter of 2025 or 2026, or (b) it employed 10 or more farmworkers, for some part of a day and not necessarily at the same time, in each of 20 or more different weeks of 2025 or of 20 or more different weeks of 2026.

Under either farmworker test, the employer must count wages paid to aliens admitted to the United States on a temporary basis to perform farmwork (H-2A visa workers). Wages paid to H-2A visa workers are nevertheless not subject to FUTA tax (p. 44). Farmworkers supplied by crew leaders, as defined earlier in section 2, are generally treated as employees of the farm operator for FUTA tax. The exceptions are where (a) the crew leader is registered under the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act, or (b) substantially all the workers the crew leader supplies operate or maintain tractors, harvesting or crop-dusting machines, or other machines the crew leader provides. If (a) or (b) applies, the farmworkers are generally employees of the crew leader (p. 44).

**Figuring FUTA tax (p. 44).** For 2026 the FUTA tax rate is 6.0%. The tax applies to the first $7,000 paid to each employee as wages during the year, which is the federal wage base; the state wage base limit may be different. Generally, a credit against FUTA tax is allowed for amounts paid into state unemployment funds, and it may be as much as 5.4% of FUTA taxable wages. An employer with the full 5.4% credit has a FUTA tax rate of 0.6% after the credit. The maximum credit goes to an employer that paid its state unemployment taxes in full, on time, and on every wage that is also subject to FUTA tax, provided the state is not determined to be a credit reduction state. The page refers to the Instructions for Form 940 to determine the credit.

In some states, state unemployment tax covers the very wages that FUTA tax covers. Certain states, though, leave some kinds of wages out of state unemployment tax although FUTA tax applies to them: the page's examples are wages paid to corporate officers, certain payments of sick pay by unions, and certain fringe benefits. For such wages the employer may be required to deposit more than 0.6% FUTA tax. The page refers to the Instructions for Form 940 (p. 44).

**Successor employer (p. 44).** An employer that acquired a business from an employer who was liable for FUTA tax may be able to count the wages that employer paid to the employees who continue to work for it when figuring the $7,000 FUTA tax wage base limit. The page refers to the Instructions for Form 940.

**Depositing FUTA tax (p. 44).** For deposit purposes, FUTA tax is figured quarterly. The liability is the taxable wages paid during the quarter multiplied by 0.6%, an amount that may need adjusting depending on entitlement to the credit for state unemployment contributions. The page refers to the Instructions for Form 940. Deposits of FUTA tax on an employee's wages stop once taxable wages reach $7,000 for the calendar year. If the FUTA tax liability for a calendar quarter is $500 or less, no deposit is required; the amount may be carried forward and added to the liability figured in the next quarter to see whether a deposit must be made. If the liability for a calendar quarter is over $500 (including any FUTA tax carried forward from an earlier quarter), the tax must be deposited by EFT. The page points to section 11 for more on EFTs.

**Household employees (p. 44).** FUTA taxes for household employees need not be deposited unless their wages are reported on Forms 941, Form 943 or Form 944. The page refers to Pub. 926.

**When to deposit (p. 44).** The FUTA tax is deposited by the last day of the first month after the end of the quarter. If the due date falls on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, the deposit may be made on the next business day. The page points to Legal holiday in section 11 for a list of the legal holidays occurring in 2026. If the liability for the fourth quarter (plus any undeposited amount from any earlier quarter) is over $500, the entire amount is deposited by the due date of Form 940 (January 31). If it is $500 or less, the employer can make a deposit, pay the tax with a credit or debit card, or pay the tax with its Form 940 by January 31. An employer that files Form 940 electronically can e-file and use EFW to pay the balance due. The page refers to IRS.gov/Pay for paying by credit or debit card or using EFW.

**Caution (p. 44).** In years when there are credit reduction states, liabilities owed for credit reduction must be included with the fourth quarter deposit. The anticipated extra liability may be deposited throughout the year, but it is not due until the due date for the fourth quarter deposit, and the associated liability should be recorded as incurred in the fourth quarter. The page refers to the Instructions for Form 940.

Table 4. When To Deposit FUTA Taxes (p. 44)

| Quarter months | Quarter ending | Deposit due date |
|---|---|---|
| Jan.–Feb.–Mar. | Mar. 31 | Apr. 30 |
| Apr.–May–June | June 30 | July 31 |
| July–Aug.–Sept. | Sept. 30 | Oct. 31 |
| Oct.–Nov.–Dec. | Dec. 31 | Jan. 31 |

**Reporting FUTA tax (pp. 44–45).** Form 940 is used to report FUTA tax. The 2025 Form 940 is due February 2, 2026; an employer that deposited all FUTA tax when due may file on or before February 10, 2026.

**Form 940 e-file (p. 45).** The Form 940 e-file program lets a taxpayer file an original Form 940 and an amended Form 940 electronically.

**Electronic filing by reporting agents (p. 45).** Reporting agents who file Forms 940 for groups of taxpayers can file them electronically. The page points to Electronic filing by reporting agents in section 12.

**Electronic filing by CPEOs (p. 45).** CPEOs must file Form 940 electronically with Schedule R (Form 940). In certain circumstances the IRS may waive the electronic filing requirement. To ask for a waiver, the CPEO must send a written request through the IRS Online Registration System for Professional Employer Organizations at least 45 days before the due date of the return it cannot file electronically. The page refers to Revenue Procedure 2023-18.

**Household employees (p. 45).** An employer that did not report employment taxes for household employees on Forms 941, Form 943 or Form 944 reports FUTA tax for them on Schedule H (Form 1040), and must have an EIN to file Schedule H (Form 1040). The page refers to Pub. 926.

**Related:** 12. Filing Forms 941, Form 943, Form 944, or Form 945 — who files Form 941, Form 943, Form 944 and Form 945, when they are due, e-file and penalties (p. 38)

text:
## Note
**Filing and paying electronically (p. 6).** Businesses can benefit from filing and paying federal taxes electronically, and the IRS offers convenient and secure programs for this, whether a tax professional is relied on or the business handles its own taxes. For e-file the page points to IRS.gov/EmploymentEfile and says a fee may be charged to file electronically. For electronic payment options it points to IRS.gov/Pay.

**Electronic filing of Forms W-2 (p. 6).** The page points to SSA.gov/employer for electronic filing of Forms W-2 (Forms W-2AS, W-2CM, W-2GU, W-2VI and Forms 499R-2/W-2PR included). Electronic filing of Forms W-2 may be required, and the page refers to the General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3. Anyone with problems filing electronically can contact the SSA at 800-772-6270. The SSA’s Regional Employer Services Liaison Officer can be reached through SSA.gov/employer/wage_reporting_specialists.htm, and these officers can help with all questions about the SSA’s payroll reporting processes and applications.

**Employers in the CNMI and Puerto Rico (p. 6).** CNMI employers are told to contact their local tax department for instructions on completing Form W-2CM; the form and its instructions are at Finance.gov.mp/forms.php or by calling 670-664-1000. The SSA’s Business Services Online (BSO) is independent of the Government of Puerto Rico’s electronic filing system, and Puerto Rico employers must go to Hacienda.pr.gov for additional information.

**Caution: a valid EIN is required (p. 6).** Whenever a return is filed or a federal tax payment made electronically, a valid employer identification number (EIN) must be provided at that time. A return or payment submitted without a valid EIN won’t be processed, and penalties may follow. The page refers to section 1 for applying for an EIN.

**Electronic funds withdrawal (EFW) (pp. 6–7).** An employment tax return that is e-filed can be paid, as to the balance due, in the same step by EFW, through tax preparation software or a tax professional. EFW must not be used for federal tax deposits. The page points to IRS.gov/EFW.

**Credit or debit card payments (p. 7).** The balance due shown on an employment tax return can be paid by credit or debit card. A payment processor handles the payment and charges a processing fee. A credit or debit card must not be used for federal tax deposits. The page points to IRS.gov/PayByCard.

**Online payment agreement (p. 7).** If you can’t pay the full tax you owe when you file your employment tax return, you may be eligible to apply online for an installment agreement. The page refers to the instructions for your employment tax return and to IRS.gov/OPA.

**Related:** 1. Employer Identification Number (EIN) — the nine-digit employer identification number and how to apply for one (p. 13)

## Note
Code section 7654 and 48 U.S.C. section 1681 (P.L. 94-241, section 703(b)) require the U.S. Government to cover over federal income taxes to the CNMI Treasury. These are the taxes withheld on payments to military and civilian employees and to pensioners who are residents of the CNMI (pp. 54–55). The federal government transfers the federal income taxes withheld or collected from those employees and pensioners to the CNMI Treasury at least once a year (p. 55).

To let the federal government cover over these taxes as the law requires, federal agencies must certify the federal income taxes withheld or collected from their employees and pensioners, following the procedures under Certification Procedures, later in the section (p. 55). Federal agencies are not required to certify local CNMI taxes that are withheld or collected, as the Caution next to it explains (p. 55).

**Caution (p. 55).** In December 2006 the U.S. Treasury Department and the CNMI Division of Revenue and Taxation made an agreement under 5 U.S.C. section 5517. Under it, every federal employer (the Department of Defense included) must withhold CNMI income taxes in place of federal income taxes, and deposit them with the CNMI Treasury, for employees whose regular place of federal employment is the CNMI. Federal employers must also file quarterly and annual reports with the CNMI Division of Revenue and Taxation. The 5517 agreement does not apply to payments to pensioners, or to pay of members of the U.S. Armed Forces who are stationed in the CNMI but whose state of legal residence is outside the CNMI. The page refers to IRS.gov/5517Agreements for more information, including details on completing Form W-2.

**Related:** Certification Procedures — the procedures federal agencies follow to certify to the IRS the federal income taxes paid to and deposited into the U.S. Treasury (p. 55)

## Note
- Return transcripts for Forms 940, 941, 943, 944 and 945 for tax years 2023 and later are now available through your IRS business tax account (F03, p. 3).
- Federal income tax withheld on nonpayroll payments (reported on Forms 1099 and Form W-2G) is reported on Form 945, Annual Return of Withheld Federal Income Tax (F10, p. 8).
- Payroll withholding (Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944) and nonpayroll withholding (Form 945) require separate deposits (F10, p. 8).
- Nonpayroll items include pensions (distributions from tax-favored retirement plans too) and annuities, IRA distributions, military retirement, gambling winnings, Indian gaming profits, and payments subject to backup withholding, among others the page lists; details on depositing and reporting are in the Instructions for Form 945 (F10, p. 8).
- Distributions to participants from some nonqualified pension and deferred compensation plans are treated as wages, so the income tax withheld goes on Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 and not on Form 945 (F10, pp. 8–9).
- Distributions from such plans to the beneficiary or estate of a deceased employee are not wages; they are reported on Forms 1099-R, and the income tax withheld on them goes on Form 945 (F10, p. 9).
- The Employer Responsibilities list includes filing Form 945 for any nonpayroll income tax withholding among the items under Annually (see Calendar for due dates) (F09, p. 8).
- The filing address for Form 945 generally turns on where your residence or principal place of business is located and on whether a payment goes with the return (F14, p. 9).
- Tax-exempt organizations and government entities have separate filing addresses, which are in the separate instructions for Form 945 (F14, pp. 9–10).
- Under the Calendar’s By January 31 date, Form 945 reports any nonpayroll federal income tax withheld; if all taxes were deposited when due, it may be filed by February 10 (F21, p. 11).
- The name and EIN on Form 945 have to match those on your information returns that report federal income tax withholding, such as backup withholding shown on Form 1099-NEC (S01, pp. 13–14).
- An incorrect EIN, or another business’s EIN, on Form 945 can lead to penalties and delays in processing the return (S01, p. 14).
- An employer must backup withhold when an H-2A worker gives no TIN and the worker’s total annual wages are at least $600 in 2025 ($2,000 in 2026); the page refers to the Instructions for Form 945 (S05, p. 19).
- A payment may accompany a timely filed Form 941, 943, 944 or 945 in place of a deposit, without penalty, in the cases the page lists; for Form 945 that case is annual total tax liability (Form 945, line 3) under $2,500 (S11, p. 31).
- If you aren’t sure you will report under $2,500 on Form 945, deposit under the section’s rules to avoid an FTD penalty (S11, p. 31).
- Deposits for Forms 941 (or 943 or 944) and for Form 945 are kept apart and never combined (S11, pp. 31–32).
- Nonpayroll deposit rules are generally the same as the payroll rules, except that the return period is a year, not a quarter; if the year’s total tax reported on Form 945 is under $2,500, no deposits are required during the year (S11, p. 32).
- A Form 945 filer’s deposit schedule for a calendar year comes from the total taxes on line 3 of its Form 945 for the second preceding calendar year, so the lookback period for 2026 is calendar year 2024 (S11.01, p. 32).
- For Form 945 filers, a lookback total (Form 945, line 3) of $50,000 or less makes a monthly schedule depositor, and more than $50,000 a semiweekly schedule depositor (S11.01.01, p. 33; S11.01.02, p. 33).
- For Form 945 filers, liability from before the business began or was acquired counts as zero in the lookback period, so a new filer is a monthly schedule depositor in the first and second calendar years; however, the page points to the $100,000 Next-Day Deposit Rule (S11.01.01, p. 33).
- A semiweekly schedule depositor filing Form 945 completes Form 945-A, Annual Record of Federal Tax Liability, and submits it with the return (S11.01.02, p. 33).
- For Form 945 filers the return period is a calendar year (S11.01.02, p. 33).
- Employment taxes, including Form 945 taxes, are deposited by EFT (S11.02, p. 35).
- If you deposited too much, the Form 945 for that year is where you choose a refund or a credit toward your next return (S11.02, p. 36).
- The deposit penalty information is written about Form 941 but applies to Form 945 as well (S11.03, p. 36).
- Before submitting Form 945, check that the total liability on Form 945, line 7, or Form 945-A, line M, equals the tax liability on Form 945, line 3, and show no negative amounts on Form 945, line 7, or Form 945-A (S11.03, p. 37).
- A taxpayer who withholds, or must withhold, federal income tax (backup withholding included) from nonpayroll payments files Form 945 (S12, p. 38).
- Withholding on nonpayroll payments reported on Forms 1099 or Form W-2G goes on Form 945 and not on another form such as Form 1040-ES (S12, p. 38).
- Withholding that belongs on Form 1042 is not reported on Form 945, and Form 945 need not be filed for years without nonpayroll tax liability (S12, p. 38).
- Your 2025 Form 945 is due by February 2, 2026, or by February 10, 2026 if timely deposits fully paid the year’s taxes (S12, p. 38).
- Farmwork wages are not reported on Form 941, Form 944 or Form 945 (S12, p. 38).
- Form 945 can be filed through the IRS e-file program, and reporting agents filing it for groups of taxpayers can file electronically (S12, p. 38).
- Only one Form 945 per year is filed by a payer of nonpayroll payments that withheld federal income tax or backup withholding (S12, p. 39).
- Name and EIN on Form 945 should read exactly as on earlier returns, and the Instructions for Form 945 explain how to prepare the form (S12, p. 39).
- A business that closes files a final return for the last year in which nonpayroll payments are paid (S12, p. 39).
- A late Form 945 for a previous year is filed on a copy of the form with a revision date showing that year (S12, p. 39).
- Withholding on nonpayroll payments such as pensions, annuities and gambling winnings is reported on Form 945, not on Forms 941, 943 or 944 (S12, p. 40).
- Return transcripts for Form 945 for tax years 2023 and later can be accessed through your IRS business tax account (B04, p. 57).

text:
## Note
A Form 941 filer is a semiweekly schedule depositor for a calendar year when the Form 941 line 12 taxes for the lookback period come to more than $50,000. A filer of Form 943, Form 944 or Form 945 is a semiweekly schedule depositor for the calendar year when the lookback-period taxes, taken from line 13 of Form 943, line 9 of Form 944 or line 3 of Form 945, were more than $50,000.

The semiweekly schedule sets the deposit date by the day of the payment. Employment taxes on payments made on Wednesday, Thursday and/or Friday are deposited by the following Wednesday, and those on payments made on Saturday, Sunday, Monday and/or Tuesday by the following Friday. The page points ahead to Deposits Due on Business Days Only.

Table 2. Semiweekly Deposit Schedule (p. 33)

| IF the payday falls on a... | THEN deposit taxes by the following... |
|---|---|
| Wednesday, Thursday, and/or Friday | Wednesday. |
| Saturday, Sunday, Monday, and/or Tuesday | Friday. |

**Caution.** A semiweekly schedule depositor must complete Schedule B (Form 941) and submit it with Form 941. A Form 943 filer in that position completes Form 943-A and submits it with Form 943, and a Form 944 or Form 945 filer completes Form 945-A and submits it with the return.

**Deposit period spanning 2 quarters (Form 941 filers).** More than 1 pay date within a semiweekly period, with the pay dates in different calendar quarters, means separate deposits for the separate liabilities. For example, pay dates of Wednesday, September 30, 2026 (third quarter) and Friday, October 2, 2026 (fourth quarter) call for two separate deposits although they share one semiweekly period, and both deposits are due Wednesday, October 7, 2026.

**Deposit period spanning 2 return periods (Form 943, Form 944 or Form 945 filers).** The period a return covers is its return period, and for the annual Forms 943, 944 and 945 that is a calendar year. When more than 1 pay date falls in one semiweekly period but in different return periods, separate deposits are needed for the separate liabilities. For example, if a return period ends on a Thursday, the taxes accumulated on Wednesday and Thursday make up one deposit obligation and the taxes accumulated on Friday a separate one, because two different return periods are involved.

**Steps to determine your deposit schedule.**
1. Identify the lookback period, as explained earlier in the section.
2. Add up the taxes reported for the lookback period on Form 941 line 12, Form 943 line 13, Form 944 line 9 or Form 945 line 3.
3. Decide from the total whether you are a monthly or a semiweekly schedule depositor, using the table below.

| Lookback-period total | You are a... |
|---|---|
| $50,000 or less | monthly schedule depositor. |
| more than $50,000 | semiweekly schedule depositor. |

**Related:** Example of Monthly and Semiweekly Schedules — examples of Rose Co. and Red Co. and the deposit schedule each has for the years shown (p. 34)
