text:
## Note
**Wages in general (p. 18).** Wages subject to federal employment taxes generally cover all pay given to an employee for services performed, in cash or in other forms. They include salaries, vacation allowances, bonuses, commissions and taxable fringe benefits, and how the payments are measured or made is irrelevant. A bonus paid for signing or ratifying a contract in connection with establishing an employer-employee relationship is wages subject to social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes and to income tax withholding, and so is an amount paid to an employee for cancelling an employment contract and giving up contract rights. Compensation paid to a former employee for services performed while still employed is likewise wages subject to employment taxes.

**Cash wages paid to farmworkers (p. 18).** Cash wages paid to employees for farmwork are generally subject to social security tax and Medicare tax. Additional Medicare Tax may also have to be withheld, deposited and reported by you, and the page refers to section 9. Wages that are subject to social security and Medicare taxes are subject to federal income tax withholding as well. You owe these taxes to the federal government whether or not you collect them from your employees. For example, if you withhold less than the correct tax from an employee's wages, you are still liable for the full amount. FUTA tax, which you don't withhold and the employee doesn't pay, may also be your liability; the page refers to section 14 for it. Checks, money orders and any kind of money or cash count as cash wages.

**More information (p. 18).** The page refers to section 6 for tips, section 7 for supplemental wages and section 15 for exceptions to the general rules for wages. Pub. 15-A gives additional information on wages (nonqualified deferred compensation among them) and on other compensation. Pub. 15-B covers other forms of compensation, including health savings accounts, group-term life insurance coverage, accident and health benefits and dependent care assistance; achievement awards, adoption assistance and educational assistance; athletic facilities, lodging on your business premises and meals; employee discounts, employee stock options and tuition reduction; employer-provided cell phones, transportation (commuting) benefits and retirement planning services; and de minimis (minimal) benefits, no-additional-cost services and working condition benefits.

**Noncash wages, including commodity wages, paid to farmworkers (pp. 18–19).** Noncash wages are food, lodging, clothing, transportation passes, farm products and other goods or commodities. Paid to farmworkers (commodity wages included), they are not subject to social security tax, Medicare tax or federal income tax withholding. You and your employee can nonetheless agree to have federal income tax withheld on them. If the substance of the transaction is a cash payment, noncash wages (commodity wages included) are treated as cash wages and are then subject to social security tax, Medicare tax and federal income tax withholding. The value of noncash wages goes in box 1 of Form W-2 (box 7 of Form 499R-2/W-2PR) with the cash wages. Noncash wages for farmwork are subject to federal income tax unless a specific exclusion applies. They are not to be shown in box 3 or 5 of Form W-2 (box 20 or 22 of Form 499R-2/W-2PR), except where the substance of the transaction is a cash payment and they are being treated as cash wages.

**Share farmers (p. 19).** Amounts paid to share farmers under share-farming arrangements carry no duty to withhold or pay social security and Medicare taxes. A "share farmer" working for you is not your employee, though the share farmer may owe self-employment tax. In general, share farming means that the farmer and the owner (or tenant) of the land share certain commodity products. The page refers to Regulations section 31.3121(b)(16)-1.

**Compensation paid to H-2A visa holders (p. 19).** For foreign agricultural workers who entered the country on H-2A visas, compensation of $600 or more paid in 2025 ($2,000 or more paid in 2026) is reported in box 1 of Form W-2 (box 7 of Form 499R-2/W-2PR). Neither social security wages (box 3 of Form W-2, box 20 of Form 499R-2/W-2PR) nor Medicare wages (box 5 of Form W-2, box 22 of Form 499R-2/W-2PR) should include it, because compensation for agricultural labor performed in connection with this visa isn't subject to social security and Medicare taxes. H-2A workers aren't statutory employees, so box 13 (Statutory employee) of Form W-2 is not checked. An employer need not withhold federal income tax from this compensation but may do so if the worker asks and the employer agrees; the worker must then give the employer a completed Form W-4, and the tax withheld should be reported in box 2 of Form W-2. These reporting rules apply when the H-2A worker gives the employer their TIN. If the worker gives no TIN and total annual wages are at least $600 in 2025 ($2,000 in 2026), the employer is required to backup withhold; the page refers to the Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC and the Instructions for Form 945. The page points to IRS.gov/H2A for more information.

**Employee business expense reimbursements (p. 19).** A reimbursement or allowance arrangement is a system for paying advances, reimbursements and charges for your employees' business expenses. How a reimbursement or allowance amount is reported depends on whether the plan is accountable or nonaccountable. When one payment covers both wages and an expense reimbursement, you must specify the reimbursement amount. These rules cover all allowable ordinary and necessary employee business expenses.

**Accountable plan (p. 19).** An arrangement is an accountable plan only if it requires employees to meet all three of these rules:
1. They paid or incurred allowable expenses while performing services as your employees, and the reimbursement or advance pays for those expenses rather than an amount that would otherwise have been paid to the employee as wages.
2. They substantiate the expenses to you within a reasonable period of time.
3. They return any amounts above the substantiated expenses within a reasonable period of time.

Amounts paid under an accountable plan are not wages and are not subject to income, social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes. Where expenses go unsubstantiated (or amounts above substantiated expenses are not returned within a reasonable period of time), the excess over the substantiated expenses is treated as paid under a nonaccountable plan. That excess is subject to income, social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes for the first payroll period after the reasonable period of time ends. What is a reasonable period depends on the facts and circumstances. Generally, these timings are considered reasonable: employees get their advance within 30 days of paying or incurring the expenses, account adequately for them within 60 days after they were paid or incurred, and return any excess within 120 days after they were paid or incurred. A periodic statement (at least quarterly) asking employees to return or adequately account for outstanding amounts is considered reasonable as an alternative, if they respond within 120 days.

**Nonaccountable plan (p. 19).** Payments to your employee for travel and other necessary business expenses under a nonaccountable plan are wages, are treated as supplemental wages, and are subject to income, social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes. Payments are treated as made under a nonaccountable plan in any of these cases:
- The employee isn't required to substantiate the expenses to you timely with receipts or other documentation, or doesn't do so.
- You advance an amount for business expenses and the employee isn't required to return timely whatever is unused for business expenses, or doesn't do so.
- You advance or pay an amount whether or not you reasonably expect the employee to have business expenses related to your business.
- You pay an amount as reimbursement that you would otherwise have paid as wages.

The page refers to section 7 for more information on supplemental wages.

**Per diem or other fixed allowance (pp. 19–20).** You may reimburse employees by travel days, miles or some other fixed allowance under the applicable revenue procedure. Your employee is then considered to have accounted to you if your reimbursement stays within the rates established by the federal government. Pub. 15-B gives the standard mileage rate for auto expenses. The government per diem rates for meals and lodging in the continental United States are on the U.S. General Services Administration website at GSA.gov/PerDiemRates. Apart from the amount of these expenses, employees' business expenses must be substantiated (for example, the business purpose of the travel or the number of business miles driven); for substantiation methods the page refers to Pub. 463, Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses. A per diem or allowance that exceeds the amounts substantiated must be reported as wages for the excess, and that excess is subject to income tax withholding and to social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes. The amount equal to the substantiated amount (the nontaxable portion) is shown in box 12 of Form W-2 with code "L." Employers in Puerto Rico report the amount in box 12 with no code.

**Wages not paid in money (p. 20).** If, in the course of your trade or business, you pay employees in a medium that is neither cash nor a readily negotiable instrument such as a check, you are said to pay them "in kind." Goods, lodging, food, clothing or services may be the form of payment in kind. Generally, the FMV of such payments when they are provided is subject to federal income tax withholding and social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes. Noncash payments for household work, agricultural labor and service not in the employer's trade or business, however, are exempt from social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes, and income tax is withheld on them only if you and the employee agree. Even so, where the substance of the transaction is a cash payment, noncash payments for agricultural labor (commodity wages, for example) are treated as cash payments subject to employment taxes. The page refers to Noncash wages, including commodity wages, paid to farmworkers, earlier in the section.

**Meals and lodging (p. 20).** Meals furnished for the employer's convenience and on the employer's premises are not taxable income and are not subject to federal income tax withholding or social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes. Lodging escapes federal income tax withholding and social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes when it is provided for the employer's convenience, on its premises and as a condition of employment. "For the convenience of the employer" means that you have a substantial business reason, other than giving the employee additional compensation, for providing the meals and lodging. For example, meals provided at the place of work to keep an employee available for emergencies during their lunch period are generally considered to be for your convenience. You must be able to show that such emergency calls have occurred or can reasonably be expected to occur, and that they have led, or will lead, to your calling on employees to do their jobs during the meal period. Whether meals or lodging are for the employer's convenience depends on all of the facts and circumstances, and a written statement that they are for your convenience isn't sufficient.

**50% test (p. 20).** When over 50% of the employees provided meals on an employer's business premises receive them for the employer's convenience, all meals provided on the premises are treated as furnished for the employer's convenience. When the 50% test is met, the meals' value can be excluded from all employees' income and is free of federal income tax withholding and employment taxes. The page refers to Pub. 15-B for more information.

**Health insurance plans (p. 20).** Your payments for an accident or health insurance plan for your employees, including an employee's spouse and dependents, aren't wages and aren't subject to social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes or to federal income tax withholding. Generally, the exclusion applies to qualified long-term-care insurance contracts too. For income tax withholding, though, wages of S corporation employees owning more than 2% of the S corporation (2% shareholders) must include the value of health insurance benefits. When it comes to social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes, a 2% shareholder's wages exclude those benefits. The page refers to Announcement 92-16 (page 53 of Internal Revenue Bulletin 1992-5).

**Health savings accounts (HSAs) and medical savings accounts (MSAs) (p. 20).** Your contributions to an employee's HSA or Archer MSA are free of social security, Medicare and FUTA tax and of federal income tax withholding if it is reasonable to believe, when you make them, that they will be excludable from the employee's income. To the extent that belief isn't reasonable, the contributions are subject to those taxes. Employee contributions made to their HSAs or MSAs through a payroll deduction plan count as wages; social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes apply to them, as does federal income tax withholding. HSA contributions made under a salary reduction arrangement in a section 125 cafeteria plan, however, aren't wages and aren't subject to employment taxes or withholding. The page refers to the Instructions for Form 8889.

**Medical care reimbursements (p. 20).** Generally, medical care reimbursements made for an employee under an employer's self-insured medical reimbursement plan are not wages, and social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes and federal income tax withholding don't apply to them. For a rule on including certain reimbursements in the gross income of highly compensated individuals, the page refers to Pub. 15-B.

**Differential wage payments (pp. 20–21).** Differential wage payments are payments by an employer to an individual for a period of more than 30 days of active duty service in the uniformed services, representing all or part of the wages the individual would have received from the employer if performing services for the employer. They are wages for income tax withholding but aren't subject to social security, Medicare or FUTA tax. Employers should report them in box 1 of Form W-2 (box 7 of Form 499R-2/W-2PR) (p. 21). The page refers to Revenue Ruling 2009-11 for more information on their tax treatment.

**Fringe benefits (p. 21).** Fringe benefits must generally be included in an employee's wages (the page refers to Nontaxable fringe benefits, next), and they are subject to income tax withholding and employment taxes. Examples include tickets to entertainment or sporting events, vacations, memberships in country clubs or other social clubs, cars you provide, flights on aircraft you provide, free or discounted commercial flights, and discounts on property or services. In general, the amount to include is the excess of the benefit's FMV over the sum of what the employee paid for it and any amount the law excludes. You and your employees may use other special rules to value certain fringe benefits. The page refers to Pub. 15-B for more information.

**Valuation of fringe benefits (p. 21).** Generally, the value of fringe benefits must be determined by January 31 of the next year at the latest. Until January 31 you may make a reasonable estimate of their value for purposes of withholding and depositing on time.

**When taxable fringe benefits are treated as paid (p. 21).** You may choose to treat certain taxable noncash fringe benefits as paid by the pay period, by the quarter or on any other basis, provided you treat the benefits as paid at least once a year. No formal choice of payment dates is needed, and you needn't notify the IRS of the dates. The choice need not cover all employees. You may change methods as often as you like, as long as all benefits provided in a calendar year are treated as paid by December 31 of that year. The page refers to section 4 of Pub. 15-B, including its discussion of the special accounting rule for fringe benefits provided during November and December.

**Nontaxable fringe benefits (p. 21).** Some fringe benefits aren't taxable (or are minimally taxable) if certain conditions are met; the page refers to Pub. 15-B for details. The page's examples:
- Services provided to your employees at no additional cost to you.
- Qualified employee discounts.
- Working condition fringes: property or services that the employee could have deducted as a business expense or depreciation expense had they paid for them, such as a company car for business use and subscriptions to business magazines.
- Certain minimal value fringes (an occasional cab ride when an employee must work overtime is one; so are meals you provide at eating places you run for your employees if the meals aren't furnished at below cost).
- Qualified transportation fringes within specified conditions and dollar limitations (including transportation in a commuter highway vehicle, any transit pass and qualified parking).
- Use of on-premises athletic facilities that you operate, if substantially all of the use is by employees, their spouses and their dependent children.
- Qualified tuition reduction that an educational organization provides to its employees for education; the page refers to Pub. 970.
- Employer-provided cell phones provided primarily for a noncompensatory business reason.

The following fringe benefits must not be excluded from the wages of highly compensated employees unless the benefit is available to other employees on a nondiscriminatory basis: reduced tuition for education, meals provided at an employer-operated eating facility, qualified employee discounts and no-additional-cost services. The page refers to Pub. 15-B for more information, including the definition of a highly compensated employee.

**Withholding federal income tax on fringe benefits (p. 21).** You may add the value of fringe benefits to regular wages for a payroll period and figure withholding taxes on the total. Alternatively, you may withhold federal income tax on the value of the fringe benefits at the optional flat 22% supplemental wage rate; for an employee who receives more than $1 million of supplemental wages during the calendar year, the page refers to Withholding on supplemental wages when an employee receives more than $1 million of supplemental wages during the calendar year in section 7. Withholding income tax on the value of an employee's personal use of a vehicle you provide is something you may choose not to do, though social security and Medicare taxes on that use must still be withheld. The page refers to Pub. 15-B for more information on this election.

**Withholding social security and Medicare taxes on fringe benefits (p. 21).** Social security and Medicare taxes are figured on the total of regular wages for a payroll period plus the value of fringe benefits. You may recover the taxes from the employee when, in a calendar year, you withhold less than the required social security and Medicare taxes but report and pay the proper amount. The page refers to Pub. 15-B for more information.

**Depositing taxes on fringe benefits (pp. 21–22).** After you choose when fringe benefits are paid, the taxes must be deposited in the same deposit period in which you treat the benefits as paid. To avoid a penalty, deposit them following the general deposit rules for that deposit period (p. 21). Suppose you determine by January 31 that you overestimated a fringe benefit's value when you withheld and deposited for it: you may claim a refund of the overpayment or have it applied to your next employment tax return, and the page refers to Valuation of fringe benefits, earlier in the section. If you underestimated the value and deposited too little, a failure-to-deposit (FTD) penalty may apply, and the page refers to section 11 for information on deposit penalties. When you deposited the required amount but withheld less from the employee, you can recover from the employee the social security, Medicare or income tax you deposited for them and included in their Form W-2, but the income tax must be recovered before April 1 of the following year (p. 22).

**Back pay (p. 22).** Back pay, retroactive wage increases included but amounts paid as liquidated damages excluded, is taxed as ordinary wages in the year it is paid. For reporting back pay to the SSA, the page refers to Pub. 957.

**Sick pay (p. 22).** In general, sick pay is any amount paid under a plan to an employee who can't work because of sickness or injury. A third party, such as an insurance company or an employees' trust, is sometimes the payer. Either way, the payments are subject to social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes. Sick pay paid more than 6 calendar months after the last calendar month in which the employee worked for the employer is outside those taxes; it is always subject to federal income tax. The page refers to section 6 of Pub. 15-A for more information.

**Overtime compensation (p. 22).** Under the FLSA, employers must generally pay covered, nonexempt employees at least one-and-a-half times the regular rate of pay for hours over 40 per week. The page points to dol.gov/agencies/whd/overtime for more information. Overtime compensation is subject to social security, Medicare and FUTA taxes and to federal income tax withholding. For tax years beginning after 2024 and ending before 2029, however, P.L. 119-21 lets individuals (employees and other workers not treated as employees) deduct up to $12,500 ($25,000 if married filing jointly) of qualified overtime compensation on their income tax returns. Qualified overtime is compensation above the regular rate of pay (such as the "half" portion of time-and-a-half compensation) that must be paid to an individual under section 7 of the FLSA of 1938. Where an employee submits an updated Form W-4, employers must use it, along with the federal income tax withholding procedures in Pub. 15-T, so the employee can account for the expected deduction and get more money in each paycheck rather than waiting until filing an income tax return to receive the deduction's full benefit.

**Identity protection services (p. 22).** The value of identity protection services that an employer provides to an employee is not part of the employee's gross income and need not be reported on an information return (such as Form W-2) filed for the employee. Services provided before a data breach occurs are included. The exception doesn't cover cash received instead of identity protection services or proceeds received under an identity theft insurance policy. The page refers to Announcement 2015-22 and Announcement 2016-02.

**Related:** 6. Tips — cash tips employees receive from customers and how they are reported to the employer and withheld on (p. 22)

text:
## Note
If an employee repays wages that were received in error, the repayment is not offset against current year wages unless the amounts were received in error in the current year (p. 43).

**Repayment of current-year wages (p. 43).** When the employer receives repayments of wages paid in a prior quarter of the current year, it reports adjustments on Form 941-X to recover the income tax withholding and the social security and Medicare taxes on the repaid wages.

**Repayment of prior-year wages (p. 43).** When the employer receives repayments of wages paid in a prior year, it reports an adjustment on Form 941-X, Form 943-X or Form 944-X to recover the social security and Medicare taxes. No adjustment can be made for income tax withholding, because the wages were income to the employee for the prior year. No adjustment can be made for Additional Medicare Tax withholding, because the employee determines liability for Additional Medicare Tax on their own income tax return for the prior year. The employer must also file Forms W-2c and W-3c with the SSA to correct social security and Medicare wages and taxes. Wages (box 1) on Form W-2c are not corrected for the amount paid in error. A copy of Form W-2c goes to the employee.

**Employee reporting of repayment (p. 43).** Wages paid in error in the prior year stay taxable to the employee for that year, since the employee received and had use of the funds then. The employee is not entitled to file an amended return (Form 1040-X) to get back the income tax on those wages. A deduction or credit for the repaid wages may be available instead, on the employee's income tax return for the year of repayment. Additional Medicare Tax paid on the wages paid in error in the prior year is treated differently: the employee should file an amended return (Form 1040-X) to recover it. An employee who asks how to report a wage repayment may be pointed by the employer to Repayments in Pub. 525, Taxable and Nontaxable Income.

**Related:** Prior-Period Adjustments — correcting an error found on a previously filed Form 941, Form 943 or Form 944 (p. 41)

text:
## Note
Section 2 of the publication covers who is an employee: workers who are employees under common law, persons treated as employees or as nonemployees by statute, farmworkers and crew leaders, the treatment of an employee as a nonemployee, and relief and classification programs. Its one part deals with a business that spouses own and operate. The chapter's own text, summarised below, runs from p. 14 to p. 15.

**Definitions (p. 14).** Generally, employees are defined either under common law or under statutes for certain situations. For details on statutory employees and nonemployees the page points to Pub. 15-A.

**Employee status under common law (p. 14).** Generally, someone who performs services for you is your employee when you have the right to control what is done and how it is done, even if you leave the employee free to act. The deciding point is the right to control the details of how the services are performed. For more on deciding whether an individual providing services is an independent contractor or an employee, the page points to Pub. 15-A. People in business for themselves are generally not employees: doctors, lawyers, veterinarians and others in an independent trade in which they offer their services to the public are usually not employees. Corporate officers who work in an incorporated business are employees of the corporation. Where an employer-employee relationship exists, its name doesn't matter, and the employee may be called an agent or independent contractor. How payments are measured or paid, what they are called, and whether the employee works full or part time also don't matter.

**Statutory employees (p. 14).** When someone who works for you is not an employee under the common-law rules, don't withhold federal income tax from their pay, unless backup withholding applies. The persons below may not be common-law employees, yet they are considered employees by statute for social security and Medicare tax purposes if the conditions under Tests, later, are met:
- An agent or commission driver who delivers meat, vegetable, fruit or bakery products, beverages (other than milk), laundry or dry cleaning for someone else.
- A full-time life insurance salesperson who sells primarily for one company.
- A homeworker who works at home or off premises following the guidelines of the person for whom the work is done, with materials or goods furnished by that person and returned to that person or to someone that person designates.
- A traveling or city salesperson (other than an agent or commission driver) who works full time (except for sideline sales activities) for one firm or person, getting orders from customers. Those orders must be for merchandise for resale or for supplies used in the customer's business, and the customers must be retailers, wholesalers, contractors, or operators of hotels, restaurants or other businesses dealing with food or lodging.

**Tests (p. 14).** Social security and Medicare taxes are withheld from a statutory employee's wages if all three tests apply:
1. The service contract states or implies that almost all of the services are to be performed personally by the worker.
2. The worker has little or no investment in the equipment and property used to perform the services apart from any investment in transportation facilities.
3. The services are performed on a continuing basis for the same payer.

Persons in the first group above (agent or commission driver) or the fourth (traveling or city salesperson) are also employees for FUTA tax purposes if tests 1 through 3 are met. Examples of the employer-employee relationship are in Pub. 15-A.

**Statutory nonemployees (p. 14).** By law, direct sellers, qualified real estate agents and certain companion sitters are considered nonemployees. They are generally treated as self-employed for all federal tax purposes, income and employment taxes included. The page points to Pub. 15-A for more information.

**Farmworkers (pp. 14–15).** In general, you are an employer of farmworkers if your employees do any of the following:
- Raise or harvest agricultural or horticultural products on your farm (raising and feeding livestock included).
- Work in connection with operating, managing, conserving, improving or maintaining your farm and its tools and equipment, if the major part of that service is performed on a farm.
- Provide services relating to salvaging timber, or to clearing brush and other debris from land after a hurricane (also known as hurricane labor), if the major part of that service is performed on a farm.
- Handle, process or package an agricultural or horticultural commodity in its unmanufactured state, if you produced over half of the commodity (for a group of up to 20 unincorporated operators, all of it).
- Do work for you related to cotton ginning, turpentine, gum resin products, or the operation and maintenance of irrigation facilities.

Here "farm" covers stock, dairy, poultry, fruit, fur-bearing animal and truck farms, plantations, ranches, nurseries, ranges, orchards, and greenhouses or similar structures used primarily to raise agricultural or horticultural commodities. Reselling activities with no substantial activity of raising agricultural or horticultural commodities, such as a retail store or a greenhouse used primarily for display or storage, are not farmwork. Neither are processing services that change a commodity from its raw or natural state, nor services performed after a commodity has been changed from that state.

**Crew leaders (p. 15).** A crew leader is an employer of farmworkers. A crew leader furnishes and pays workers (on their own behalf or on behalf of the farm operator) to do farmwork for the farm operator. You are a crew leader if you pay the workers (for yourself or for the farm operator) and no written agreement between you and the farm operator says you are their employee. For FUTA tax rules the page refers to section 14. A crew leader is not considered the farm operator's employee for services performed in furnishing farmworkers and as a member of the crew.

**H-2A agricultural workers (p. 15).** H-2A workers are not statutory employees, so on Form W-2 don't check box 13 (Statutory employee).

**Treating employees as nonemployees (p. 15).** Treating an employee as a nonemployee, and so not deducting and withholding social security and Medicare taxes and income tax, generally leaves you liable for those taxes and for the income tax that should have been withheld. You may be able to figure your liability with special section 3509 rates for the employee share of social security and Medicare taxes and for federal income tax withholding; which rates apply depends on whether you filed required Forms 1099. If the tax is paid under section 3509, the employee share of social security tax, Medicare tax and income tax withholding can't be recovered from the employee. Liability for the income tax withholding exists regardless of whether the employee paid income tax on the wages. You still owe the full employer share of social security and Medicare taxes, and the employee remains liable for the employee share of those taxes. The page refers to section 3509 for details and to the Instructions for Form 941-X, Form 943-X and Form 944-X. The section 3509 rates can't be used when you intentionally disregard the requirement to withhold taxes from the employee, or when you withheld income taxes without withholding social security or Medicare tax. Section 3509 is also not available for reclassifying statutory employees.

Where the employer issued required information returns, the section 3509 rates are:
- Social security taxes: the employer rate of 6.2% plus 20% of the 6.2% employee rate, a total of 7.44% of wages.
- Medicare taxes: the employer rate of 1.45% plus 20% of the 1.45% employee rate, a total of 1.74% of wages.
- Additional Medicare Tax: 0.18% (20% of the 0.9% employee rate) of wages subject to Additional Medicare Tax.
- Federal income tax withholding: 1.5% of wages.

Where the employer did not issue required information returns, the section 3509 rates are:
- Social security taxes: the employer rate of 6.2% plus 40% of the 6.2% employee rate, a total of 8.68% of wages.
- Medicare taxes: the employer rate of 1.45% plus 40% of the 1.45% employee rate, a total of 2.03% of wages.
- Additional Medicare Tax: 0.36% (40% of the 0.9% employee rate) of wages subject to Additional Medicare Tax.
- Federal income tax withholding: 3.0% of wages.

**Relief provisions (p. 15).** With a reasonable basis for not treating a worker as an employee, you may be relieved from paying employment taxes for that worker. To get the relief, you must file all required federal tax returns, information returns included, in a way consistent with how you treated the worker. You (or your predecessor) must not have treated any worker in a substantially similar position as an employee for any period beginning after 1977. The page points to Pub. 1976, Do You Qualify for Relief Under Section 530.

**IRS help (p. 15).** To have the IRS determine whether a worker is an employee, file Form SS-8.

**Voluntary Classification Settlement Program (VCSP) (p. 15).** Employers who now treat their workers (or a class or group of workers) as independent contractors or other nonemployees, and want to reclassify them voluntarily as employees for future tax periods, may be eligible for the VCSP if certain requirements are met. Apply by filing Form 8952. The page points to IRS.gov/VCSP for more information.

## Business Owned and Operated by Spouses
- Business Owned and Operated by Spouses — spouses who jointly own and operate a business may be partners in a partnership; the qualified joint venture and community income exceptions (pp. 15–16)

text:
## Note
Once taxes of $100,000 or more accumulate on any day of a monthly or semiweekly deposit period, they must be deposited by the next business day, whether you are a monthly or a semiweekly schedule depositor. The $100,000 threshold for a next-day deposit is measured before any reduction of the liability for nonrefundable credits (p. 34).

For this rule, accumulation does not carry on past the end of a deposit period. Example: a semiweekly schedule depositor has $95,000 accumulated by a Tuesday (in a Saturday-through-Tuesday deposit period) and accumulates a further $10,000 on the Wednesday. The next-day rule does not apply, since the $10,000 falls in the next deposit period; the $95,000 is deposited by Friday and the $10,000 by the following Wednesday (pp. 34–35).

Conversely, once at least $100,000 has accumulated in a deposit period, accumulation stops at the end of that day and starts afresh the next day. Example: Fir Co., a semiweekly schedule depositor, accumulates $110,000 on Monday and must deposit it on Tuesday, the next business day. On Tuesday it accumulates another $30,000. That amount is not added to the $110,000 and is under $100,000, so Fir Co. deposits it by Friday under the semiweekly schedule (p. 35).

**Caution.** A monthly schedule depositor that accumulates a $100,000 tax liability on any day of the deposit period turns into a semiweekly schedule depositor from the next day, and stays one for at least the remainder of the calendar year and for the following calendar year (p. 35).

**Example (p. 35).** Elm, Inc., began business on May 4, 2026. It paid wages for the first time on Wednesday, May 6, accumulating a $40,000 liability, and paid wages again on Friday, May 8, accumulating $60,000, which brought its total to $100,000. In its first year the lookback liability is treated as zero, so the lookback rules alone would make it a monthly schedule depositor. But because $100,000 accumulated on May 8, it became a semiweekly schedule depositor on May 9, and it remains one for the rest of 2026 and for 2027. It is required to deposit the $100,000 by Monday, May 11, the next business day.

**Related:** Accuracy of Deposits Rule — the requirement to deposit 100% of the tax liability and when a shortfall draws no penalty (p. 35)

## Sources & References

- Accuracy of Deposits Rule — the section on the accuracy of deposits rule (p. 35)
- When To Deposit — the section that defines the term deposit period (page link, p. 32)

text:
## Note
This part of section 17 lays out the steps federal agencies must take to certify to the IRS how much "federal income taxes" were paid to, and deposited into, the U.S. Treasury (p. 55).

**Who certifies, and when (pp. 55–56).** Every department and agency of the federal government, and every service and social organization associated with a military or civilian federal entity, that withholds federal income taxes on payments to employees and pensioners of the United States (or an agency of it) as the section provides must certify to the IRS each calendar quarter. The certification gives the total federal income taxes withheld that have been deposited into the U.S. Treasury. A separate certification is required for federal income taxes creditable to American Samoa, the CNMI and Guam, as applicable (p. 56).

**What the certification contains (p. 56).** Unless the section provides otherwise, a certification should be a letter that includes:
1. Pub. 15, cited as the authority for the certification;
2. the name of the federal agency or department that certifies;
3. that agency's EIN;
4. the calendar quarter and fiscal year covered;
5. how many individuals the certification covers; and
6. the aggregate dollar amount of federal income taxes withheld on all those individuals.

**Certification for other agencies (p. 56).** A federal department or agency that certifies for another department or agency must list the name and EIN of each subordinate or designated federal department or agency it covers, with the required data for each. That certifying agency must send its certification at least once a year, by February 14 at the latest.

**Military personnel not stationed in the territories (p. 56).** Federal agencies that certify for pay of military personnel who are not stationed in American Samoa, the CNMI or Guam, but whose state of legal residence is one of these territories, must further provide each servicemember's name, SSN, amount of annual salary paid, and total amount of annual federal income tax withheld.

**Agreement with the quarterly return (p. 56).** The amounts in the certification must agree with the federal income tax withheld that the agency reports on its quarterly federal tax return(s) (Form 941).

**Quarterly due dates (p. 56).** Certifications are due quarterly, within 45 days after each calendar quarter closes, on these dates:
- May 15 for the first quarter, which ends March 31;
- Aug. 14 for the second quarter, which ends June 30;
- Nov. 14 for the third quarter, which ends September 30;
- Feb. 14 for the fourth quarter, which ends December 31.

**Where to mail it (p. 56).** Federal agencies should mail the certification to the Internal Revenue Service, Revenue Systems and Analysis, at the address the page prints: Attn: OS:CFO:FM:RA:S (77K St), 1111 Constitution Ave NW, CFO/FM - Mail Stop 6167, Washington, DC 20224. The page also lists the fax number 202-803-9691.

**Related:** Federal Income Taxes From American Samoa, the CNMI, or Guam — which federal income taxes the certification procedures cover (p. 55)

text:
## Note
**The requirement (p. 17).** Employers must obtain each employee's name and SSN and enter both on Form W-2. An SSN has nine digits in the pattern 000-00-0000. Resident and nonresident alien employees are covered too. You should ask the employee to show their social security card, though the employee need not do so if the card is unavailable. When an employee can't provide the card, you should verify their SSN and their eligibility for employment as discussed later in the section under Verification of SSNs.

**Caution on the card (p. 17).** A card stating "Not valid for employment" must not be accepted, since an SSN issued with that legend doesn't permit employment. You may photocopy the card if the employee provides it, but you aren't required to. Without the correct employee name and SSN on Form W-2, you may owe a penalty unless you have reasonable cause. On the requirement to solicit the employee's SSN, the page points to Pub. 1586.

**Tip (p. 17).** Often a replacement social security card can be applied for online, with no visit to an SSA office. For some applicants an SSN application can be started online before a visit to an SSA office. The page points to SSA.gov/number-card.

**Applying for a social security card (p. 17).** An employee who is legally eligible to work in the United States but has no social security card can get one by completing Form SS-5 and submitting the necessary documentation. Form SS-5 is available from the SSA website at SSA.gov/forms/ss-5.pdf, at SSA offices, or by phone at 800-772-1213 or 800-325-0778 (TTY). The employee has to complete and sign it; the employer can't file it. If the employee has used up their yearly or lifetime limit on replacement cards, you may be asked to supply a letter with Form SS-5.

**Where to get and file Form SS-5 in the U.S. territories (pp. 17–18).** The page lists the U.S. SSA offices located in the U.S. territories (American Samoa, Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands and the U.S. Virgin Islands), each with an address. More information is on the Social Security Office Locator page at secure.ssa.gov/ICON, and the page adds that entering your ZIP code on that website finds your nearest SSA office in Puerto Rico.

**Applying for an SSN (p. 17).** Suppose you file Form W-2 on paper and an employee has applied for an SSN but has none when the form is due: enter "Applied For" on the form. For electronic filing, enter all zeros in the SSN field (000-00-0000 when creating forms online, 000000000 when uploading a file). Once the employee gets the SSN, file Copy A of Form W-2c with the SSA to show it, and give Copies B, C and 2 of Form W-2c to the employee. Online, up to 25 Forms W-2c per Form W-3c can be filed in a session, and the number of sessions is not limited. The page points to the SSA's Employer W-2 Filing Instructions & Information webpage at SSA.gov/employer. Advise the employee to correct the SSN on their original Form W-2.

**Correctly record the employee's name and SSN (p. 17).** Record each employee's name and SSN as shown on their social security card. When the name on the card is wrong (for example, after marriage or divorce), the employee should ask the SSA for an updated card. Keep reporting wages under the old name until the employee shows you the updated card with the corrected name. When the SSA issues an updated card after a name change, or issues a new card with a different SSN after a change in alien work status, file a Form W-2c correcting the name/SSN reported on the most recently filed Form W-2. Earlier years need no correction if the previous name and number were used for the years before the most recent Form W-2.

**IRS ITINs for aliens (pp. 17–18).** An ITIN must not be accepted in place of an SSN for identifying an employee or for work. ITINs are available only to resident and nonresident aliens who aren't eligible for U.S. employment and need identification for other tax purposes. An ITIN is a nine-digit number formatted like an SSN. It begins with "9", and its fourth and fifth digits fall in the ranges "50–65," "70–88," "90–92" or "94–99" (for example, 9NN-7N-NNNN). The page points to the Instructions for Form W-7 and to IRS.gov/ITIN for more information. A person with an ITIN who later becomes eligible to work in the United States must obtain an SSN. If that person is currently eligible to work in the United States, instruct them to apply for an SSN and follow the instructions under Applying for an SSN, earlier in the section. An ITIN is not to be used in place of an SSN on Form W-2 (p. 18).

**Verification of SSNs (p. 18).** Employers and authorized reporting agents can use the Social Security Number Verification Service (SSNVS) in two ways: to verify instantly that an employee name matches an SSN, for up to 10 names and SSNs (per screen) at a time, or to submit an electronic file of up to 250,000 names and SSNs and usually receive results the next business day. The page points to SSA.gov/employer/ssnv.htm. A person can hold a valid SSN without being authorized to work in the United States. To confirm the employment eligibility of newly hired employees, employers may use E-Verify at E-Verify.gov.

**Accessing the SSNVS (p. 18).** Access to the SSNVS goes through the SSA's BSO, and BSO users need a social security online account. An existing Login.gov credential or ID.me credential can be used; someone with neither will need to create one. The page points to SSA.gov/bso.

**Related:** 1. Employer Identification Number (EIN) — the nine-digit employer identification number and how to apply for one (p. 13)
